lIElt SONG. "And I. would sing," she said, "some wondrous thing. To lift high souls to higher planes of thought, And I would wear a crown of fame all wrought With jewels, and the world would hear me sing." And, while she spoke, the sunlight fell around, And crowned her with its glory, and a bird Filled the bright space with music, while she heard And wondered, and was silent, as spell-bound. Then cried she, "God !" she cried, and must I sing While no one heedeth, even as but now This bird bath sung and asketh never word Of praise?" Then from her heart, song, triumphing In joy, arose, loud, clear, and on each bough The blossoms burst, and all the springtime heard. BEM/ GRACE SMITH.

- Utility is the true test of excellence. Learning makes a man fit company for himself. Victory belongs to him who is constant in faith and courage. Every man has just as much vanity as he wants understanding. It is the diamond miner who is the most successful discoverer of strata-gems. It is astonishing how quickly the merit of a picture can be determined—after we know the astist's name. It is a mistake to say that rain falls alike on the just and the unjust. The latter always has the umbrella. "Well, Johnnie, do you enjoy going to school?" "It's pretty good fun. I like coming home the best, though." "She is begging 'the question," as the bachelor observed of the elderly spinster who was fishing for an offer. Every one that can administer what he possesses has enough: and to be wealthy is a burdensome affair, unless you have it wisely under your fingers. He that bath gained an entire conquest over himself will find no mighty difficulties to subdue all other oppo- sition; and this is a complete victory indeed. A more glorious victory cannot be &Tied over another man than this, that when the injury began on his part, the kindness should begin on our.. An Irishman, seeing a very small coffin, exclaimed, "Is it possible that that coffin was intended for any living creature ?" " Ah," he said, as the postman handed him a letter. "An epistle !" "No," said his wife, as she opened the envelope, and a bill fluttered to the floor; "not an epistle, a collect." A person once said to his minister, the Rev. Mr. o—, that it was impossible for a man to carry on business in this imperfect world and be honest, and get a living. Die, then," was the emphatic reply_ Mrs. Wundah "I did not know there were such things as artificial whales." Mr. Wundah : "Well, there are not." Mrs. Wunclish "But where do they get this artificial whalebone the papers speak of?" "They have decided that 'phonograph' is in the feminine gender," said Mrs. Liabley's husband. "I wonder why ?" asked Mrs. Gabley. "Because it always has the last word. Instead of laying down the law with absolute certainty, the true thinker is better pleased to put his convictions to every test. Even when he is fully persuaded of their truth, he has no desire to force them upon others, know- ing such a method to be utterly unavailing. . We are ruined, not by what we really want, but by -what we think we do; therefore never go abroad in •search of your wants. If they be real wants, they will -cpme home in search of you, for he that buys what he -does not want will soon want what he cannot buy. The Hon. E. Everett, the American F-enator, once had his health proposed thus by the artist Story, "Here's to Learning—when Ever-it rises it grows." Everett, spring- ing to his feet, at once exclaimed, "I beg to amend. Here's to Learning—whenever it rises it grows,ibut never above one Story." Jones is nothing if not•gallant. Mrs. B. is exactly the same age as her husband, but she will not admit it. "My husband is forty," she said to some friends the other day. "You wouldn't believe it, but there's actually ten years' difference in our ages." " lmp)ssible, dear madam !" hastily interposed Jones, anxious to say something agreeable; " l'm sure you look every day as young as he -does." There is a well-known saying that every time a cock crows a lip is being told somewhere in the world. " AcCording to that," observed a well-known journalist, the other evening„ when the saying had been mentioned in conversation, "it would Wm that the most menda- cious period of the day is sunrise, for that is when the cock crows most." "Precisely," said a gentleman of eno t heti calling, "for that is when they begin to publish -the morning papers, don't you know." COCMNRY v. Yottesuing.—An old gentlemen hailing from Wharfedale, upon visiting London, rose early one morning before the domestics of the hotel where he was staying were astir, purposely to have as quiet a stroll as possible along the streets of the big City. A cockney on taking down the shutters of a shop espied our friend as a "yokel." and accordingly accosted him with (un- doubtedly thinking of making an early bargain out of him). "Good morning, sir; is there anything I can show you?" Our friend from the dale turned in the shop and was shown a variety of articles, until the man of the ,counter became slightly irritated, saying, "Is there nothing I can show you to suit this morning?" "Yes," was the reply, "there is. I'll take a penn'orth of Rom- lbelds moor turf, if you've got it, to light the fire, for I e, an't get 'Pm out of bed where I'm staying." The master just coming through an inner door at the time, and seeing at a glance how matters stood, said they hadn't such a thing as Rombalds moor tuif, but they had some loggerheads. Our old friend thereupon burst into a loud "Ha, ha, you must have had good sale for them lately, ifor I only see two left." , "POOR MAMMA !"--150t. many things in the life of a 'boy seem more important. to him than his first getting into trousers. It is to be doubted, indeed, if he is likely ' to find much in his after life that will give a joy so keen and unmixed; and when Master Jamie, having reached • the mature age of "most five," as he put it, was given his first pair of knicker-bockers, the whole family were naturally called upon to rejoice with him, It was after his first transports of delights were over, and he was able to speak of the great event with calmness, that Jamie came to his mother, and, after parading up and - down before her two or three times, said, in a tone of perfect satisfaction: "0, mamma, pants make me feel so like somebody! Don't I look real grown up, mamma?" - -Hie- mother smilingly told him that he• certainly did, and that she could not feel that he was her baby any more. "Didn't it make you feel crown up, mamma," Jamie began, "when you—" He stopped short. It had evi- • dently come to his 'mind that his mother had never known this deep delight which so filled his soul. Be looked at her a moment, an expression of the deepest pity coming over his/face, and then he took her hand in both of his and laid it'against his cheek. "Poor mamma!" he said, softly. "Poor mamma! If you'd been my little girl, I'd have let you wear pants just the same as if -you'd been a boy." A CLE`NiER THIEF.—It is an unusual experience to find an anecdote involving theftand deception which rouses -not only amusement but admiration of the culprit's -cleverness. Yet such a story is told by Mansfield IParkens, whe himself was a witness of the incident. 4t Tante= I triw a Illon wll9 was exhibiting three kIl apes, who performed several tricks at his command. I entered into conversation with him' and he told me that 'his male ape WRS the most dexterous thief imaginable„and stole every day a sufficient amount of food for his subsistence. In proof of this he begged me to watch the animal for a few minutes. I did so, and presently the keeper led him to a spot where a date seller was sitting on the ground, with his basket beside him. Here his master put him' through his evolutions, and altheugh I could perceive that the ' monkey had an eye to the fruit, yet so completely did he disguise his intentions that no careless observer would have noticed it.. He did not at first care about - approaching the basket, but gradually brought himself nearer and nearer, until at last he got close to the owner. . . .

In the midst of one of his feats, he suddenly started up frOna the gtound, on which he was stretched, and, utter- ing a cry, as if in pain or rage, fixed his eyes full on the face of the date seller; then, without moving the rest . of his body, be stole as many dates as be, could hold in one of his "hind hands." The date seller, thus stared out of countenance, and having his attention diverted by this extraordinary movement, knew nothing about, the tbeft till a bystander told him of it. Then he joined' heartily in the laugh raised against him. CORING A TENOR.—The company were in Havana, and at a critical juncture in the manager's a ffairs Brignoli took it into his head that it would be the swell thing to 5a9 sick.- The Marquis de Aguas Cearas, president of tile AVuntamiento, sent a doctor to visit) the distin- guished tenor, and to reportithe result of his investiga- tions. Unatild tO discover any alarming svmptons -except an insatiable appeUGQ Or Macaroni and a senti- mental longing for a dolce far niente, the gentlemanly young doctor ordered Brignoli to take a substantial dinner and in the evening a drive to the opera, and to , sing his part in the usual manner, and predicted to him a full restoration of health by following his advice. The silver voiced tenor shared the doctor's opinion as to the prescription df a good dinner, but demurred from the I order of singing in the evening. The judge upon hear- ing the doctor's report, sent a gentle warning to Brig- ', noli, who, however, answered that the doctor who bad visited him Seemed. like Crispino, to be more a cobbler tnan a doctor, and did not understand his illne"s. where- upon the magistrate despatched another doctor from the military hospital, with two attendants. After having felt Brignoli's pulse, looked into his throat, and examined his eyes, the new doctor solemnly declared, with a shake of hi" head, "Really some precursory :.'symptoms of yellow fever," but added that by employ- ing 200 leeches immediately on the shoulders of the patient the great evil might be averted. "Mama Mi 3 screamed Brignoli, with his clear, beautiful tenor voice, reaching with ease on that occasion the high B. "200 leeches ! You are a fool. but not a doctor! lam per- fectly well!" "No," replied the doctor, " you are sick, and cannot sing to-night," giving at the same time in- structions to his attendants for the operation. "Clear out," vociferated Brignoli, "I will show you whether and how I can sing this evening." And he did sing, better than ever. div.p: " CA.PITAL " CHAT.
The Speaker is suffering from his old trouble, varicose veins in the leg. The complaint is extremely painful, and often compels Mr.d'eel to keep his legs extended on a cushion in front of the chair.

Mr. Henry Tate, sugar refiner, of London and Liverpool, whose benefactions have been most munificent, has announced his intention of giving 5,000/. to London and a similar sum to Liverpool towards promotion in those cities of home nursing of sick poor.

Bing George of Greece, although only forty-four,' has become a grandfather. His daughter, Princess Alexandra,who was married on the 16th of June, last year, to the Grand Duke Paul the Czar's youngest brother, has just given birth to a daughter, who will be called the Grand Dueness Maria Paulovna.

The first lady physician in the, Austrian Empire has just 'received her appointment. Fran Doctor Rosa Kersebbaumer is the name of the lady on whom the Emperor of Austria has conferred this high honour, and'she lives in Salzburg. Frau Ker- schbaumer has gained reputation in her profession as a specialist in diseases of the eye.

A " Herald " man has succeeded in interviewing the Pope. Louis XIII. encourages jounalism, says that dancing and the social question are the two problems to be solved, and as a practical solution of the latter suggests the formation of committees of working men in every diocese, to meet on fast days and discuss moral and social questions.

- Mr. Stanley is expected to arrive at Dover from Calais about four °clock on Saturday afternoon. He will be received on hislanding at the Admiralty Pier by the Mayor and Corporation, and according as time will permit accompanied either to the Town Hall or the Lord Warden Hotel, where an address will be presented. A special train will be placed at his disposal by the Chatham and Dover Railway Company, and he will travel to Victoria.

The House of Lords has a father as well os the House of Commons. This is Lord Cottesloe, who last month entered upon his ninety-third year. He was, as usual on Budget nights, in his place in the Peers Gallery over the clock on Thursday week. This venerable nobleman entered the House of Commons in 1827, and in 1834 he was appointed Secretary to the Treasury. For more than italf a century he has made a point of hearing every Budget speech.

Primrose Day this year thoroughly revealed the fact that the custom has developed into a mere " fad " of the upper and a section of the middle classes. The workmen—barring a few youths—had nothing to do with it, save that a few wore it openly in jest, and proclaimed their Radicalism with at. The wear-; ing was most frequent in the City in the =ening, when the flowers were fresh, but in the West-end in the afternoon, the Primrosers were few and far between.

Mr. John Burns is resting at the seaside, out of the reach of letters and all other troubles. His health and spirits have been greatly *improved by his short holiday. He will be back in time for the May Day celebration, and he may even be here in time to congratulate Mr. Stanley on his arrival. The great traveller and the trade union leader are old friends, and Stanley has written a cordial letter just to show that he does not . take the County [Council speech of Mr. Burns to heart.

Mr. Gladstone, on Tuesday afternoon, drove through South London ut) Lambert-road, Brixton- ' rise, and took tea with Mr. and Mrs. Broadhurst. On account of the state of his health, Mr. Broad- hurst is about to leave his present residence and to live in Cromer when not compelled to be in London. Mrs. Gladstone had expressed a wish to visit Mr. and Mrs. Broadhursebefore they left Lambert-road, and had arranged to do so on Tuesday; but as she was too unwell to leave home, Mr. Gladstene drove up alone, and stayed with the bon, member and his wife fully an hour.

The promoters of the Watkin Tower have under consideration a proposal which, though it is some- what suggestive of Jules Verne, is submitted by a well-known engineer, and is said to be quite practi- cable. The Tower is to be not less than 1,200 feet high, considerably loftier than its prototype.at ' Paris. At this atmospherie level the air, even aver Lopdon, is absolutely pure, and it is proposed that by means of machinery specially devised for the purpose a supply of fresh air shall be drawn to the street level, and thence distributed to houses and public buildings as water and gas now are.

Mr. Morton and two or three more M.P.'s on the right side of the House have brought in A bill to make every return ticket by rail or steamboat available for twelve months. Good luck to them 1 But why stick at this small instalment of the right of railway passenger? Why not clauses to compel Parliamentary fares by every train; the issue of third-class season tickets; the provision of seats for all passengers, especially passengers by workmen's trains ; lighting ot all carriages in such a way that every passenger can see to read; and so on, and so on? The private member's bill is oft en a monument of praiseworthy intention, but it is apt to lack comprehensiveness.

In spite of the sanguine announcements of experi- ments which have been published from time to time coloured photographs remain still much in the position of blue roses and other unrealised dreams of the scientific world. Dr. Norris, who in an Out- burst of enthusiasm assurrd his comrades at the dinner of the Birmingham Photographic Society that he should die happier if he could but live to see colour photography established, does not look, he tells us, to practical photographers to make this great stride in the photographic art, but rather to some of those original thinkers who" know no dangers and recognise no impossibilities." -

--- - Commenting on the presence of the Grand Duke I and Grand Duchess of Mecklenburg-Strelitz at the demonstration of the Primrose League, on Saturday, at Covent Garden Theatre, the London correspon- dent of the " Manchester' Guardian" gives the politics of some royal persons as follows :—The Prince of Wales is a Unionist; the late Duke, of Albany was a vehement Tory; the Princess of Wales sided with the Liberals 'on the Eastern Question; Princess Mary was called "The Queer f of the Jin- goes " ; Princess Louise IS a Radical; but all these illustrious persons have confined the expression of their opinions to private life and the society of intimate friends. They have been neutral alike in word and in act. They havenever lent the sanction of their presence to the official celebration of a great plitical organisation.

During all the hours of the day before Patti is to sing she is practically mute. From her first waking moments she adheres to a strict vow of silence. Caroline, the German maid who has been with her for twenty-six years, knows all "her lady's" needs and wants without a prompter, and this valuable woman is an impassable barrier to intrusion upon the great singer's solitudeand silence. Her manager keeps his diAance discreetly. Nothing but the

sudden taking off of the tenor whom Patti expects to support her that evening would be considered a valid excuse for intruding upon her seclusion. And even in such an extreme case it is quite likely that _

the lady would express her wishes a's to a substitute in writing rather than by word of mouth. She is very conscientious about what she gives to the pub- lic. It is not enough for her that her voice should be unwearied when she sings; she will have it absolutely fresh.

Mr. Handel! Cossham was present throughout Tuesday night's sittings in the House of Commons, voting in each of the three divisions on Mr. Lea's motion with respect to Sunday closing in Ireland. He appeared in his usual health when he entered the library of the House of Commons at eleven o'clock on Wellnesday. After the first seizure 'which *took place in the library, he was able to walk into one of the side corridors, where he proposed to lie down. He was taken thence under the doctor's direction to the National Liberal Club, where he had rooms, and where he died. The only remark he made after his seizure in the House of Commons was," I wish I were at home.'

Referring to Mr. Gladstone's speech on the Irish Land Bill on Thursday,a correspondent says :—There was a great rush for the Strangers' Gallery, among those present with admission cards being the young son of a well-known member to whose pre- sence a pretty story pertains. Appealing on Wed- nesday to the Speaker's secretary for a lgood place for the boy, the father said—" I should like him to hear Mr. Gladstone before he dies." Mr. Ponsonby, naturally mistaking the drift of this remark, ob- served that Mr. Gladstone was in excellent health and strength—not likely to die for a long while yet. " Ah," said the father, " I was not thinking of his dying ; that's out of the question. 1 wasthink- ing of my boy."

Owd Scroggins lives up tort Arley, an varry seldom goos furr away. He doesno believe i' newe, pappers at o ;he seys ther no good to onybody. When th' lad cos on a Setterday wi't th' ' Examiner" he'll not tak one, becos he conno think what th' wo'ld wants wi sich things as newspappers for foak to bother their brains'wf.

Ileowever, he went to Warriton one Setterday, an brovit o' his family wi him in a two-boss waggin. He Still thowt as heaw George Thurd wur King, an wanted to know iv th' Hinglish ud taen Wayterloo, and iv so, wheer had they ta,en it? He'd sowd his corn for hauve o' what he should ha' done, an when he went to put th' brass i'th bank they towd him it wur o bad. Th' only brass he had wur a lot a' thrip'ny-bits, an thoose someb'dy ud gen him for sixpunses. His owd woman smookt a clay poipe, an hoo wouldno beleeov ut ony other soart un do for smookin WI. _ _

One o'th lads went to th' blacksmith's shop to get mezzur'd for a pair o' clogs. Th' owdest lad thowt th' Market-heawse wur a church. After hengin his hat cn a hook, he Beet hissel deawn uppo one o'th butcher's stalls, an lis- ten'd to a fella sheawtin green-stuff, an thowt he wur t' preycher. He coom eawt afoar th' sermon wur o'er, an sed he didno think mich abeawt th' preycher. One o'th dowters went to th' Post Offis wi a lot o

yung onions and wanted to trade urn for a letter. Hoo'd a choilt wi her ut hoo carried in a box, an boo Rept stoppin neaw an-•agean to rock it on th' flags. When it cried, hoo shov'd an owd stockin in it meawth an sung it. to sleep. When th' owdest lad wur last seen he'd co'd for a glass o' "sody an wayter," an stood soakin ginger- breyd in it an pooing lung faces. Th'' shopkeeper hadno understood him reet, so he'd gen him a mix- tar o' weshin soda an wayter, an it tasted gradely strung o' sooap.. But th' lad ud yerd tell o' "sody an wayter," an he wur tarmint give it a fair trial. Th' owd fella ad swept one o'th hoses for a don- key becose he sed i wouldnO heyt so mid]. ' Th' owd woman stood lewkin at black puddins aboon an heawr. div.head: DEVIL'S PLOT.
div.p: THE DEVIL'S PLOT.
AN APPEAL ON BEHALF OF MRS. LEWIS.

[Owing to a defect in the law' Mrs. Lewis, who has worked and is working nobly in the temperance cause in Blackburn, has had heavy legal expenses to meat in de- fending her reputation from a publican's gross and unfounded attack. She obtained at the trial an apology, the withdrawal of all imputations, and £5O towards her expenses; but, as she is still very much out of pocket, a fund is being raised to cover all expenses. The Rev. Charles Garrett, in sending a guinea last week to the "Alliance News," said : "Mrs Lewis is doing a good work that angels may well envy, and the dastardly attack upon her has not been made because she is Mrs. Lewis, but because of her Inost successful temperance work." The following lines have been contributed by the Editor of this journal, who has forwarded a subscrip- tion, and will be pleased to aalirwledge other subscript- Lions.]

Id hat! Are you men with wivestand daughters dear, With sisters whom you love as lilliptself, And will you look on idly while a *ter Is wronged, because the law is halt and lame? Fair phty ! There was a time when at the word

'he pulse would leap, and every heart beset To compass it ; Shall we now coldly say We care net if the play be fair or foul P And foul it was as well he Devil knows, For who but he, with wanton, wicked wil., Could counsel thus his spiteful spiteful minions : "She wins your victims ; you must strike her down— "Not openly, hut subtly and by stealth ; "Strike in the dark, and strike with. poisoned Ateel ! " Soft as the Devil whispered, he was. heard, And craftily the Devil's work was done. The blow was struek—struck where the pure in heart Can least defend themselves, yet feel the hurt As one that overwhelms the shuddering soul. The poison works; the sons of Belial grin ;. They, wallowing in the mire themselvea"have made,. Would shout for joy iflbut a speck of it Should chance to stain .a passing angel's wing. But foul is foul, and fait is fair, and you— Who in the light of day Have Seen the fain, Once fouled, made fair again—will you notsay— " She shall not suffer threugh the Devil's plot ; "She shall go forth uporylber mission high,. "'With powerful help of purse, and pen, and • voice; "With strenghtened hands and blessing onlrer work "" Then give—give freely—make the burden lit;.• Nor rest until the flinty road she treads Is pleasant as a pathway strewn with flowem.
BREATHED BUT WAS NOT'ALIVM.
We-regret that we cannot, in the space alloteci to uev, give the following story in full. lo see the writer and talk with him wculd, to Viousands of Englishmen, be

_ worth the cost and trouble of a journey to- America To condense the facts into, small compassk is a task of marked difficulty. Yet we must attempt it for the sake of the interest that it is certain to inspire. The state- ment was voluntarily given and will be Piarnd to con- tain more useful knowledge to most of uathan an ma- count of Stanley's researches in Africa. It is better to let the narrator give his experience in his own %vont*, which we do in the subjoined extract front.an article which attracted wide attention in the UniteiStates. Ile says:. 'On New Year's, Day, 1.883, }weighed 1851 pounds. My veins were fultof good blood.. My head was clean muscles strong,, nerves steady. It was easy to work, it Was sweet to sleep. Life was- a pleasure, as. God intends it to.be to every man. Between four and five years later I wean poor, emaciated, broken wretch; useless to others, a burden to myself.. All this happened through an ignorance almost unpardonabls in these days. of education. Aliout the Ist. .of February,: 1883, I began to feel out -of sorts. I felt heavy and dull, couldn't work, and went about like a man in a bank of fog. These were rambling feelings of uneasiness in the chest, sides, and lower part of the back. My appetite became poor, and the kidney secretions scanty, and of. a dark 6otouz. I said to myself, I have eanght cold, and it will sooniffear off. I was wrong ; it did not wear /off, and in two months I was down with thedropsy. "With. this I suffered the agonies of death for four months. The lightest food lay on ay stomach like cold iron. There was no power or motion. there. It was , like a watch with the mainspring broken, Then carne a perfect fleck of things to disgust and frighten me: -foul taste in the mouth, risings. of nauseous gas in the throat, sometimeoa sour and choking kind of saliva or.raucus,

. - yellow skin, cold ettremities, coated tongue, spells of whirling.dizziness, and palpitation of the heart, which seemed to threaten death, as the wind blows out a candle. Then loss of sleep, and the horrors of dragging night hours while listening to the unceasing. ticking of the clock. Neither Dickens nor Hawthorne could have- described it. I was in this condition nearly. five yearsi.. What a living death:! I walked. in Valley, of the Shadow, breathing, but not alive. "Yet I made a fights. Every remedy I heard of I tried.. [let nothing go by. Friends andt physicians. combined in vain to help me. Then came a, cough. I thought it was consumption, and so did others. But it was-not. Let me toll, you that thonsanda SLR treated. for consumption whosolungs are sound as al steel boiler/ They should be doocared for somothing else. But wait!. By this time my stomach was insuch a stateL threw up even sweet milk. The doctor said I must got betfim at once, or die soon, But what chance hacUP. 'You. see none, the doctor:saw none, I saw none. "For all that ham a well man to-day. How L became SD iS a wonder tome, and will be untith solve-the last noystery that awaits all of us. The facts are these: I 'could no longer walk; I could only totter and stagier, only to fall an a chair or on, the bed. A, friend came in and said, Alderson, you are in very bad form.. I wish I had known it months ago.. But I'm afraid it'a too late now." What would you, have done 7-'1 asked., 'This,' he replied. •I should have made, you take Mother Seigel's Clarative Syrup—nothing else. I have seen it cure lots of such cases,, though none as bad as yours.' Let natty even nowl said. It was done. One bottle seemed, to do me no. good. Weeks went by and I kept on. I then got better. I began to sleep, and ate a little. I got out, of the land of the nightmare. One day. being hungry, at the house of a neighbour, I thought- lessly ate a full meal of hearty food. I feared it would kill me; it was the first for months. Hours passed. Death? No; only comfort, warmth, and strength. I continued with Mother Seigel,' dear old soul! and got well.

"1 have only to add, nine-tenths of our diseases are merely indigestion and dyspepsia. The other apparent ailments are nothing but symptoms of that. Pluck up the poison :Got, the bad treo perishes, and the only thing that will kill it is Seigel's Syrup. That I know. " D, Q. MonasoN.

Certainly Elizabeth Ann thought she was good looking, and to solve all doubts upon the subject, she frequently repaired to a little false-faced looking-glees made of exceedingly bad glass, and hung up at onrond of the dresser. She never looked in that glees to see if she was pretty, but kept up a pleasant fiction that it was on purpose to see if her cap was straight, and if this were so, Elizabeth Ann must have worn caps of the oroekedest construction and wickedest disposition, foi they were nearly always awry. No sooner had the parlour door closed than Eliza both Ann wanted to see if her cap was straight; and ail she wasthere she rearranged the cherry-coloured ?dereo. that formed a bow at her neat collar, smoothed down a few obstinately crimpy hairs, gave her apron a hitch, and then smiled at herself and made her eyes twinkle. The room looked very bright and cosy, velth its well spread tea-table, flowers, pictures, and glistening furni- ture. The curtains were drawn, the lamp lit, and the cat and dog were quite reads, to afford the visitor a kindly welcome, while the canary burst ';ertle in a jubilant song. " I am so glad to see you, Alfred," said the little woman, pressing her visitor down into a Beet. °' Diu do look so tired and worriedthough, and you must want your "Well, I 8.191 a bit tired and worried," he added, as the little widow pulled the belle-a needlers3-promed- ing, for Lizzybeth was alreedehat the door-with the tea-urn, her cheeks now glowing like the- eherry ribbons, and looking as hot.aeethe detours g.iece of rotundity she bore. "That's right, Lizzybeth e now the tea-calms," cried the little widow, as she hastened to warm tho tea-fee with its proper modicum from the hissingeuen, and then emptying tie water into the cups- liberally shovelled in tire tea from the '!oil-liaed caddy: at her ride.

"I did think it PO long before you come,'said the little woman, looking across the table at her guest, and blushing rosily with amiability and pleasure. " hope you have not been much worried."' "Horribly," he said,,gloontap, agate toolethe cup of tea she offered from her hands' a cup of ' tea by the way that gave promise of the treatn tent MrssAppleby's second lard would receive—for it was very strong, very sweet; and for her visitor's benefitoshe had not skimmed the milk, but ,skimmed off ,the thickest por tion of the crams. "Oh, I' am sorry, dear,'"she said, tenderly, as. regardless of self, she now proceeded tc hand the hot cake which Lizzybeth brought in, and placed, upon the heated sibp basin. "Make haste with the toast, Lizzybeth4' she cried, parenthically,. "and bring up the brass footman as well." "Yea, mum," said the maid; and then; as the door closed, " Which I just won't, then. I . shall bring up one thing at a time, for I ain't going to leave you two togetherlonger than I can help, so come now." Here Lizzybeth relieved her feelings its the passage by making another "face "at the parlour door. "Is it about your poor dear. mother's % affairs," said Mrs. Appleby, as soon as they were alone once more. "Yes—yes—yes," he said, drearily. "Oh, Mary, Marysl'm afraid it'a all over.". ' "No, no, no; don't be.destiondent about it," said the little.woraan, tenderly_ "Perhaps things will turn out better than you think." s "rna afraid not," he replied: "But it down and have some tea, too, or II shall not enjoy mine." Mrs. Appleby retook her seat with essmile, and filled her own Cu!). "t w:sh all the lawyerawere hung!" said the visitor, sarnestly. Oh, don't Fay- such things as that, dear," said the lady, whose stiff silk. dress rustled as she popped stF again to take the cup her guest had-just emptied. "More toast, mum," said Lizzybetlo, coming in. "No, no, Lizzsbeth; ,Lnisnoto ready yet," said sthe lady. "All right, mums"' said the, maid, and she wb.isited off again with the plute of •hot toast. "I can't help saying it," ha continued. "'The rascals! Th ssaandrele ! It'd so very hard ti find that all your hopes are dribbling away in consultations and stamps, awl exalninatiens,, and references, and goodness knows what besides. , The law's a Yeast, very deep well." 'Yes, dear, ills," she said, with a sighs "but, pray, make a sxod tea. Try, some of these sardines ; they are the sort you said you. lilted SO well." The visitorwould have .00rne sardines, hut he de clined to hese strawberry, jam with them, and Appleby was just taking hisoup for refilling, ,when the door openedsagain. "Did you, ring, mutur said Lizzybeths "No, Lissybetb." Must have been nest door," said Liszybeth ; and she descended again. The visitor's troubles. were no doubt great, but non quite so large as his appetite, which wasexcellent, and the more heartily he ate, the greater the satisfaction ix the widows tho . tools it all as a compliment to her

repast. But no. maidea coulra have been , more attentirs than Lizzybeth, who was constantly zoming up wi4l relays of hot cake and toast, to see iirmore hot water. was required forth& urn, or a fresh aupply of cream; and, truth to telh.sbe passed a gr,ati deal of the time hovering between the top of the, staircase and the parlour door. Airlast, however; the tar. was ab. an end, th*Mbhi cleared, the hearth neatly xw.pt up, and, with a.amile, thelittle widow brought out a cigar box, insisting. upon her visitor taking one, and me:king himself vita at home. And now,, perhaps from indigestion, the, visitor began to look exceeding y dolt and dispirits& The widow conversed, but it was of reo use: he grew more and more depreised, and he sighed deeply. If the widow had se, n that the sighs were those of . *loving swain, she would Ltito felt flattered; but they ' Varo WW-Clerttly the sighs of one in trouble, and that was a very &fferect thieg., Sh-, talked o:: being hopeful, of waiting to see how -the lawyers brought matters out; and several times it was upon the good little woman's lips to say that he was wit to trouble bitneelf about money, for that she would have enough for all; but though deeply in love with her handsome swain, she bad a little of that- worldly possession kr IDA n as prudenee,and, while be ng generous to a fault, the idea of money in connection with their intimacy jarred upon her unpleasantly. Lizzybeth contrived several reasons for visits to. the . parlour. There was the tax paper that had been left and not brought up, There was the change that Mr Wilkins's man had raid her early in the day, out of' that half crown, and which she bad put upon the dresser shelf, and "forgot all about." A quarter of an hour after she was obliged to come and BA missus whether she would like any potatoes cooked for supper, and soon after receiving her o.rmmands upon this point, she made her appearance with the little copper kettle of hot water to place upon the hob. This was followed by a tray with tumblers, when poor Lizzybeth was so forgetful that she had to go down for teasttoons, and even then she forgot the sugar-tongs. The evening was wearing on,. anCr he bad another' engagement to keep—one where heknew thdt he mart not fail; so at last he leaned his head upon his hand, n'id at looking at the fire. Mrs. Appleby had some fancy work in her hand SS she sat opposite to him; and she hid been growing more and more uneasy about his seate. That he bad something upon his mind she was sure; so,softly laying down her work, she rose, crossed to his side, and stood with her plump little hands resting upon his shoulder. "Don't you think we have known each other bag-. enough now, Alfred, for you to confide in me? Iru,„u have some trouble on you:, mind. Why don't you ten' me?" "Oh, there are some things a man with any priae , or feeling in him cannot teil. Mary," said tbieloeng man, piteously; and as he congratulated,himself upon bow cleverly he was acting he raised his-eyes to the wall, and started really, for it seemed as if the portrait of the late Mr. Appleby, la a blue coat and braes , buttons, was gazing down at him very sternly, as reading him through and through. "Why not? 'Why should you keep anything froln I me?" "Pride," he said, quietly; .and there was a beauti- fully ingenuous expression in. his countenance, az he looked her full in the face. "Then it's about money," she-said, sharply. " You Want money." "No," he said, with a sad smile, "si don't want , money. It is my lawyer who says we mast pay net' , tabs things if this unfortunate little property is not to • be lost for ever, and I can't help feeling that I should be far wiser if I wrote to him or went to him, and said I would have no more to do with it, for be bad bad my last sovereign, and / was no bette- off." , "And do you think so, der ?'5 said Mrs. Appleby. . I "Yes," he said firmly, "I do,. and I will pal tm

more." It was a desperate stroke, bath-is-often these despere" strokes which win. "Then I don't think tio, dear," she said Srinlyi It is to get yourrights, and a hundred pounds that is wanted for the lawyer, it s'oall be found.. Dow rnuo.a does he want now?" "It is thirty-nine pounds thirteen and fourpeuP9, said Martin, shaking his heud, "but no could r tak.e Ft of 3 our money: I should feel that I Wf graded in your sight, and 1 wild -never look,it fees again." She laughed, and,/ parting hit hair, kissed very affectionately on the forehead. Thea leavir room, Martin at thinking his eyes rose and more- met those of the portrait so sternly fixed him, that he shifted his. chair impatiently, wondered whether he shnukl get the meney.. Ha was not long left in doubt, for the little came-bustling hack. but, only to send a appointment through him. as she exclaimed: " so sorry, Alfred, I have not get enouf have only thirty-seven pousds in the house," "That would be plenty,. if I could take. it," 131 with a trngic air; when she pressed him ani much declining, he did ;aka it, and soon. tOrter that he must go, leaving without noticing lila who hurried up to open the, door. div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT BANK QUAY.

On Tuesday evening a meeting in support of Mr. Bea- Man's candidati. re was held at the Workingmen's Mission, Bank n - -"ay. There was a good attendance. The chair Was taken by Mr. T. Birchall, and amongst others present Were Councillors W. Pierpaint and J. Shaw-Green ; Messrs J. naYward, J. W. Hayward, G. Legge, and Clayton (Liberal agent.) - The CHAIRMAN read a letter from Councillor F. A. ;Roberts, 'who said the Tories had thrown down a chal- lenge to the North-west ward to declare its political nolours and that it was now the duty of every Liberal in tile ward to reply to that challenge by doing his utmost . 1.9 get every elector to poll. (Hear, hear.) Continuing, tneihairinan said that since their last meeting there had _Dee a variety of criticism. Several oracles had spoken,and the usual amount of misrepresentation on the part ntw their opponents had taken place, but that they knew .naa inseparable from the Tories. Amongst others that 7,ory Paper, which was described not long ago by its frivn advocate in the celebrated action, Bradlaugh vesus uself,in language which,if he were to use it, he would be ebsi,arged with discourtesy. So far as the remarks of :lab PaPer concerning himself were concerned he should tot trouble the meeting by any allusion to them, except aesaYing that he was glad the editor evidently remem- _ r d pretty keenly a tap on the knuckles he gave him lltc,ine four or five years ago when he charged him (the tmairman) with a meanness he was not capable of, and which ought never to have been made before hear had been taken to substantiate it. (Hear, .) That paper had also been trying by a rries of verbatim reporting to pour some little N n'erript on their friend, Mr. Thomas Morris. e°W they all knew that Thomas Morris was in who was always straight both in his utterance and t:3l is conduct. (Hear, hear.) He made no pretension being an orator, but he said clearly what he had got 7744,Y and said it in his own natural way. (Hear, hear.) .s:at if it was tried to make Mr. Morris look blunt and „a,lleouth they all knew the reason why it was done. He 'mould like to see the same paper try verbatim reporting ll'ir. John Roberts. and if it did so, and gave Mr. John lit "überts' grammar and the 66 h6s "in the place Mr. Roberts th P ftt, --elm, with a few other peculiarities of that kind he I"Ze,Chairman)would pay for the printing. (Laughter and tiPause.) Mr. John Roberts was making a great deal h "Pita' out of his connection with the Infirmary, but ill23lthe Chairman) did not think that was a fair proceed- eras not right that the Infirmary should be made battle ground by anybody.and as one of the Board , diernagement of the institution he protested against it • M. Rh" (Hear, hear.) He did not think the course pre Roberts had taken had been at all a dignified or a one in his position. He was a little surprised on • lust hold of one of their Infirmary reports which had 6 s been issued. It had evidently been sent to one of ;ltl: working-men's committees and he found that it was ' gi,,laPed with the words "from John Roberts." He (Mr. ',ran) had been under the impression that those re- Were sent out by the Infirmary to people interested, : Ro'Lthat was not quite sufficient for their friend, Mr. .' nvght 'ens, who must have his name stamped on them. That e. i , l-... f •-• just a little bit of vain ambition on the part ' „• Roberts, but it was one of those straws which ;',7"wed which way the wind was blowing. (Hear, hear, , 7,A.u.aPPlause.) , ~Zr• Rxamam, on rising to address the meeting, was librarsyPeee, a h, , Zilted with loud applause. In the course of an admir- Mr Beaman advocated the freeing of the ' of th nd the sanitary improvement of the dwellings Pour. He was glad that power had been invested ~ ...., ueir hands under the Artisans Dwelling Act. Any 12 inajers could, if, after repeated representations to the ✓ ir7,„ Powers that be "no attention was paid to them, ' 0.„-'"°rialize and secure the intervention of the Local seUernment Board. Mr. John Roberts in his address ▪ ",,a great deal about improving trade but he did not lloW it could be d)ne. He (Mr. Beaman) could tell one way to do it, namely, by theabolition of royalty •ef .„,"".• (Applause.) Mr. Beaman referred to the question The fling royalties, and asked if it was fair and just that . inatreadY enormously rich landlords—men who in some 6 flees had no more moral claim to the land than he anyone in the meeting had—should not only grab the 'd, but that which a bountiful providence had placed ' • erneath it ? Was it fair that these men should put I:1111th or more tor every ton of manufactured iron into already overgereed purses than a puddler and his ; .„,s4l,lerhand *received in wages? If these rents were 7' nced and diverted into their proper channel, namely, national exchequer, and expended for national pur- ' real they would relieve taxation to an incalculable , hZ,.,eee- (Applause) What held good with the mines ' 11,24 go Od with the land in the main. This question of l • „_ nearned increment must come to the front, and that iroMily too. Works, factories, properties of all descrip- , la°rinda had to bear their share of local taxation, but the „„ upon which they had beon built was exempt. He [ ', iTntended that if the land bore its fair share of taxation l' Would conEvderably lighten the burdens of the local • ayers. (Applause.) 1/7.1*,.; G. LEGGE moved :---" That this meeting considers oamuel Johnson Beaman a fit and proper person to _present the North-West Ward in the Town Council, and I edges itself to use all legitimate means to secure his• (Applause.) He (Mr. Legge) considered it was • Wrong of Mr. Jahn Roberts to try to make political lout of the Infirmary, which was subscribed to by , all p • arties and sects. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Legge also !Poke kA strongly in favour of the enlargement of the baths. A PPlauß ) th istr. -e• • L. o J. HAY WARD, in seconding the proposal, said he LI, ire light that as working-men they knew what was the 1,%,131-line article. Having made some amusing compari- P 4 irk% between Mr* Roberts' candidature and incidents in ' Wa iticaen's " Oliver Twist," Mr. Hayward said he thought -rs t' , • gist Mie working-men were doing something in earn- [ Ile • He had been canvassing lately, and his heart had .- in l'er been so stirred as it had been during the past week ienvisiting some parts of the town. He could not have r „, agined that within a few yards of his own door so it aeh dirt could be seen or so much poverty exist ; and as, he thought, quite time that these questions were ;Toughly ventilated. (Applause.) kouncillor Wm. PIERPOINT, in supporting the resolu- an, referred to the meagre representation of the work- in the Town Council. The manufacturers, °, were able to take care of themselves, already had .e, largest share of the representation in the Council-12 7 l' of the 36 members to which the town was entitled. e ereallopkeepers, another large and important class, sh...verY well represented, and had six seats. The ridters, the brewers, the wine and spirit merchants, ~_ e publicans had six seats ; which were, in fact, a deal more than their share. The "gentleman" , l ' hatiftaa---the so-called " gentleman " class on the register— , representatives, but the largest class of all, the .7' (erring-class interest, had only one' representative. ceili.ea; Mr. George Woods had taken ex- -65)h 'len to Councillor Flood's presence in the Council walnber, and had said he had no right there. Mr. 3,1),,,°1id8 had said that, Mr. Flood did not represent him. he (Mr. Pierpoint) could say that Sir Gilbert ,iaeenall did not represent him. (Hear, hear, and ap- e;lse, ,)„. He also thought the town of Warrington was be,"„ 111-represented by Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Hear, to 1;.'• Mr. George Woods said Mr. Flood did not attend the,la duties, but he believed that he could say that 14,•% was not a member of the Committees on which l°od served who attended oftener or more assidu- . ItY to the duties than he did. (Loud applause). E. WRIGHT, in supporting the motion, said that I , ell Mr. George Woods implied that Councillor Flood egi 'ran eeted his duties, he must either have spoken in igno- ceeete or deliberately said what he did to mislead the , kstn,°l.a. (A Voice: "To mislead.") If he spoke in smelance he should apologise, but if he spoke delibe- , he„.'Y, what could they say about such a man? (Hear, gro, and applause.) 7, ReiLliticillor .1. SHAW-GREEN said he knew Mr. Beaman's t,.t,„ tworth, and the ability he would be able to bring t in tl'ar on the questions which had to be discussed ' nam:e Council Chamber, and he was convinced he would '‘ trna,e his mark as a member of the Corporation He ' • ram'"? Mr. Beaman would be returned by such a large , 3•lngirl't,,,v that the Conservatives would not contest the .1.„, -West Ward again. (Applause.) resolution was put to the meeting and unani- -kr, sit). aAreeti to, and a vote of thanks was accorded to Itt„,:lrenall for presiding, on the motion of Mr. J. W. -"man, seconded by Mr. FIELDHOIISE.

div.p: Vry hard working man. He had, perhaps, been more successful than sonic working-men, hut so rev it, was no discredit to a person to get on in the wor,ld. It was always a pleasure to him to help his fellow working-men in whatever way he might be able. If on Friday all his friends did their hest, he would be returned to the Coun- cil. (Applause.) So far as politics went, he did not mean to enter into any. It was well-known that he was and always had been a Conservative, but he promised that if he were elected he would do his best, whatever might come before the Council, for ;lie interest of the ratepayers. Heasked their support, and would venture to say that they would never rue the day they voted in his behalf. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN WHITE remarked that Mr. John Crosfield had said that politics ought not to be introduced in those elections, but a much higher authority—Mr. Gladstone —had. distinctly stated that it was desirable that in municipal and county council contests politics should be introduced. For his own part, he did not see how they could be kept out. There was, possibly, no man living in Warrington at the present time who had done more for the Conservative party than had Mr. John Roberts. That was one reason why he should be elected, but there was a greater. It was from his business education, practical knowledge, straightforwardness, and integrity of character. Mr. Roberts was a man who would do his duty when sent to the Council. (Hear, hear.) An important matter which needed looking after just now was the commencement of the Warrington docks. If pressure was not brought to bear on that question, Warrington would be left out in the cold, as it was when the railway system was intro- duced into this country: If energetic and capable men were not sent into the Council, the docks would, five years hence, be no nearer commencement or completion than they were at the present time. (Hear, hear.) The , ratepayers did not want to send •men of "lump-post" policy—(laughter)—to the Council, but men who would look to the future and not sacrifice the interests .and wel- fare of the town to a little parsimony. Mr. Roberts was the right kind of man for that work, and he, therefore, asked the ratepayers to give him their support. (Ap- plause.) The meeting closed with the passing of a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: NESTING IN IZOLLESTON-ST. SCHOOLS
div.p: NESTING IN IZOLLESTON-ST. SCHOOLS

Another meeting in aid 04 Mr. Roberts' candidature was held in Rolleston-st. schools on Thursday evening. Mr. James Smethurst presided, and there were also on the platform, besides the candidate, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Alderman Sutton, Councillors Muir and Hepherd, Messrs. A. Woods, W. Spinks, P. Naylor, tee. The CHAIRMAN, in the course of his remarks, said if they had to reply to all the insinuations that had been thrown out against the Tories they would have nothing else to do that night. It had been said by Mr. Birchall that Mr. Roberts was making political capital out of his connec- tion with the Infirmary, but this he (Mr. Smethurst) denied. He defied those on the other side to prove a , single instance in which Mr. Roberts or any one on his behalf had referred to the Infirmary before the thing was mentioned at the Liberal meetings. He contended 1 that it was not right for Messrs. Pierpoint and Flood to interest themselves so much in the return of the Liberal candidate seeing that they were returned to the Town Council as representatives of the Ratepayers' Associ- ation, and as such received the votes of some Conserva- tives.—Mr. J. P. TAYLOR moved a motion pledging the meeting to support Mr. Roberts.—Th:s was seconded by Mr. J. BANNER, and supported by Councillor MUIR, the latter stating that as the battle was being fought pn political lines he hoped all Conservatives would support Mr. Roberts. He thought that many Liberals would also vote for Mr. Roberts because of his personal worth—Mr. W. SPINES supported the motion and referred to the need for improved baths in Warrington. Mr. T. Masorr and Mr. P. NAYLOR spoke in favour of Mr. Roberts, the latter remarking that Mr. Beaman had only been brought %rut because he was a Radical to the "score." Mr. Naylor also alleged that Mr. Beaman gave no support to the workmen's associations, and that he had only lived in Warringtcn eight years. Both of these statements were characterised as untrue by one of the audience.—Mr. S. BARLOW, who was one of the audience, said he would not vote on either side as he entirely disapproved of the municipal elections being fought on political lines.—The Chairman at this point read a note, which had been I handed up to him from the audience, to the effect that Mr. Beaman had that afternoon been to the Secretary of the Ironworker's Association and offered himself as a inember.—Alderman SUTTON having supported the motion it was carried with acclamation.—ln responding, Mr. ROBERTS referred to the remarks made by Mr. Birchall at the Liberal meeting with regard to his send- ing out the Infirmary report to the members of the Workingmen's Committee with the words" from Jelin Roberts" stamped on the back. In doing this, he said, ,he had done nothing but what was usual. He could assure them he was not deserving of the criticisms that , had been passed upon hi m.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. A. Woods, brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.
div.p: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.

The friends at Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, have this week' been celebrating the occasion of the re-opening of their place of worship, after it has been throughly renovated and beautis fled. It had for some time been apparent that the building was in need of re-decoration, and a determined effort was made by the members of the congregation to raise by snbscription among them- selves a sum of money to provide for th6,carrying out of the wotk. By this means promises were obtained of over £3OO, and, as the estimated cost of the work is £420, arrangements were made for hold- ing special services, with a view to raising the balance required.. A deseriptiota of the decorations was given in our last week's issue. The re-opening services commenced on Sunday. The preacher in the morning was the Rev. John Yonge, and in the evening the Rev. James McDougall, of Manches- ter. Mr Hamilton White; of Retford, was' at the organ on both occasions. There were large congregations, and at the evening service an anthem was well rendered by the choir. The Rev. J. Yonge's sermon in the morning was founded upon Isaiah lx. 13, "The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree and the box together to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious." In the course, of an eloquent sermon the rev, gentleman asked the con- gregation to present that sanctuary to God as an act of worship. Years ago that house was built for God. for the worship of his name, for the preaching of his saving truth. It was built in a style and at an outlay propor-.. tionate to the means and social position of' the Christian men and women who combined to build it, and now once again it had been renewed and re-ornamented, and he thought the general feeling would be one of pleasure and thankfulness that with the means they had been able to produce conspicuous talent and faithful work had com- bined to clothe the building with such a large degree of comeliness and beauty. The rev. gentleman urged the congregatioe to seek to beautify their personal lives. The collections for the day amounted to £79 13s. 2d. On Wednesday evening Mr. Hamilton, White, of Ret- ford, gave au organ recital at the church, there being a good attendance. Mr. White, who is organist of West Retford Church, is a talented musician, and gave a splendid display of his power over the instrument. The programme was as fellows :—Overture to Sacred Drama " Athalie " (Mendelssohn) ; Priere et Berceuse (Guil- mant) ; Legende et Allegro Symphonique (Guilmant) •, song, "Jerusalem," Mrs. R. H. Pearson: Toccata altd Fugue in D. Minor (J. S. Bach) ; Fantasia Pastorale— solo, violin, and organ, " Meditation," R. H. Pearson and H. White ; March in C Minor (from the Piano Works) (F. SPindler) ; Cantilene in A flat (A. Mailly) ; and Grand Offertohie in D (Batiste). 'The overture to the sacred drama " Athalie," by which the programme commenced, is an arrangement for the organ by Mr. W. T. Best, and orchestral contrasts are aimed at throughout. The two following items, " Priere et Berceuse," and " Legende of Allegro Symphonique" are amongst the best pieces written for this instrument by the celebrated organist of the Madeleine, Paris. The first has some nice effects for the softer stops, and the last is far above the average of French compositions for the organ. 'F ho Toccatta and Fugue in D minor are among the finest examples to be found in the works cf Bach, and the "Fantasia Pastor- ale" is a light and graceful composition, which, It is scarcely necessary to say, delighted the hearers. All the items were played with skill, and in her song Mrs. R. H: Pearson appeared •to great advantage. The collections for the everting:amounted to £5 2s. Bd. On Thursday evening, when the Rev. C. A. Berry, of Wolverhampton, preached, a large congregation assembled. The rev, gentleman occupied the same pulpit a few months ago, and his high reputation as an eloquent and earnest preacher drew together on that occasion a large assemblage. At, the special service held on Thursday it was very noticable that many worshippers from other churches were present, and that several ministers of other denominations hap come to hear Mr. Berry. The preacher took for his text the words con- tained in the 17th and 18th verses. In the course of a sermon delivered with an impressiveness that rivetted the attention of his numerous hearers, he printed cut that it was not enough to merely know Christ historically. He was a living pres,•nce ; a saving presence. They had not done their duty to Christ when they summed Him up, analysed Him, and •.explained Him. There was too much tendency in these daps to think we were religious if we said that ,Christ was great, and good, and beautiful. That langu- age seemed to him to border very near upon blasphemy. . If a thing was good, they could not help seeing that it was good. There was no virtue in calling things by their proper names. The virtue came in in this case when, seeing how great, and good, and beautiful Christ is, we say to Him "Come and dwell with us ; Thou art our Lord • Thy death is the mastery of our sin : Take our life, our heart, our all." That was virtue, and that was faith. At the conclusion of his sermon, the Preacher said that a collection would be taken in behalf of the funds of the church, and especially the fund for its decoration and cleaning. About £59 were required to complete this fund. Was it too much to ask their friends to discharge the liability that night and leave the church free to its spiritual work. While the collection was being made, the choir sang an anthem. The amount collected was £l5 12s. 5d., making a total amount collected at the rs-cpsiihag services of £lOO 15s.

div.head: SIR W. HARCOURT AND ALLOTMENTS.
div.p: SIR W. HARCOURT AND ALLOTMENTS.

Sir. W. Harcourt speaking at the annual meeting of the Allotments and Small Holdings Association, in London, on Wednesday, said that County Councils were not fit to deal with allotments, and that the condition of the British agricultural labourer was worse than in any other country. What was wanted was the elevation of. his incral condition, and to give him a sense of stability, security, and independence. He denied Mr. Jesse Colling's charge that the Liberals took office on the ques- tion of allotments and then threw it over.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY.
div.p: THE SALVATION ARMY.

General Booth made a statement at a meeting of the Salvation Army in Manchester on Tuesday night with reference to the finances, strength, and work of the organisation. Their income, he said, now amounted to over £250,000 a year, and the Army contained more than 9,000 officers and 3,700 corps in distant and neighbouring parts of the world. Among other extensions, contem- plated and in progress, General Booth mentioned that the Army had purchased a site opposite the new Palace of Varieties in Manchester' at a cost of £14,000, on which they intended to erect abuilding.

div.head: ALLEGED DEATH FROM NEGLECT.
div.p: ALLEGED DEATH FROM NEGLECT.
INQUEST AT WARRINGTON:

On Tuesday morning Mr. Samuel Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lancashire, opened an inquiry at the Warrington Workhouse, relative to the circumstances of the death of a lad named James Gavin, who.it is alleged had been neglected by his parents. The case was investigated a few months ago by the borough magistrates, with the result that the mother, who is the wife of a puddler, was committed to prison for two months with hard labour. It was stated during the magisterial inquiry that the boy was sufferingofrom burns received several weeks before, and from want of food. The child was re- moved to the Workhouse Hospital, where it received every attention, but was unable to regain its strength, and died on Saturday morning last. After a consulta- tion with Police-Inspector Cox, the Coroner said he was afraid they would not be able to finish the inquiry that morning, because the mother of deceased had been com- mitted to prison for two months with hard labour for neglecting her child. He gathered from the police re- ports that that was previous to the burning, and that death had nothing to do with the neglect. But he under- stood from the police now that the child was burnt, and that then the alleged neglect took place, so that the neg- lect might have had something to do with the death .f the child. After hearing one ortwo witnesses, he thought the better course to adopt would be to have a post- mortem examination of the body made, to decide whether neglect had had anything to do with the death. (To the Inspector) : Who is this witness P—lnspector Cox: This is the mother.—The Coroner: She may be charged. Is there anyone else you can call who can identify the body —someone who cannot be criminally charged with the death P—lnspector Cox said he could call another wit- ness—Harriet Dutton, a married woman, living at 27, Warburton-St., said she had known the deceased child, who was the son of Thomas Gavan, a puddler, living at No. 5, Arnold's-yard, off flaydock-et. She believed the deceased was seven years of age. She was present when the child died, and was the first to see it after it had been burnt. She had seen the body of the deceased that morning.—Nurse Daniels deposed that the child died in the Workhouse Hr:spital at five o'clock on Saturday morning last.—The Coroner: That is all the evideace I shall call this morning. We will have the fullest inquiry when we meet again.—The inquest was then adjourned till Tuesday morning next, at 11.20.
TIIE EXAMINER, SATILRDAY, APRIL 26, 1800
MURDER AND SUICIDE.

Agnes Ruston, aged 22, of Parkgate, near Rotherham, plunged into the canal near her home a few days a.o, with her child, aged eight months, and they were boh drowned. At the inquest held on Tuesday the jury returned a verdict that the mother murfiered the child and committed suicide while temporarily insane.
MR. DILLON REALISES £30,000 FOR
IRELAND.

_ Mr. John Dillon, on arriving at Southampton from his American and Australian tour, told a representative of the "Freeman's ' Journal" he had realized by it £30,000 for evicted tenants in Ireland. The only opposi- tion was from the Melbourne Press, but it did not inter- fere with the meetings. He never visited a country, not even the United states, where there was such an appear- ance of general comfort among the people as in Australia and New Zealand.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSB OF LORDS.—Monmsv. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. INEQUALITY OF SENTENCES.—Lord HERSCHELL called attention to the inequality of sentences passed in cases of like gravity, and asked if the Government would appoint a Royal Commission, or Committee, or by some other means make inquiry into the present system of punishment and the principles ,Fhich should guide its administration ; also whether it was possible to diminish the unequal incidence of punishments, and render them more effective.—The Loan CHANCELLOR, while recogniz- ing the importance of the subject, and that the question was worthy of consideration by the Government, said it was one not for inquiry by a, Royal Commission or Com- mittee, but for debate. Lord Coleridge was averse to excessive punishment, and would welcome the formation of a Court of Criminal Appeal.—Lord Norton considered , the present system of dealing with criminals was not sufficiently deterrent.—After some further discussion, Lord Herschell hoped the Government would give the matter their earnest attention, and the subject then dropped. The House adjourned at twenty minutes to seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. In the absence of the Speaker through indisposition, Mr. Courtney took the chair at three o'clock. THE PORTUGUESE IN AFRICA.—Sir J. FEROUSSON told Mr. Stanley Leighton that the Portuguese Government knew of no intended expedition to the Shire country, but had sent orders to the Governor of Mozambique to keep their officers below the Rua. POSTAL REGULATIONS.—Mr. RAISES, in answer to Mr. 0. V. Morgan, said that he was aware that circulars were sent from this country to be posted abroad and that unfastened envelopes might be used for covers, and he was considering whether or not the book post regula- tions in this country could be modified in that and some other respects. IRISH LOCAL GOVERNMENT.—Mr. BALFOUR, in answer I to Mr. Lea, said the possibility of presenting a Local Government Bill for Ireland this session depended upon the progress made with other Government business. The , Bill would not contain provisions giving power to local authorities to control the further issue of liquor licences. —Mr. Las gave notice of a motion on the subject of legislation for Ireland on the liquor question. WELSH SUNDAY CLOSING COMMISSION.—MT. W. H. Smrra said that the Government did not intend this session to recommend Parliament to take any steps upon the report of the Welsh Sunday Closing Commission. IRISH LAND BILL. Mr. BALFOUR formally moved the second reading of the Irish Land Purchase Bill. Mr. Naomi. moved its rejection, although the bring- ing forward of such a measure demonstrated the justice of the claim made nine years ago on the formation of the Land League that an occupier's ownership might to be established. He, however, contended that the measure was an insufficient one, as it would benefit only one- fourth of the tenantry ; that it exhausted local credit without consulting the Irish people; that it made no suitable provision for the congested districts, and that it was unsafe for the Imperial taxpayer, and that the counter guarantees were illusory, insufficient, and un- availing. His proposal for the settlement of the land question was to give the landlords so many years' pur- chase on reducing the rents on the judicial tenants to a satisfactory level, and let him use the money in paying off the most onerous of his encumbrances. Mr. MADDEN, the Attorney-General for Ireland, re- garded Mr. Parnell's speech as in substance one for the second reading of the Bill. The principle of the measure was that it did not deal with an estate in its entirety, but with each individual tenant. Since 1889 there had been a concensus of opinion in support of the principles of State-aided purchase of land in Ireland, and he be- lieved the real object of the opposition to the present Bill was to endeavour to inflict injury upon the Govern- ment. He argued that the security provided by the Bill was free from risk, and that this was the first measure ever introduced which dealt in an effectual manner with the congested districts. Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN did not consider the Govern- ment's scheme to be advantageous for Ireland, as it in- cluded all tenants, good and bad alike, and permitted the clearing out of landlords from whole estates. When once the Government began this system of land purchase, it was impossible to fix any limit to it. The debate was continued by Mr. Ambrose, the Earl of Cavan, Mr. F. F. X. O'Brien, Mr. T. Lea, Dr. Wallace, Mr. .1. A. Bright, and others, and was adjourned. The House adjourned at 12.20. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack at half-past Ave o'clock.—The St. Anne and St. Mary, Manchester (Union and Benefices), Bill was read a third time and passe, and the House rose at twenty-Eve minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TITESDAY. . .

Mr. Courtney, the Deputy Speaker, took the chair at ten minutes past two o'clock. QUESTIONS.—MT. W. LONG, replying to Mr. James Ellis, said the power of levying tha police rate was vested in the County Council, and not in the Standing Joint Committee. Mr. Goscsuw, replying to Mr. Wil- liam Johnston as to whether he would postpone the date for the operation of the reduction on the tea duty until June Ist, in order to enable the retail dealers to reduce their existing stocks, said he hoped to communicate his decision to the House next day. Mr. MarrifEws replied to questions by Mr. Pickersgill as to the way in which the chaplain of Strangeways Prison, Manchester, dis- charged his duties, and as to the flogging of a violent prisoner there. Mr. W. H. SMITH, in answer to Mr. Bonsor, said the Government would take care that the general provisions of the new licensing bill should be made known before the second reading of the Budget Bill was taken. WAYS AND MEANS.—III Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. Picton strongly criticised the reduction of the tea duty by 2d. per lb.„ as not calculated to benefit the people whom Mr. Gdschen had in view. Mr. GOCHEN defended the proposal, and the resolution was agreed to. Mr. GOSCHEN intimated that he would to- morrow announce hi decision as to postponing the reduction of the duty on currants or allowing a draw- back. The South Indian Railway Purchase Bill was read a third time and passed. SUPPLY.—The House went into Committee of Supply, and the vote of £17,640 for the cost of the suppression of the slave trade and of the liberation of African cap- tives on the East coast of Africa, gave rise to consider- able discussion. The sitting was suspended at five minutes to seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WetnasnAv. The Deputy-Speaker, Mr. Courtney, took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock. SUNDAY CLOSING IN IRELAND.—The HOURS proceeded

div.head: SHOCKING MURDER OF AN OLD
div.p: SHOCKING MURDER OF AN OLD
WOMAN.

An Alresford correspondent states that Mrs. Sansom, a widow, sixty-three, was found on Tuesday in her house, her face covered with blood, and with discolora- tions upon hei throat. She received, medical attention, after which she became sufficiently conscious to relate what had happened. During the previous night she had heard noises in the lower part of the house, and went downstairs to discover the cause. There she was con- fronted by a man, who knocked her down and threaten- ed to murder her. Beyond this little or nothing is known. The unfortunate woman died on Wednesday morning from the injuries. On searching the house it was discovered that a bole large enough to admit a man had been made in a window at the back of the house. A cap, too, has been found in the room the window of which was broken. It has been identified as one worn on Monday by a young man named Wright, who is now in custody. ,

div.head: BRUIN GOES TO CHAPEL AND MAKES
div.p: BRUIN GOES TO CHAPEL AND MAKES
A SCENE.

- _ On Sunday morning, during Divine service, a huge brown bear, which had escaped from the stable of a public-house, in which its owner, a travelling showman, was located, entered a Nonconformist chapel, situated on the high road between Barnes and Mortlake. Women shrieked, and children cried, and there was a general rush for the door. Bruin, however, whose neck was or- namented with a thick chain, which somewhat impeded his progress, took things calmly, and made its way to thechoir stalls, where it lay down and surveyed the sur- roundings with apparent satisfaction. The pastor of the chapel, whose high and commodious pulpit had suddenly become occupied by several lady members of his congre- gation, desirous of ministerial protection, was in the midst of his discourse at the time of the animal's appear- ance, and had chosen for his text the words, "Be not afraid." The sermon of the reverend gentleman was brought to an abrupt termination, and from his elevated and safe position he discussed with the members of his flock remaining below, ways and means for the bear's expulsion. Fortunately, the anxiety of pastor and people was set at rest by the arrival of the owner of the animal, and Bruin was got out of the chapel with ease, and taken back to its quarters. The congregation re-assembled for general hand-shaking and mutual congratulation.
