With the consideration of the Intoxicatiia Liquors ?Ire- land) Bill. Mr. Thomas Lee moved the second reading of the Bill. Mr. MARONY, in seconding, said the measure had the support of a nearly unanimous public opinion in Ireland, Mr. PETER Mecnosim.p moved as an amend- ment, that it was inexpedient to proceed further with the consideration of a measure which proposed to place further restrictions upon an important Irish trade. The Attorxey-General for Ireland supported the second reading. The House divided on the second reading, when there were : • For the second reading Against

Majority for the bill The second reading was therefore carried. Miscxzzsxxous.—The Women's Disabilities Removal Bill was withdrawn. The report of the Committee of Ways and Means (22nd inst.) was agreed to. The Pauper Lunatic Asylums (Ireland) (Officers' Superan- nuation) Bill was read a second time. Mr. Cozens-Hardy obtained leave to introduce a Bill, which was read a first time, to remove the disabilities affecting members of county councils in respect of contracts for the supply of road materials. The Customs and Inland Revenue Bill was brought in and read a first time. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THMISDAY. The Lard Chancellor took his seat at a quarter past four o'clock. NEW PEERS.—Viscount Falmouth and Lord Napier of Magdala subscribed the roll and took their seats on suc- ceeding to their titles. THE BILLS OF Sem; Blzz.—The Lord Chancellor, in moving the second reading of this bill, said its object was to correct an interpretation of a clause in the Bill of Sale Act by which certain documents relating to com- mercial transactions in the city of Liverpool and else- where had been held to come within the Act. The bill was read a second time. MERCHANT SHIPPING ACTS AMENDMENT BLLL.—Lord HERSCHELL moved the second reading of a bill to amend the Merchant Shipping Acts relating to the load line. The bill provided for the compulsory marking of the load line at such a level below the deck line as might be approved by the Board of Trade, and that the maximum load line in salt water to which it should be lawful to load the ship should be indicated. The bill, he said, was an attempt to carry out the recommendations of the Royal Commission which reported on loss of life at sea. After some conversation, the bill was read a second time, and referred to the Committee on the General Bills. The House adjourned at 5.20 HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TatrasnAY. The Deputy Speaker (Mr. Courtney) took the chair at three o'clock. QURSTlONS.—Questions were asked with regard to the lobster fishery in Newfoundland, and also on several of the Budget proposals. Mr. Goschen saw no reason to defer the reduction in the duty on tea or on currants. THE IRISH LAND BILL.

_ The debate on Mr. Balfour's Irish Land Purchase Bill was resumed by Mr. Gladstone, who felt compelled to oppose the Bill, particularly after the remarkable declar- ation of Lord Salisbury that the plan of the Government was not intended to impose any burden on the British taxpayer. a statement so strangely at variance with the project now brought before the House. He held that they could not approach a settlement of the question so long as Ireland was under coercive law, and pointed out , that the voice of Ireland was against the Bill. lie asked the Government if they had sufficient temerity to pledge the national credit to the extent of £33,000,000 for one class in Scotland, and then to impose repayment i of the money in default upon the Scotch counties n de- fiance of the prote,stsof the majority of members. Nor did he see how they could use British credit for this purpose in face of the fact that the recorded opinion of the country at the last general election was alto- gether against such an application of funds. He dwelt then on the evils of State landlordism, which in- volved great pecuniary risks and conditions shack- ing to humanity and fraught with political dangers. Under the guise of a voluntary arrangement, in fact, the landlord, who was the stronger party, would be able to bring irresistible pressure to bear on the tenant anxious to buy his holding, and the great boon, devised for the tenant's benefit, would really be to the landlords gain, for he would get the lion's share of the spoil. He pro- tested against embarkation in such pecuniary risks, against a plan that, instead of lending itself towards the settlement of the Irish problem, plunged the country into further pecuniary conditions and political embarrassments. Mr. GOSCHEN followed, contend- ing that the Government were really anxious to give the Irish tenants a chance, and had taken such precautions that it was unlikely any burden would fall on the shoul- ders of the British taxpayers. Mr. Vesey Knox, in his maiden speech, emphatically condemned the Bill. Mr. Dillon took part in the debate, and characterised Mr. Parnell's proposal as a statesmanlike scheme from "the one living man who had the power to settle the Irish land question." At midnight the debate was adjourned.

div.head: DARING BURGLARY AT WIDNES.
div.p: DARING BURGLARY AT WIDNES.

On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Henry Hall, of Pollard-st., Liverpool, and Edward Houghton, of Charter-st., Manchester. were charged with having burglariously entered the premises of Mr. D. .T. Brookes, tailor and outfitter, Victoria-road, and stolen two overcoats, one dress coat, two vests, two pairs of trousers, one black felt hat, and one pair of 1 hoots, valued at £7. It appeared that on Sunday Mr. Brookes went from home at noon, leaving the servant in charge of tho place. The servant went to bed about nine o'clock, and about half-past ten Mr. Brookes returned home. On entering the kitchen he saw the prisoners who are two rough looking fellows, and they immedi- ately ran into the yard. Mr. Brooke followed, and saw Hall on the wall, and attempting to assist his confeder- ate to attain a similar position. A threat to blow his brains out caused Mr. Brooke's to step back, and, blow a whistle of which he was possessed; and Sergeant Laing, who was in the vicinity, arrived on the scene in time to se' t Hall drop into the road way and run away. The officer chased and captured the thief and having secured him in the police station returned to Mr./Brooke's shop and made a search of the premises, with the result that he found Houghton concealed in the outhouse. Both prisoners were wearing stolen apparel. In the kitchen were found an axe and a ha•nmer, and an examination revealed that the prisoners had effected an entrance to the premises by scaling up to the roof, and taking a few slates off, and removing the plaster. They thus gained admittance to the third storey of the build- ing. The prisoners, who are suspected of being con- cerned in other burglaries, were remanded for a week.
SUNDAY TRADING AT RUNCORN. THE HERBALIST AND HIS MEDICINE.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday,before Mr. ' C. Reynolds and G. L. Wigg, an elderly man named Thomas Wood, of Holloway-road, appeared to answer a summons charging him with having exercised his worldly calling on Sunday the 13th April, the same not being a work of charity or necessity. The defendant is a seller of various herbs and herb beer, and he had been several times warned about plying his trade on Sunday. On the date mentioned P.C.'s Woodrow and Malkin watched his premises from a place of concealment. From five o'clock, until half-past seven in the evening, they saw six men and women enter the premises, and on each occasion the defendant came to the door and looked to see if anybody was about. About half-past eight three women went in, one having a jug. The constables followed and in a room apparently fitted up to accommodate casual callers, the women were seated, each with half pint glasses of herb beer." There was also a quart jug filled with herb beer.—The defend- ant said he contended that it was medicine and not herb beer.—P.C. Woodrow said the woman who left the house was wiping her mouth (laughter) and the defendant said it was herb beer.-1 he defendant denied this. He said the woman told him her husband was ill, and she brought an ounce of castor oil. He had been in practice 35 to 40 years as a herbalist,and he had never had it doubted that he had as much right to give medicine as any other doctor in the town or to give a death certificate, and there was no law to prevent these things. It mattered not whether it was herb beer, or anything else, if it was I given for the purpose of relieving the sick. It was a work of necessity.—Mr. Reynolds: Your contention would apply to stout, beer, &c.—Defendant : If it is given with the intention of doing good to a person who is sick.—Mr. Reynolds : You have no diploma.—Defend- ant: I have no diploma from a medical faculty. I have a diploma from the medical Herbalists Society of Great Sritain.—The defendant called his daughter Sarah Woods, who said the women told her they were not well and could she give them something which would do them good. She gave them some medicike called sar- saparilla.—Mr. Reynolds said there was no doubt the defendant had committed an offence against the act and he would be fined ad., and costs 11. s. 6d., as a warning that he must not sell on a Sunday. If he came there again he would be fined more.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The annual meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday afternoon, at the Town Hall, Widnes. The chair was taken by Mr. F. H. Gossage, and there were also present Messrs. B. Brown, D. Wright, J. Midwood, J. Hargreaves, J. Houghton, G. J. Neil, S. Sadler, E. Carey, T. S. Timmis, F. C. Liddel, and J. Taylor. THE CHAIRMANSHIP. —At the commencement of the meeting, Mr. Wright proposed the re-election of Mr. Gossage as Chairman of the Board. After what was said at the last meeting, he thought they were in duty bound to ask Mr. Gossage to again take the position. Be had made a good chairman in years past,and had always been considerate to the members. Mr. Brown seconded the proposition in complimentary terms, and it was carried unanimously. COMMITTEES :—The following committees were then appointed :—Highway :—Messrs. Sadler, Houghton, Neil, Liddell, Taylor. and Dr. O'Keeffe. Gas and Water: —Messrs. B. Brmen, Wright, Timmis, Liddell, Hayes, and Taylor. Health :—Messrs. Carey, Cook, Wright, Timmii, Neil, and Hargreaves. Finance :—Messrs. Midwood, Cook, Hayes, Houghton, Hargreaves, and'Dr. O'Keeffe. General Purposes ;—The Chairman of the Board, the Chairman of Committees,andMessrs.Wright, Liddell, and Dr. O'Keeffe. Ship Canal Committee : Messrs. Gossape, Carey, and Liddell. Widnes Brine Supply Committee :—Messrs. Carey, Liddell, Sadler, and
Hayes. This was all the business before the Board.

The claim of Dowager Lawrence to be the rightful heir to the Towneley Hall estates, Lancashire, now held by Lord Norreys and othlsrs, was on Tuesday dismissed by the House of Lords as vexatious and orrirassive. A man named Rawdon, who has been several times imprisoned for threatening and otherwise annoying Lady Conyers and her daughter, was on Thursday re-com- mitted for six months for a repetition of the offence. A fire occurred on Thursday morning at the pottery works of Messrs. Thomas Forester and Sons, at Longton. The damage is estimated at £12,000. Among the pro- perty destroyed are many of the present season's moulds.

div.p: SERIOUS FIRE AT AN OIL REFINERY,

But there has been no addition to Parliamentary machinery; it goes lumbering along as it did half a century ago; a slow coach in an age of railways. Take, for instance, the present Session. There are about MO local and personal bills to be dealt with—if they can be dealt with. But why, to name one of them, should the time of the Imperial Parliament be occupied with the consideration of the clauses of the Warrington Extension, Water and Improve- bent Bill? Such a measure ought to be relegated to an English Home Rule Parliament, where it -would have a chance of receiving, what it will not receive at present, that discussion which its impor- tance demands. Then in addition to these local bills,there are over one hundred public bills brought into the House by private members, besides a score .nf measures which may be termed Government ineasures. Of these hundred and odd bills, but a fraction have any chance of becoming law, and all because the Imperial Parliament has more work to do than it can get through. It is disgraceful :to us to go fooling along in this insane fashion. 'The remedy is—sub-division of labour—four Home ' Itule Parliaments, and one Imperial Parliament.

Mr. Parnell MR. PARNELL, on Monday night, and the when the second reading of the Land Bill. Irish Land Bill was proposed in the Rouse of 'Commons, took upon himself to move its ejection; and in doing so he adduced reasons Which cannot fail to make an impression upon the people of this country, who are being made res- - Ponsible for the working of an unworkable scheme. ItaQems to us that it ought to be regarded as an Bitiot that no land purchase scheme can be success- 'nil in Ireland which is not acceptable to the people 'of Ireland. Even if the proposed machinery were .Petfect, it could not be efficiently worked unless the representatives of Ireland were prepared to. 'Work it. But it is not perfect; on the contrary, it ja so inadequate and defective that the Nationalists, 'With the prospect of having to govern Ireland Under Home Rule, would be false to themselves 'and to their supporters if they did not protest 'against its being foisted upon them. Mr. BALFOUR takes credit for limiting the risk to 40 millions, as f.that were not a very large sum when there is littlel or no prospect of its achieving the end in view. But, as Mr. PARNELL showed, the scheme, M its entirety, involves an expenditure of 166 millions. Admitting that no more than a sum of 40 millions is advanced, what does it mean? Why, that one out of four only of the tenant farmers of Ireland will get the benefit "of the bill! This is a serious statemeneto make, hut it was backed by statistics which cannot be 'Shaken. Will that settle anything? It seems to ns that it will make confusion worse confounded for it must be remembered that the three men who 'cannot have the benefit of the bill will become res- Ixinsible for the money which has been advanced to the fourth man. This will certainly breed dis- satisfaction. It puts a premium upon a strike against the scheme; and if the people of Ireland tail to keep up payments under a system which; they have not asked for, and against which they protest, it is obvious that in•the end the people of , ngland will have to pay the piper. It may be aid that the Irish landlords as a body will at any tate profit by the Bill ; but not even this can honestly ;lac said in its favour ; for, judging by 'Past experience, the money will find its way into the pockets of about one-ninth of the landlords, and these the largest and least needy. div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Several letters are again unavoidably held over.

It looks as if the battle of compensation to brewers will have to be fought over again. Mr. Goschen will have to be watched. It is something, however, to remember that the Government have been beaten once on the question, and that they can be beaten again.

--- Primrose Day is already on the decline. Some of the swell Tories of the metropolis are getting ashamed of trotting round and displaying a bunch of primrose% on the 19th April. They are beginning to think that" that sort of thing, don't you know, is all very well for the common herd, but not for us, you know."

In a year or two, there will be the same signs of " the frost" in country places. It is the usual way with devices and badges. Where are the Blue Ribbons that were, a few years ago, seen everywhere? Gone, like last year's Snow, in all except a few places. A craze has its birth, life, and death, whether it connects itself with a ribbon or a flower.

_ The Tories are actually learning a little of some- thing about Lord Beaconsfield. They have said nothing this year about "his favourite flower." It has taken a long time to dram the legend out of their heads., In a few more years, they will smile as ordinary mortals do at the absurdity of asso- ciating the primrose with the memory of the man who said he liked peacocks better than primroses, and who mocked sentiment about the flower by suggesting that it was good for a salad.

The Primrose "Knights and Dames" still talk, to be sure, about maintaining the principles which that great statesman" advocated ,• but they do not say what the principles were. Can it be that they know nothing about them.? They might, for instance, let it be known that he once said a Con- servative Government is an organised hypocrisy, and that Conservatism itself is the mule of politics which engenders nothing. What is the use of "principles" like these if they are not to be blazoned abroad on Primrose Day?

Mr. Balfour is not to have a walk over for East Manchester, for there is every prospect of Professor Munro being adopted as the Liberal candidate. The Irish Secretary was returned, in 1866, by a majority of 644 • but bigger majorities than that have since melted away under the abominations of Mr. Balfour's administration in Ireland.

The "Pall Mall Gazette" says "The bimetal- lists are obviously making progress," but the pr o- gress is not amongst the working classes. The sub- ject is beyond them; the only two metals they are familiar with are copper and silver. Their oppor- tunities of studying gold in its relation to silver are indeed small. Would they were larger

The ingenuity of the Tories in slandering their opponents at election time would be wonderful if it were not so common. If they cannot win by fair means, they never hesitate to try foul. What could be worse than the attempt to associate the Liberal candidate with the stoppage of the Paddlers' Shilling, when he had nothing more to do with it than the man in the moon P

But lies are sometimes like boomerangs in turn- ing on and striking the user. It was a lie to give it out that Mr. Beaman was opposed to extension of hotel accommodation in the Bewsey district. Not that it would have been any discredit to him if he had. But as a matter of fact he signed a memorial in favour of extending such accommoda- tion. He has been fallen foul of for a purely imaginary offence. Did Mr. John Roberts sign the memorial? Will somebody tell us that?

However, the electors have shown themselves capable of estimating the slanders at their true value; and of estimating the candidates, too, at their true value. A Liberal majority of 189 is not merely a beating—it is a thrashing. Mr. John Roberts is the rejected of North-west Ward, as he was the rejected of the North-east Ward. He will have to go on tramp to another ward; he is evidently not wanted in the two wards where he was said to be "so popular."

He was, to be sure, to carry all before him. The Radicals were shaking in their shoes, and couldn't even find a candidate. How does it look now—that boasting before the armour was put on? We grant that the Liberals are not in as good form as they might be; but they are still to be reckoned with. They know where their love lies, and can show a tanner a thing or two in the way of tanning a hide. But enough of this; the Tories needed 6a lesson—and they have got it.

Two more cases at Runcorn which point to the need of reform in the matter of Police Court costs. On Monday a seller, of herb-Peer was ordered to pay a fine of 6d. and lls, costs for selling his liquor on Sunday; and a fish-dealer was fined 6d. and 20s. costs "for cutting up ray in the market contrary to the bye-laws." In both cases, the penalty was excessive; while the ridiculous contrast between , fines and costs is Calculated to bring the law into contempt.

The " Ship Canalers " are exceedingly fond of quoits, and some of them are very clever with the 1 disc. It is an ancient game, for it is practically identical with old-time throwing of the discus. Has the " quoit " any relation to the Lancashire word" Keik," which is used when coals are tipped from a cart. Foster, in his "Life of Dickens," uses the word in a similar sense when he says :--' If you could have seen the physician and nurse quoited out into the passage?'

A so-called "Ship Canal navvy" was brought up at the Lymm Police Court, on Tuesday, and sent to goal for begging. He didn't know his way about, for he tried it on at the house of P.C. Buchanan, and got more than he bargained for. But it may well be doubted if the beggar was a navvy. The genuine navvy doesn't beg; he has no need to do; for go where he will, if he can, when he is out of work, find a mate who is in work, he is sure of a meal and a lodging. The virture of the navvy in this respect is unfailing.

The interior of Wycliffe Church, WarringtOn, has been made "beautiful exceeding," and at the re-opening services, on Sunday, the collections in aid of th 3 Renovation Fund amounted to the handsome sum of £BO. On Wednesday evening last, there was an Organ Recital; and this was followed on Thursday evening by a sermon by the Rev. C. A. Berry. The result is that the total in connection with the services now reaches £lOO 15s. id., which is in addition to over £3OO pre- viously promised.

At St. Silas's Church, Liverpool, on Monday, a wedding party of four *ere pelted by an irate female on-looker with small bags of flour. As the bags consisted of thin paper, it goes without saying that the bombardment was most effective. It is supposed that the green-eyed monster had prompted the attack. Pelting with flowers is not unusual at a wedding, but to be pelted with flour is altogether new and altogether disagreeable. The flour-girl may consider herself fortunate that she didn't get herself locked up.

April 22nd is known as Cuckoo Day in this part. of the country. True to time, the cuckoo was heard in Latchford on Tuesday. "To left and right," as Tennyson has it, "the cuckoo told his name to all the hills." The bird is welcomed as the harbinger of spring; but not by the feathered tribe, 1 for they know its trick of depositing its egg in another bird's nest. Shakespere alludes to this habit when he says: The hedge sparrow fed the cuckoo so long That it had its head bit off by its young.

The Riviera from being a Paradise threatens to become a plague spot. It is said that the air is "sick," it has been so acted upon by consump- tive visitors. Something of the same kind has happened in Australia ; there have been so many consumptive sojourneis that the dust of the cities is believed to contain a large proportion of tuber- culosa microbes. The remedy now is to go "up the country," where the air is pure and healthful. So

div.head: HE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 26, 1800.
div.p: HE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 26, 1800.
, with the Riviera ; those who are in doubt must Ileave it, and—go to Jericho.

• --- But a visit to the Holy Land is not without its drawbacks—at times. It is all very well to moon and moralise about Jerusalem; but when people happen to be made prisoners, as was the case, the other week, with Mr. and Mrs. Hill and party (of Liverpool), there is a sudden conviction that "There's no place like home." Mr. and Mrs. Hill were pounced upon by a gang of rascally Arabs when within two days' journey of Jerusalem ; and they were kept prisoners until messages were sent to the British Consul, who had to pay a stiff sum for their ransom. Such a robbery as this gives new meaning to Longfellow's lines about Folding their tents like the Arabs, And so silently steal away.

FEMALE TMLEVES WIDNBS. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday Sarah Bates (16), Sankey-st. ; Eliza Lewis (13), Waterloo-road, and Ann Jane McCann (13), Sankey-st., were charged with steal- ing four pieces of timber valued at 4d. the property of Messrs. Gasket! Deacon and Co., chemical manufacturers. On Friday morning P.C. Murray was in the works and saw the prisoners carrying away the timber. On seeing the consta6le the prisoners dropped the timber and ran away. Each of the prisoners was fined 10s., and Lewis, who had been previously convicted was warned that she would be sent to goal if she again offended against the law.—Mary Tansey, Victoria-st., and Ann Jane Gibson, Sutton's-lane, were charged with stealing 1301bs of scrap iron worth is., the property of Widnes Alkali Company. About noon, on Friday, P.C. Holbrook met the prisoners coming from the Widnes Alkali Works and as each was carrying a bag, he stopped them and found the bag con- tained scrap iron of which they could not give a satis- factory acconnt.—Gi bsort said no one had told them they should' not take the iron away.—The prisoners were committed to goal for seven days. Reynolds, and Mr. G. L. Wigg, Mr. Alfred Buck, chemist, Bridge-st., and his two daughters, Miss Clara and Miss Eva Buck, were summoned for having on the 15th inst assaulted William Henry Povey, errand boy to Messrs. Tyler and Sons. boot 'dealers, Bridge-st., There was a cross-summons charging the boy with maliciously damaging some clothing belonging to Mr. Buck.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys appeared for the complainant, and Mr. F. A. Lake represented M. Buck; —lt appeared that the, two shops had a common yard, and on the day mentioned Mr. Hill, the manager of Messrs. Tyler' ; shop, sent the boy out to shake carpets. At the same time a quantity of white linen and sheets belonging to Mr. Buck were hung on a line to' dry, and as the boy would not desist from shaking the carpets, Mr. Buck got hold' of him by the shoulders and shook him. It was also alleged that the Misses Buck dealt likewise with the-boy—Mr. Lake in cross-examination sought to show that carpet shaking was usually indulged in when Mr. Buck's linen was exposed—Without calling upen the defence the Bench dismissed the summonses for assault and Mr. Buck withdrew the summons for malicious damage. FALLING OUT OF A RAILWAY CABItIAGE.—.2I,B6B

DABL&Gigs. On Wednesday morning, the jury awarded £1,368 damages against the London and North-Western Railway Company to Mrs. Dow, widow of a Shanghai merchant, for personal injuries. She was travelling from Ruston to Liverpool, and as the train was run- ning round Runcorn curve she threw some water out of a teapot from the window, when the carriage door flew open, and she was precipitated on to the I ine.--Application to 8' ay t xecution. Yesterday morning, in the Queen's Bench. Baron Iluddleston and Justice Grantham had before them an application in the case of Dow v. The London and North-Western Railway Company. The accident happened owing to one of the new handles, which is inside as well as outside the door, being opened, and while there was no absolute evidence as to how the door was opened, the suggestion of the defendants was that the lady herself opened it in order to empty a tea- I pot, but owing to the great rush of wind, the train travelling at a high rate of speed, she fell out. The 1 Solicitor-General said he was astonished when he heard that the learned judge at the tria4Mr. Justice Denman,. would not stay execution, and he' now asked the court to grant an interim stay. Pending a motion for a stay, their lordships granted the application, the motion to be argued next week.

div.head: AT UPTON _ROOKS.
div.p: AT UPTON _ROOKS.

Before Mr. Brock and Major Gaskell, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Robert Baldwin, land:ord of the beerhouse pt,m Tavern, Upton Rocks, Widnes, was sum- moned for having, on Thursday night, the 3rd inst., per mitred card playing for money, to be carried on on his. premises. P.S. McCracken. of Itainhill, stated that on the night in question, about a quarter-past ten, he and P.C. Heaton were passing the Tavern, when they heard a noise in the tap-room. they went to the window,and the blind being too narrow they could see a portion of the room. They saw Evan Baldwin (hr tiler to defendant), Joseph. Cookson, and George Sparks sitting at a table playing a, game of cards called "Nap." They watched four games,. and heard Evan Baldwin call "2," Cookson said " Pass ;: you have done me out of a (mod •2 ' " ; and George Sparks called "3 " and got them. A voice asked "Any- one got nap yet ?" and the defendant replied "Nobody's . won Much yet." They heard i•noncy pass after each game, and witness heard a person say "You owe me a , halfpenny." After watching about ten minutes,they went in the house, and found six persons seated round the table. Thos. Baldwin was putting the pack of cards in his pocket, and Sparks took something off the table,, which the sergeant thought was money.—P.C. Heaton corroborated.—Mr. Knowles said card-playing could take place in a beerhouse, so lore" as there was no gambling on the games, and he contended that there was no direct evidence that money passed on this occasion. Be did not call aay witnesses.—Mr. Brock said the evi- dence was conclusive that money passed, and a fine of 40s. and costs, 135., was imposed. " LIZZIE'S "144TH APPEARANCE. At the St. Helens Town ' Hall, on Monday, Eliza- beth Tither, was again brought up for drunken- ness. She made her 144th appearance before the Bench, and was fined the usual 58. and costs, or seven days imprisonment. SPRING FASHIONS. spring Fashlons.-4. As W. DurroN, 16 and 18, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. CHESHIRE ALLOTMENTS. The labourers of Tarvin, Cheshire, recently peti- tioned Colonel Howard Vysa•to grant allotments to them; and they have just had their request acceded to. The land has been stamped out in plots of eighteen roods in the church field, which was selected as being most convenient for the appli- cants. The rent is fixed at the reasonable sum of ..£2 per acre, and no tehant will be permitted to sublet. REGISTER Gas.—J. S. Garland, 51, Bridge-street, War rington.—Advt.

LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. The agenda for the Lancashire County Council has been issued. It shows that the sessions will be held at Preston on May 1. The reports of a num- ber of Committees will be received, river conserva- tors appointed, and it is proposed to grant £250 on, account of costs and expenses to he incurred in opposing the Manchester City, Extension Provi- sional Order. Several other grants are proposed for asylum and other purposes. SPRING FASHIONS. Spring Raelliont'.'—.T. &W. DurroN, 16 and 18, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Adtt. • MARRIAGE OF MISS BRUNNER. Northwich was en fete on Tuesday in celebration of the wedding of Miss Grace Brunner, eldest daughter of Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., of Wilmington Old Hall, to Thomas Buckley, of Thrapstone, Northamptonshire, member of the medical profes- sion. The tradesmen of the town erected four arches in the principal streets, and the members of the Gladstone Club, of which Mr. Brunner is presi— dent, also erected a handsome arch and presented the.bride with a handsome drawing-room clock. div.head: WALKER'S BREWERY SHARES.
div.p: WALKER'S BREWERY SHARES.

The expectation that a great rush would be made for the shares in Walker's Brewery Company has been justified. So great has been the demand that the lists of applications, 'which were to have been kept open until Thursday night, were closed i on Wednesday at noon, and t is estimated that both the preference shares and the debentures.have been applied for many times over. In one London bank alone in the course of the morning ..E.86,000. was paid in over the counter as deposite money. Sir A. B. Walker is in Liverpool in good health,, and much gratified at the proof afforded of public con- fidence in the concern. _ . .

div.head: RUNCORN RU HAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RU HAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The annual meeting of this Authority was hold at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Colonel Ashton, Messrs. Mclntyre, Enowles, Lowe, Brandrethr J. Whitlow, , Hewitt, J. .Stokes Lewis, Turner,, K. Aaron, W. Whitlow, Weir, H. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linakee (assistant clerk), and J. Farrington (sanitary inspector.)—Mr. Aaron proposed that Colonel Ashton be re-elected chairman for the ensuing year, for the reason that he not only attended the meetings regularly but guided the members in the right way.—The- Rev. J. W. N. Tanner seconded the motion; and remarked that they could not have a better man to guide them, through the difficulties, dangers, and troubles of the Board.—The motion was carried unanimously, and Colonel Ashton ,on taking the chair, thanked the members for the honour they had again conferred upon him, and said he was very pleased to occupy the position. He only wished he deserved all that Mr. Aaron and Mr. Tanner had said of him.—The Sanitary Inspector reported that several nuisancesin the township of Kingsley had been remedied at a cost of £29, and the account was passed.—The Medical Officer reported that a case of typhoid fever, and a case of scarlet fever had broken out at Netherton, and he would deal with the outbreak in the osdinary course..
CAMDEN 'WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RU.NCORN..

The anniversary services in connection with this schoa were held on Sunday, in Sr. 'Paul's Chapel. Thd Rev. R.. P. Downes, the editor of " great Thoughts," occupied the pulpit both morning and evening and delivered two eloquent discourses to crowded congregations. Special music was rendered by theehoir of Str.: Paul's Chapel. assisted by the scholars from. Camderr School and formed a most enjoyable , feature of the services. The collections realised over R... 36. On Monday evening, Mr. Downes delivered a lecture in the Public.Hall„on "The greatest character in history." A.crowded.audience assembled and Mr. P. Speakman, C.C.,.oecupied the chair. In introducing the Lecturer, the Chairman, who had a cordial reception, said he was much obligeclfor the honour -conferred upon him in ask- ing him to take tho position he occupied, and remarked that it wasariew departure in Sunday. School work to engage the Public. Hall. He did not believe himself that any local religious institution should separate vory much from their places of worship, as some people were apt to say that it was for mere money-making and nothing more, but' he could assure them it was not so in that case. He had been connected with Camden Sunday School many years. There were now 570 children on the books, and all these children had gone through the class he had the privilege to teach. He impressed upon the audience that the object of Sunday Schools was to make the scholars honourable members of society, and exhorted those parents•who had the interest of their offspring at heart, to let them join, the Sunday School whose inter-sts they were rnet to, serve that night. (Applause.)—Mr. Downes then delivered his lecture in which he gave a graphic and powerful narration of the life and character of Jesus Christ. At the conclusion, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to him on the motion of Mr. Fred Norman,.seconded bst Mr. T. Simister ; and on the pro position of the Lecturer, seconded by the Rev. J. Judson a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman, Mr Downes remarking that he was glad to find that a gentle- man immersed in businesslike Mr. Speakman, had also the interest of a Sunday School at heart.

div.head: FISH DEALERS AND RUNCORN MARKEY.
div.p: FISH DEALERS AND RUNCORN MARKEY.

• At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, .Tolin Morris, a fish dealer, was summoned by the Board 'of Commissioners for acting in the market contrary to the byelaws. He was further charged with neg- lecting to comply with the reasonable diroctions of the market superintendent, Charles Dutton.--Mr. FA. Lake prosecuted, and said one of the byelawa for the regulation of the Markets stated that no person should cut up ray or skate in the market. He • under- stood that this was a large, coarse fish, from whichithere was a great deal of offal, and slime of a very offensive nature. Another byelaw was to the effect that any per- son resorting to the market, either as buyer or seller,who should neglect to comply with the reasonable directions of the superintendent of the market, should be liable, for the first offence., to a penalty not exceeding 20s. On the 15th inst., Mbrris was cutting up some ray at his stall in the market.. He was requested by Mr. Dutton tobleanse the fish in the place which has recently been specially built at considerable expense, for the purpose of cutting up. and washing and cleaning fish. There was a. bench for cutting up fish, proper slabs and water taps-for washing the fish, and tubs to receive the offal. The defendant refused to clean his fish in that place, and said he should cut up as much as he liked ondiiiistaAl. Mr.lDUtton,.and Mr. H..!. (Dice, chairman of the riieneral Purposes Committee: of the Board of Commissioners gave evidence to prove this statement.—Mr. Once said it was unpleasant to have to attend court as witnessdn a case like that.,—Mr. Reynolds : It is part of ,the privilege of doing public work, and has got to be dorfe.—The defend- ant said he was cutting the fish up on a boc lid and not on. the stall and lie put the offal in a basket on the stall. Re alleged that the summonses were taken, out through spitc.—flecalled Mr. Hankinson who turnedout a witness for the prosecution, and Mr. Reynolds said. the case was very cleat, and it was ridiculous to talkabout spite.— Mr.. Lake said he only asked for a nominal penalty as it was the first case.—The defendant wasordered to pay ed. and costs in each case • is. Od.—The defendant said he would go to gaol before he would pay the money.

div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMIUSSIONERS.

A special meeting of this Board was held, on Monday evening, at the Town Hell. Mr. J. W. Ligh churn presided and there were present Messrs. Fisher, W. Mellor, E. Timmins, W.. llankinson, White, F'. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secre- tary.) THE NEW RATE.. On the proposition of Mr. E. 'raison, seconded by Mr. W. Fisher, the seal of the Board affiaod to a general dis- trict rate of 2s. 2d. in the £ for th& year ending March 25th next. •

THE 81115 CANAL AND. SEWERAGE. The members discussed in committee, a scheme for conveying the sewage of the. district under the Ship Canal, into the river Mersey. On resuming, the Chair-; man mentioned that according to section 11 of the I Manchester Ship Canal Act, which stated that the Ship. Canal Company" shall compensate the Commissioners for any increased expense to be incurred by theman maintaining and working, their present sewers, and the amount of such compensationtif not agreed between the company and the Commissioners, shall be settled by the Local Government Board,. on the application of either party." The Chairman said the Commissioners were. giving up their claim fbr compensation upon the. under- standing that the Ship Canal Company undertook the maintenance of the sewers themselves. If the company had given the Commissioners compensation, they would probably have offered the compensation in a lump. stun.. —Mr. Timmins 'thought the Commissioners shbuld not impedsthe progress of the company and he proposed that the following resolutions be passed :--" That this Board hereby approves the plans of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, dated 26th Febrivoy„ 1893, a the °Walls and works for conveying the sewage of the sanitary district under the Ship Canal and the river Mersey, subject to such modifications as have been agreed upon and which are indicated in the specifi- cation and to be shown upon the detail drawings to be submitted by the Company's engineer. That the following offers of the Manchester Ship Canal Company be accepted, subject to their being em- bodied in an agreement. (a.) The said Company to undertake the maintaining and working of the proposed nevr intercepting sewer and outfalls, in lieu of compensation to be given to the Commissioners as pre- scribed by section 75. sub-section 11, of the Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1885. (b) If it should hereafter be found that any sandbank will interfere with the proper flow of the sewage into the deep, so as to cause a nuis- ance, the said company undertake at the request of the Commissioners to make a second outfall from the syphon under the Ship Canal to some point between the position shown on the said plan and a point to be determined by Mr. Newton and shown on a plan to be annexed to the agrecinent."—The resolutions were seconded by Mr. Fisher and carried,—lt was further resolved, on the
motion of Mr. Imison, seconded by Mr. Fisher, that the reports and letters of Mr. Newton on this matter be entered on the minutes.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

POOR RATES IN RUNCORN DISTRICT. The Runcorn magistrates on Monday sanctioned the levying of a poor rate of is. in the £ for the respective townships of Clifton, Sutton, and Norton, and of is. Id. in the £ for Halton.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. At the Runcorn Police Court, on Wolnesday, before Mr. G. L. Davies, Thomas Carr was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for drunkenness, and on Thursday, before Major Hazlehurst, a Harpist named Bamphlin was fineda simi-

lar amount for an offence of a like nature. RUNCORN AND DISTRICT rEERS* ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY. An appropriation meeting was held on Tuesday even- ing, in the offices of Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, solicitor. Mr. J. J Speakman presided. The ballot resulted in No. 351 being drawn, and as there were no shares alloted to that number, the appropriation reverts to the society

according to rule. _ DRAMATIC LICENSE FOR RUNCORN PUBLIC HALL. A special Sessions was held at Runcorn Police C )urt, on Monday, for the purpose of hearing an application fora dramatic license to the Public Hall. The magis- trates on the Bench were Messrs. C. Reynolds, H. Rey- nolds, G. L. Davies, and G. L. Wigg. Mr. Arthur Salkeld made the application, and Superintendent Large having no objections, the license to perform stage plays was granted. Messrs. W. Whittaker and Thomas Brewer became sureties for the propercarrying out of the terms of the license.

MARRIAGE OF MISS WRIGHT, OF RUNCORN. On Tuesday morning, at Runcorn Parish Church, Miss Martha Timmins Wright, second daughter of Mr. Robert Wright, of Greenway-road, Runcorn, was married to Mr. Albert Wm. Guest, third son of Mr. Wm. Guest, of The Poplars, Relsby. The Rev. A. Maitland Wood, vicar, performed the ceremony. The bridesmaids were —Misses Fanny and Susie Wright (sisters of the bride), and Mr. Arthur Geo. Guest, brother of the bridegroom, officiated as best man. The bride was given away by her father. The happy couple were the recipients of many valuable presents ; and during the morning left for Rhyl. where they spend the honeymoon.

. MARRIAGE OF Miss lAIISON, OF RUNCORN. Runcorn Parish Church was on Wednesdy afternoon well filled by an audience gathered to witness the mar- riage of Miss Imison, eldest daughter of the late Mr. John lmison, to the Rev. William Fielding, 8.A., of St. Catherine's College, Cambridge. curate of Aston-by- Sutton. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, the vicar, assisted hy the Rev. E. Mars- den, vicar of Aston. The bride, who was attended by Miss Amelia Imison (sister), Miss Dorothy Cunningham and Miss Kathleen Imison (neices), as bridesmaids, and she was given away by Mr. Edwin Imison, her brother. Mr. Smith, of Blackburn officiated as best man. Amongst the numerous and costly presents, was a handsome ladies' bag given by the Sunday school teachers of the National Schools, where Miss Imison was held in high esteem as a superintendent. During the afternoon the happy couple departed for Oxford en route for the Chan- nel Islands, where they will spend the honeymoon:

• WIDNES DIVISION CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION. The annual meeting of this association was held in the Widnes Conservative Club on Monday evening, presided over by Mr. W. J. Stewart. There was a good attend- ance. A telegram was read from Mr. T. C. Edwards- Moss, M.P., who was unable to be present owing to the illness of his father. On the motion of the Chairman, the following resolution was unanimously adopted :—" That this meeting desires to express its regret at hearingof the serious illness of Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss, and wishes to convey its heartfelt sympathy with Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., and other members of the family in their great anxiety." The rules of the association having been adopted, the following gentlemen were elected officers for the ensuing year :—President, the Right Hon. the Marquis of Salisbury; vice-presidents, Messrs. Gilbert Winter Moss, A. Fletcher, E. Banner, G. H. Robinson, G. l'ilkington, and Sir Andrew B. Walker, treasurer, Major W. Hall Walker; chairman, Mr. W. J. Stewart; and members of the Executive Committee, Messrs. Husband, White, Lewis, iGorst, Charles, and Rimmer. A vote of thanks haying been accorded to Mr, W. B. Woodnorth, the registration agent for the division, and to the Chairman for presiding, the meeting ended. In reply to the communication asking him to accept position of president to the club, Lord Salisbury thus replies to Mr. Stewart, the chairman of Committee.— "Dear Sir.—l am very much flattered by the proposal which you have sent to me that I should become the president of the Conservative Association of the Widnes division, which has been recently organized. I am afraid it is not in my power to take any practical part in your operations; but I shall have great pleasure in accepting the honour which you have been kind, enough to offer me." PRESENTATION AT GOSSAGE'S WORKS, WIDNES. On Tuesday the employers of Messrs. Gossage and Sons, of Widnes'. to the number of 700, assembled in the cutting and packing room of the works, for the purpose of making a presentation to Mr. and Mrs. E. F. Gossage in cornmemmation of their marriage. The room had been decorated for the occasion. The presents consisted of a handsome timepiece, adorned with. emboosed scene from " Hamlet " ; case of carvers complete, with ivory handles and sterling silver mounts ; and a cabinet of cutlery containing tone dozen ot each kind. The coin- , bined monogram of Mr. and Mrs. Gossage appeared on a ' plate on the cutlery cabinet, and on the plate on the case of carvers. On the timepiece was engraved "Presented to Mr. and Mrs. E. F. Gossage upon the occasion of their marriage, by the employes of Messrs. Gossage and Sens with best wishes for their future welfare." Mr. W. Hartland made the presentation on behalf of the men, and expressed a hope that Mr. E. F. Gossage would keep the name of the Gossage family as high in the esteem of the workpeople and the people of Widnes as it stood at the present time.—Mr. E. F. Gossage thanked the employes of the firm both at the Widnes Works and at Blackstock-st., Liverpool, for the presents, and accepted them as a token of good wishes towards him- self and Mrs. Gossage.—Mr. W. Jackson, in a speech, referred to the liberality of the firm in supporting local institutions and said to their employes they were always fair and considerate. As an evithince of this he might state that since the works started there had never been a strike amongst the men. All their differences had been amicably settled and he thought Mr. Ernest Gossage would follow in the steps of his father.—Mr. F. H. Gos- sage said he was sorry Mr. Timmis was not present to hear the elogistic remarks. He was glad they were able to give their workpeople as much work each day as they could well get through,and that the firm had always beep able to place confidence in the men to be present at their work when required. The proceedings then. terminated,

div.head: ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE CLASS, RUNCORN.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE CLASS, RUNCORN.

Under the auspices: ,of St. John's Ambulance - Association Jr., McDougall has recenbly 'Conducted a class of over 30 students, with the object of impart- ing sufficient knowle,lgo to enable them to render first aid to the injured. Dr. McDougall, who had the assistance of Dr. Clifford, delivered a series of highly interesting- lectures, combined with practical in- struction in the manner of dressing broken bones, and other wounds. In the ranks of the students were in- chided Mr. Superintendent Large and Inspector Bowyer, and nearly the whole of the constables. The examina- tion took place on Friday evening last, Dr. Lees, of Chester,being the examiner. At the conclusion of the pro- ceedings, Dr. Lees spoke in the highest terms of apprecia- tion of the intelligent and efficient manner in which the members of the class had distinguished themselves, es- pecially in the practical part of the work, and remarked that it must have been very gratifying' to Dr. McDougall to give lectures to so intelligent a body of students. He had examined hundreds of classes, but none had given him greater pleasure and none had displayed more efficiency than the class he had had betere him that day, and he felt surethat under the tuition of the same lec- turer the member* would not only win certificates and badges but would ultimately . obtain the St. Jetin's Am- bulance Medal.—ln illustration of the practical utility of the instruction given, it may beinentioned that valuable aid was a few weeks ago rendered to a football Wayer, who had broken his leg, by Mr. Harry Wright and P.C. Woodrow. On Saturday night last, Inspector BoWyer found a man named George Seyinour,of Mason-st., lying helplessly on the pavement in Regent-se. Be made an , examination and discoveredthat the man was suffering from a dislocated ankle and a fractured leg, the bone below the knee being broken. With the assistance of P.C. Woodrow, the Inspector bandaged the injured , limb and,then conveyed him to Dr. McDougall's surgery on the police ambulance cart. The doctor expressed his appreciation of the manner in which the bandaging had been done, and said the injured man had been saved a compound fracture and six or seven weeks in bed in consequence. The examiner'areport was received yesterday from St. John's Association,. and shows that 26 out of 29' students have passed, a very gratifying percentage. The success- full members of the class who are awarded certitPates and • badges. are :,--Soperintendent Large, Inspector Bowyer, P.S. Woolley, P.C's. Boyle, Brew,, Bullock, Crowder, Dutton, Fryer, Jackson, Woodrow, liaise ; Messrs. J. Clare, W.Collier, W. Challiss, D. Edwards, W. Garrett; H. W. Handley, E. Newton, T. Page. H. Page, H. Wright, Thos,. Pierpoint, C. Woolley, W. Wright, and C. Manning.

div.head: RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN.

The adjourned vestry meeting of the township of Runcorn wa4 held on Thursday night, in Bethesda Lecture Hall.. Mr. E. Imison presided,, and there were present Messrs. W. Handley, H. Coleburn, J. Littler, W. Jones, and W. Sutton (s.ssistant over- seer).

TER BURIAL BOARD. Mr. W. Jones (assistant secretary to the Burial Board), read the annual financial statement of the Burial Board. The year was. commenced with a balance in hand on general account of £lO6 4s. id.; sinking fund account, £5 10s. Eld.; and interment fees, £377 17s. ;.graveburial certificates, £l.B 16s. 4.d.; sale of graves £1.195. 6d. ; rent of field, £l7 Us. ; cash from overseers general account, £6O ;sinking fund account, £l2O ;.dividends on t onsols, £25,; sale of consols, £349; total, £1,087 3s. sd. The expenditure included the following items :—interest on mortgages, £224 15s. 10d. ; salaries and wages £192 13s. Od. ; maintenance and repairs £l7 185. Od. ; rates, taxes, and tithes, £ll 16s. Od. ; and mortgages paid off, L5OO. There was a balance in hand of £lO4 6s. 11d.— Mr. Handley proposed the adoption of the.accounts, and remarked that it was satisfactory to find that the debt on the Cemetery was £5OO less than it was last year.— Mr. Mellor seconded the motion, which was carried. THE CHURCH VESTRY AND THE CHARITIES. Mr. Sutton reported that at the last meeting a resolu- tion was.passed, requesting the trusteesof the endowed and parochial charities to furnish a copy of the accounts to that meeting. Since then the Vicar had presented the accounts of the Rigby, Alcock, and other charities, to the church vestry, and they were entered upon the church minutabook. Mr. Fisher, secretary and.treasurer to the Liptrot Charity, wrote stating that the trustees had perused the terms of that charity, and, were of opinion that the charity was not parochial in the sense of the Act of 1855, and that they were not bound to forward their accounts to the churchwardens. Mr.Fishei pointed out that the Act of 1855 only required an account to be sent to the churchwardens and not to the overseers.— Mr.. Handley said it was quite clear from his reading of the Act, that these accounts ought to have been pro- duced, in accordance with statute, at the first vestry meeting after the 25th March. Nothing could be clearer; than, the terms of the Act of Parliament with regard to 1 these charities. The Vicar, when he produced the ac- counts to the church vestry, appeared to have overlooked , the fact that they were asked to be produced at the meet- ing that night, seeing they were not produced at the first vestry meeting. The accounts had, however, been produced; there was no, getting behind that f act— but, from what transpired at the church vestry, it ap- peared to be a sort of privileged meeting it being con- vened by the churchwardens for the consideration of church business, as proved by the fact that certain per- sons were asked to retire after a portion of the busineas had been transacted. He did not draw attention to this in any contentious spirit, becawe he had not been actu- ated by that spirit in drawing attention to these chari- ties. If their vestry Clerk entered the accounts on the minute book of Ilia township so that the ratepayers could have access to it, then the spirit of the Act of Parliament would be fulfilled. It would be very incon- venient for people to. go to the Vicar and ask for the production of the chierch.minute book, which they would be entitled to do at any time they chose. With regard to the Liptrot Charity. he did not know the foundation of the trustees. opinion that they were not hound to fur- nish an account to the vestry. It was quite clear that no charities were excepted by the Act, and the Liptrot Charity appeared as a public charity in the returns pub- lished by the. Charity Commissioners. Mr. Fisher stated in his letter that the trustees had authorised him to allow any ratepayer to see the accounts, but Mr. Handley thought the Act of Parliament contemplated that the proper place to see them was in the vestry or township minute book. He proposed that the assistant overseer be requested to copy from, the churchwardens' minute book into the township minute book the charity accounts submitted to the Church vestry, and that he send a communication to Mr. Fisher point- ing out that the Liptrot Charity appeared in the list of public Charities issued by the Commissioners, and requesting him to send an account to the vestry meeting held in June.—Assistant Overseer : It will be no use.— Mr. Handley: I dare say not, but still I hope it will Let us give them credit for wishing to comply with the Act. —Mr. Coleburn seconded the resolutidh. He saw from the report of the Church Vestry that one prominent member questioned the right to hold a vestry meeting in that building at au, which was tantamount to setting at

defiance the order issued by the Local Government Board. He was glad to see that the Vicar had the good sense to continue the meeting. Referring to the fact that at a certain point Dissenters were asked to retire, he contended that Dissenters were parishioners, and as parishioners had a right to take part and interfere in church matters, as any persons who called themselves- , "-Chairch folks." He thought it was a great insult, "to Wesleyans especially, to be requested to retire. Mellor said church people did not go to Dis- senters places of worship and interfere with their business. Any business in connection with a parti- cular church ought to be conducted by the people who attended that particular church. He quite approved of the charity accounts being made public, but he contended that the church accounts were not a public matter.—Mr. Handley said no outsider wished to meddle in church affairs.—Mr. Mellor said Mr. Cole- burn's remares were calculated to lead to a different opinion—Mr. Cpleburn said every parishioner hada right to attend the Parish Church Vestry, and take part in the public business relating to the church, and leave when the private business catne on.—Mr. Mellor: Dissenters were not asked to retire until the finances of the church were brought forward .—Mr.Littler said there was only one person who objected to meeting in Bethesda and he did not receive any support from the meeting.—The Chairman said he did not think they were justified in reviewing the proceedings of a meeting held purely for church pur- poses, and Mr.Coleburn's objection would have come with greater force at the meeting, to which he referred. At the time the ratepayers contributed to the church through a rate, they had a right to take part in the proceed- ings of the church, but there was now no church rate, and the funds were provided solely by the people who attended the church; and it seemed to him not fair and reasonable that outsiders should interfere with the disposal of a fund to which they had not contributed anything.—A question was asked whether the Vicar should not be consulted be- fore the charities' accounts were copied into the town- ship book, and the Assistant-Overseer replied that there was no need to consult the Vicar in the matter at all. It was public property. So far as he was concerned, he thought this resolution was not required. The accounts were in one public book, and any ratepayer could see them.—During further discussion, it transpired that the church 'minute book had come into the hands of the Assistant-Overseer by accident, and that the Vicar was absent from home and could not be consulted, and Mr. Mellor moved and Mr. Littler seconded w resolu- tion that the question with regard to copying the charhy amounts into the township bock be deferred until the June meeting. Under the cir- cumstances, Mr_ Handley accepted this amendment, which was carried.—Mr Handley then proposed his reso- lution with regard to the Liptrot Charity .—Mr. Mellor : Who are the trustees?—Mr. Sutton : The ViCRT, Dr. Preston, Mr. Lake, Mr. G. Timmins, and Mr. J. Brund- rit.—Mr. Handley: They are all estimable men, and well qualified to carry out the terms of the Trust, and I am sure will • do, to the best of their ability.—Mr. Handley then read the scheme of the Liptrot Charity,from an official copy in his possession, and said there was nothing to con eey the idea that the charity was outside the term of the Act of Parliament. He remarked, in answer to. Mr. Coleburn, that he had no reason to doubt that the funds had been expended rightly.—Mr. Coleburn seconded the motion.—The Chair- man said he thought the resolution a reasonable one and observed that Mr. Handle/ had produced some most interesting information with regard to these charities, and they owed him a debt of gra' itude, for, the trouble he had taken in bringing torward this question of charities. He had not been actuated by any doubt that the money was misappropriated or misapplied in any way ; he had merely contended for the accounts to be made public and to be presented and kept in a proper place. It appeared to hint that it would ba much better it official records were kept of these things, whether it was in the township book or the church vestry minuto book was not for him to say.—The motion was carried unanimously and a vote of thanks to the chairman- con- cluded the proceedings.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

AMICILT ON A CONSTABLE. On Thursday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, laboucer named George . McCabe was brought up on a charge of drunkenness. He was also charged with hav- ing assaulted Constable Cooper. The officer apprehended prisoner an the first charge, and as he was taking him to the Bridewell prisoner became violent and com- mitted the assault. The magistrates ordered him to pay a fine of 10s. and costs, or to go to prison for a fortnight in default. A PIPE AS A MEANS OF ATTRACTION. A. young woman of questionable chavacter, named Ellen McCormick, was before the Warrington magistrates on Monday, charged with having been drunk in Butter- market-st., on Saturday night. —P.C. Monaghan, who proved the case, said that when he took the prisoner into custody she was smoking a clay pipe.—Alderman Harrison (to the prisoner) : Are you an habitual smoker? —Prisoner: No, sir.—Alderman Harrison: I should think not: I should think a clay pipe in your mouth would not add to your psrsonal appearance.—The Chief Constable remarked that the pipe was used as an attrac- tion. The prisoner was one of the worst of her class.— The Bench sent her to gaol forl4 days,Svith hard labour.

Victoria-road, under the license held by her late husband; 1 and William 011agan was granted similar permission to 1 sellat the Crown Vaults, Widnes, recently occupied by Rebecca Hagan. . . Scßoot. BOARD CASES.-Mr. G. H. Danby, Clerk to Widnes School Board, prosecuted a number of parents for not sending their children regularly to scho9l. In several cases attendance orders were made and in others, the usual penalty of ss. was imposed. ASSAULTS.—Ann Curchin, James Weir, and Margaret Weir, all of South-st., were summoned for assaulting Ann Sant, of the same neighbourhood. Mr. Husband appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Knowjes defended. The solici- tors had arranged that the summons against the defend- ants Weir should be withdrawn, and that Curchin should plead guilty. It appeared that the parties were interested in a case at the court on Thursday last, and in cotese- , quence of the evidence by the Mrs. Sant's husband the ' defendants lost the day. Afterwards whilst Mrs. Sant I t was hanging clothes, Mrs. Curchin assaulted her —Mrs. ' Knowles said she allowed her temper to overcome her.— She was fined 10s, and costs 7s. 6cl. _ _ . _

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was inflicted upon the following :—Catherine Doyle, Oxford-st.; Michael Glynn, Sankey-st.; Margaret McCann, Sankey-st. ; John Fowler, Palm-st. ; William Brindley, Carlile Terrace; Thomas Cunningham, Derby- road; John Cleary, Lunt's Heath; Margaret Walsh, Church-st. ; and Mary Walsh, Bold. Patrick Quinn, of Sankey-st., was fined 7s. 6d. and costs.—Bridget Rigby, 28, Oxford-st. : Margaret McCann, Sankey-st. • Mary Ann Glynn, Sankey-st. •, and Ellen Hunt, Nelson-st., were each charged with committing breaches of the peace and were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months. Doo r LARGE.—Richard Howling Nest Bank-st., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing his dog to be at large umnuzzled. HIGHWAY Oasrancrios.—Richard Eden, John Poole, and Edward Griffiths, draymen, to Messrs. Greenall Whitley, and Co., Brewers, St. Helens, were summoned for having on the 11th inst., obstructed Farrant-St., Widnes, by allowing their drays to remain there an un- reasonable time. Each defendant was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. CHIMNIES ON FIRE.—For allowing the chimney of their respective dwellings to be on fire, Edward Taylor, Mersey-road; and Win. Snelson, 58; West-st., were each fined Is. and costs.

div.head: Nu DE PRISONER'S MIDNIGHT WALK.
div.p: A Nu DE PRISONER'S MIDNIGHT WALK.

A rather excitable man, who gave the name of Charles Robinson, was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Monday on a charge of drunkenness. The case was proved by P.C. Hollingworth, who told the magistrates that on Sunday night he was called by the-landlord of a lodging-house in Old-road to eject the prisoner from the house. Prisoner had been lodging there for the past fortnight, and on Sur.day night he wen in drunk. With difficulty he was persuaded to go to bed, but was no sooner in the room than he began breaking the bed to pieces. When the officer came prisoner ran out with no clothes on into the street, and shouted "murder." He could not be induced to dress himself, and was at last taken to the police station in a nude condition. Prisoner was sent to jail for a month, with hard labour. ROBBING AN EMPLOYER. The Warrington magistrates on Monday had before them a case in which a young man, of respectable ap- pearance, named Frederick Falshaw, was charged with robbing his employer. Prisoner is a glasscutter, and has been lodging in -Nicholson-st. He has been employed by Mr. Pemberton, ef Market-place, and it was alleged against him that on the 19th inst. he stole a plate of silvered glass, and five plates of sheet glass; also, on the 15th inst., a quantity of gilt moulding, and, further, at divers times during the past four months, 32 paint brushes, a quantity of mixed paints, varnish, mouldings, gas burners, &c. During the past few months a variety of goods had been missed from the prosecu- tor's shop, hut no suspicion attached to the accused, until one day last week lie gave some evasive and un- satisfactory replies to inquiries respecting some mould- ings and glass he was cutting. A watch was set, with the result that on Saturday the prisoner was apprehended. At his lodgings a numerous assortment of articles, be- longing to the prosecutor, were discovered, as well as a bunch of keys. one of which fitted Mr. Pemberton's shop door.—The Mayor said the Bench were of cpinion that it was a very had case indeed. The prisoner had been trusted implicitly by his master, and had rewarded him by roboing him of everything he could get hold of. He would have to go to prison for thrce months on each charge—nine months' hard labour in all.

div.head: MINOIt CASES.
div.p: MINOIt CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATIIRDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett and L. Vbisey. MiseELLANrous.—William Jones, a navvy, was fined ss. and costs for drunkenness, and Catherine Taylor, for having been guilty of improper behaviour, in Scotland- road, was sent to prison for a fortnight. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb) and

Alderman Harrison. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—James Simpson, Mersey-st. Saturday night, fined ss. including costs; James Coulson, Wit- derspool-road, SundAy morning, fined ss.includin,, costs; Henry Percy, Arpley-st., Sunday morning, fined 55. in- cluding costs ; Margaret Smith, Buttermarket-st., Sun- day night. committed for 14 days' hard latour ; Joseph Hindle, Irlarn-st., Sunday night,fined ss. including costs; and Elizabeth Ellen Fleming, Buttermarket-St., 12th April, committed for one month with hard labour. ATTEMPTING A RESCUE.—Thomas Carrow, navvyi Stockton Heath, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-St., on Sunday night ; and Walter Cresey was charged with having attempted to rescue Carrow from the custody of the police. Con- stables Bell and Cooper were taking the prisoner Carrow to the Bridewell. when they were stopped by Cresey, who attempted to rescue his companion.—Prisoners pleaded guilty, and were discharged -on payment of a fine of 55., including costs, each. A NEWSBOY IN TROUBLE.—A newsboy named William Spencer was fined Is. for shouting newspapers in the streets on Sunday, the 13th inst. TEE MUZZLING ONDER.--desse Plant, forge labourer, Aikin-st., was summoned for having allowed his dog to be unmuzzled on the 7th April.—The Bench ordered him to pay a fine of 205., including costs. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. Robert Garnett and B. M.

Crosfield. DRITICKENNESS.—Thomas Burke (32), labourer, Old- road, Latchford, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk in Mersey-street, on Monday evening. Jane Water- worth (21), described as an imbecile, living in Back Stamford-street, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Buttermarket-street, on the previous night. The Bench ordered her to be detained for 24 hours and then liberated on her promise to return to her aunt's house. Mr. Garnett recommended the girl to attend some place of worship, and to get to know the minister's wife, who would, he said, no doubt take an interest in the prisoner's welfare. ScHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES. The following par- ents were summoned -for failing to send their children regularly to school :—P. Kilmarten, labourer, Latch- ford, -fined 2s. 6d. ; William Roylance, wire drawer, Longford-street, ss. ; William Johnson, filecutter, Orford- lane, ss. ; Thomas Healey, labourer, Haydock-street, 55.; Michael Gleeson, labourer, Dutton-street, 2s. 6d. ; Thomas Percival, fnrgeman, General-street, 25. 6d.; John Robinson, tanner/Nelson-street, ss. ; Patrick Dolly, labourer, Winwick-street, ss. ; and Thomas Barton, labourer, Hardy-street, fined 45., being is. each for four children. TEURSDAY.—Before Majors.. Pickmere and Litton, and
Captaln Ridgeway.

DRUNICENNESS.—Thomas Jones and James Smith were brought up for this offence, and were each lined ss. and COStS. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gnrnall. VAGRANCY.—James and Annie Pickett, husband and wife, and Winifred Burke, were brought up in custody on a charge of having been found sleeping in a straw shed in Folly-lane, on the same morning. The two former were discharged with a caution, and Burke was sent to prison for a month, without hard labour. CHARGES OF ASSAULT.—WiIIiam ROWSO/1 was vm- moned for having assaulted Joseph Birchall, on the 19th inst., and James SUtCliffe was summoned for having assaulted Bodelia Birchall, on the same date. Mr. P Davies appeared for the defence. Both cases were dis- missed.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. P. Stubs. DRUNKENNESS.—Edward McClare, a labourer, was charged with being drunk at Golborne, On the 20th inst., and was committed to prison for seven days in default of paying a fine of ss. and costs.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds, Mr. H. Reynolds, and Mr. G. L. Wigg. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon each of the following : William Smith, Thomas Bevan, James Hales, Edward Kelly, John Perrin, Henry Oldham, and Alexander John- son. OPERATIC ARTISTES Commirren.—Superintendent Large said last Monday Joseph Hudson and Edwin Worth,voca- lists in O'Beirne's Opera Company. were each fined ss. and costs, for falsely representing themselves to be bond fide travellers at the Castle Hotel, Halton, on Good Fri- day. The case was heard in their absence, and Mr. Bur- ton appeared for the defendants. The money had not been remitted, and he (Mr. Large) asked for a commit- ment to enforce payment of the penalty.—The magis- trates signed the necessary cornmital. ROBBERY BY A Seiton.—Thomas Davey, a young sailor, was charged with stealing two coats, a pair of trousers, two vests, four shirts, and a pair of overalls, value 135., the property of Henry Forster. The pri- soner was also charged with stealing a suit of oilskins, worth 1554 the property of Thomas Quirks. The articles were stol.n from a ship in the docks, and on Sunday P.C. Woodrow apprehended the prisoner, as he was leaving the tidal basin in a schooner. He was then wearing some of the stolen articles, and the remainder were found in his bunk.—The prisoner was remanded for a week, in order that inquiries might be made into his antecedents BEGGING.—WiIIiam Gibbons, a young man, was sen- tenced to seven days' hard labour, for begging, on Saturday night.
