Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches rlayed. on Saturday must be sent to the head office. Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY. Simms v. FRODSHAM.—This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday last. Sutton won by three tries and four minors to one minor. This completes Sutton's list of card fixtures. They have played 25 matcnes, won 18, lost 5, drawn 2. Scored 24 goals, 39 tries, 8.8 minors, against 4 goals, 9 tries, and 22 minors. WARRINGTON " A " T. STOCKPORT "A."—This return fixture was played on the Wilderspool enclosure on Satur- day, before a capital assemblage of onlookers. Stock- port winning the toss, Warrington commenced, and for some period the play was monopolized by the forwards at midfield, until Webster receiving a capital pass from Rowe kicked into the visitors' territory. The visitors indulged in ROM smart passing, but Ashton making his mark drove them back with a lofty punt to the quarter flag, where some pretty transfers between Rowe, Mather, and Heesom brought severe pressure to bear on their opponents. Goodall and Heathc.ote were equal to the occasion, however, getting the ball well out of danger, and after some tali kicking by Lally, Knowles, and Bur- rows for their respective sides, a minor was forced by a drop at goal by Webster. Following the drop out, Mather got grandly away and passed to Heesom, but the latter's pass was missed, and a grand chance lost. Afterwards, Webster by a run and kick gained a lot of ground, and from somescrimmaging in the Stockport nuarters,Mather gave Heesom a chance, which the last-named was not slow to avail himself of, and a capital try resulted. The drop out found Stockport by some smart play attacking strongly, and after Holmes had floored Naylor, a capital drop by Burrows resulted in a goal. After this reverse, the home team, who had played in lazy fashion, wakened up, and Ashton passed wide out t.. Ile ,soin, but nothing came of it. Fletcher, Downs, and Board, now shone in a long dribble, and Boscow was tackled at the quarter flag. A kick took the ball furtherinto Warrington lines, where Mather receiving from Rowe dashed away in fine style, but slipped after clearing all opposition. Rowe did the trick directly afterwards, no goal being kicked. Soon afterwards Isherwood, Molyneaux, Nield, and Ashton dribbled finely, and the last-named getting possession, ran over grandly, from which Heesom landed a goal. Half-time was now signalled, and after a brief rest the ball was restarted. After some quick loose play, Welsby, Knowles, and Wilkins, headed a rush well into their opponents' territory, where Welsby, made a good bid for a try after a smart run. Stockport were now severely pressed, but the ball was taken in the loose to midfield,and after it had bobbed about from one to another, Webster finally secured ahd getting away from two or three oppo- nents, got a grand try behind the posts, from which Heesom kicked a goal. The kick off was followed by a splendid rush, in which Isherwood, Kaowles, Molyneux, and Ashton were very prominent. This was somewhat neutralized be a rtin up the right by Brookes, and being supplemented with a dribble, in which Mason, Goodall, and Kitchen were notable, the outlook see.ned ominous, until Webster sailed round and saved splendidly to mid- field. Isherwood subsequently got away from a miskick, but was promptly tackled, and then ensued some very fast play. Goodall cleverly tackled Webster on the line, where after some scrimmaging Mather doged over, no goal resulting. Very soon after this Bowe made a final run, and from a pack the same player passed to Mather, who secured his second try, which Heesom converted. As the score indicates, the visitors were having all the worst of it, and after a dashing piece of play by Nield, the enthusiasm of those present was fairly roused by a magnificent left foot drop by Webster, which sent the ball sailing over the bar. From this point the game tamed down a lot, but from a pass by fleathcote. Brookes was not stopped until he got well in Warrington quarters. Here a very fine piece of play by Knowles, who dribbled from a pack and screwed right across the field to Webster, enabled the latter to make a long run, and from a kick Ashton, who had followed well up, almostscored, Goodall saving in the nick of time, the final score being Warring- ton 4-3-3 to 1-0-1. Teams: Warrington : Botcow, back ; Lally, Heesom, and Webster, threequarter-backs; Rowe and Mather, half-basks; Nield, Molyneux, Isher- wood, Welsby, Knowles, Holmes, Wilkins, Barnes, and Ashton (captain), forwards. Stockport: Goodall, hack; Brookes, Burrows. ani Downs, threequarter-backs ; Naylor and Heathcote, half-backs ; Mason, Downs, Downs, Beard, Morley, Fletcher, Goodall, Kitchin, and Ingram, forwards. WARRINGTON v. STOCKPORT.

"A grand game" was the general verdict of the large crowd which assembled at Dale Green, Stockport, on Saturday, when the above clubs met in the return engagement. Only a fortnight had elapsed since the clubs first met, Warrington on that occasion winning by one goal and three tries to nil. For the present occa- sion Warrington placed astrong team in the field. There were however not wanting a few who pinned their faith on the Cheshire men, and it was argued, and argued rightly, that as they were playing on theit own ground, this point was one half towards securing a victory.

The Stockport men mustered strongly for the occasion, and splendid weather prevailing, some five thousand people were present when Fair. Turner set the oval in motion against a slight breeze. The attempt to respond by Ritson was baffled by the 'quick following up of the Warrington forwards, when from a pack Antrobus stole away, and although promptly collared, he passed across to Lawless, who kicked to Massey, the last-named apply- ing the saving clause. A minor in less than a half a minute and against a stiff breeze was evidently too much for the homesters for after Barnes had met the drop out a judicious kick by Parrott. was ably seconded by a smart rush of the home forwards, but the danger was only of a temporary nature, far a penalty kick takes by the Warrington skipper was well taken by Lawless, who sprinted grandly until the safe clutches of G. Massey brought him to mother earth. Sterling play by Povey, Berry, and W. Dillon improved Warrington's position, and then some finessing among the visiting backs saw Ritson intercepting, and despite the endeavours of Evans and Lawless to stay his career; he succeeded in getting clear, and a capital try was the result. The Stockport supporters went into ecstacies over this success of their favourites, and cheer after cheer was heard, but the kick at goal was a failure. Following the restart, some ground was gained by Murray passing to Ritson, but this effort was placed' in the shade when Bate dodged round a pack and a short run and kick and quick follow- ing up and safe tackle of Wickman placed the Warring- tonians on the aggressive. A fine piece of play by J. T. Massey was duly appreciated. and then a neat transfer from Antrobus to Barnes almost brought about the downfall of the Stockport goat. The Warringtonians were now playing in grand style, tackling safely and never giving way in the least, while the backs, whenever opportunity afforded, rarely failed to .make headway. Dillon dribbled well, and Fair Turner headed a forward movement which had a like result of all the previous efforts of his side. How- ever, the Warringtonians had not fought in vain, for some tine passing by Bate, Antrobus, and Barnes ultim- ately found the oval in the possession of Lawless, who was soon in his stride, and pushing Ritson on one side he raced over the line, and a grand piece of play resulted in the sides being on even terms J. T. Massey failing at the place. The drop out found play at the half-way flag, where a long succession of scriminages and line-outs were witnessed-. Eventually Randles and LittlewoNl got clear of a line-out, and although Povey dribbled well, a judicious kick and run by Cockrell was followed by a smart dribble by Dain and Bailey, and the visitors had all their work cut out to prevent the Stockport men from scoring. J. T. Massey had a rare chance from a pass by Bate, but unluckily overran the ball, and Nevins took up the opening, a sharp kick send- ing the oval near the home line. The home forwards

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 26, 1890. WARRINGTON IMPROVEMENT BILL.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 26, 1890. WARRINGTON IMPROVE- MENT BILL.

relieved the danger' passing smartly and causing Evans some anxiety. The Warrington "stonewaller " was equal to any emergency, and defended his charge as only he can, and although Murray had a near shave for a drop at goal, and Cockrell tried to force an opening, the "wirepullers " knew their man, and rarely allowed him to gain more than ten yards at the most. The game was rushed back to the half-way flag, when half time was called with the score—Warrington 0-1.1; Stockport, 0-1-0. With the aid of the wind score—Warrington, at once ' made things lively for the homesters. Potts kicked off, I and Barnes with a long kick sent the oval in touch near the Stockport line. A fine run by Massey was spoiled by his holding the oval too long, and although Bailey got away, and by feigning to pass made considerable ground ' the effort was staved off, and a good kick by Evans caused Stockport to beat a hasty retreat, and Lawless, Bandies. and Barnes missed rare chances of scoring. Indeed, the play of Warrington was very erratic at this juncture of the game, for one minute we had pre- sented brilliant expositions of the passing and dribbling art, and then the next minute, when all that was requi- site was to put Coe finishing touch on the effort, the chance was mulled by the apparent eagerness to score, and all the previous efforts were wasted. After J. T. Massey had compelled a minor, a series of exchanges between Barnes and Antrobus saw the first-named running between the posts, but the point was overruled through the pass forward. A similar fate befel Lawless' who rounded his opponents after grand passing bekweeu Bate, Antrobus, Barnes, Nevins, and Littlewood. Eventually the oval was got near the Stockport line, and Nevins struggled over, Barnes' kick at goal striking the upright. Follow- ing the drop out the play was at the home quarter flag, where Nevins secured from a line-out, and dashing along he foiled'Ma.ssey in his endeavours to stay him, and an- other try was the result, Fair Turner this time placing a a goal from near the touch line. This acted as a damper on the Stockport men, and they rarely passed their own quarter flag. A grand piece of work by Bate was follow- ed by Bandies and Massey having narro* shaves for tangible scores. Lawless again put ins capital run, and in response the home forwards worked the oval to near the half way flag. Towards the close Stockport rallied, and in the last two minutes of the game Schofield , notched a try, Massey failing at the place. After this ' time was called, the oval being at centre. Warrington winning a finely contested game by one goal, two tries, three minors, to two tries. That Stockport are an improving team can easily be gathered from the fine game they played the Warring- tonians, but judging from Saturday's exhibition War- rington had always the measure of them. Superior combination existed in the visiting ranks, and to this is the victory due. Where the Warringtonians excelled most was at half back, for both Wickman and Parrott were outclassed when compared to Antrobus and Bate, who time after time got the oval away without any ap- parent extra effort. Barnes and Evans had not much work to do, but Lawless and Massey were fully employed and to say the least theyacquitted themselves admirably. The forwards were ably led on by their captain, Nevins. Dillon and Berry being the pick of the remainder. Teams :—Warrington: J. W. Evans, full back: J. Massey, T.Barnes, and J. Lawless, three-quarter backs; W. Antrobus and .T. T. Bate, half backs ; W. Nevins, W. Randles, W. Povey, R. Littlewockl, T. Donoghue, E. Dillon, W. Dillon, R. Berry, and Fair Turner, forwards. Stockpert : Cr. Massey full back •'F. Ritson, J. Murray, and E. Cockrell, three-quarter backs ; E. Wickman and H. Parrott, half backs ; C. Schofield, J. Potts, Dr. Smith, J. M. Mills, J. K. Dane, R. Mcclure, W. Du ckers, W. Bailey, a nd J. Teare' forwards. Referee, Mr. H. Lord Broughton Football Club.

SPECIAL MEETING OF THE TOWN COUNCIL. On Wednesday evening a special meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held at the Town Hall, for the purpose of considering and confirming the propriety of the promotion of the Warrington Extension Water and Improvement Bill. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb), presided, and there were also present Aldermen Harrison, Crostield, Chandley, Burgess, Sutton, .Wright ; Councillors Monks, Blackhurst, Tinsley, J. Taylor, Garner, J. Shaw Green, Fleming, W. Piernoint, R. T. Fair- dough, J. Fairclough, Greenall, llepherci, Marsh, Muir, Hutchinson, Voisey, Flood, .Jenkins; Messrs. Whittle (town clerk), Dr. Gornall (medical officer), and Longdin (borough surveyor.) THE LATE COUNCILLOR GREENING. The MAYOR said that before proceeding with the regu- lar business of the meeting, he wished to propose a resolution to the effect that the Council received with deep regret the announcement of the death of Mr. 'John Greening, and desired to record the loss that had been sustained by his death, and to express appreciation of the valuable services rendered by him to the borough during a period of upward 3 of sixteen years. Alderman BURGESS seconded the proposition, and said that by the death of Mr. Greening the Council had lost a very valuable servant indeed. The resolution was then carried.

THE IMPROVEMENT BILL. The MAYOR proposed—" That this Council do hereby confirm the propriety of the promotion by the mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of Warrington, acting by the Council, of a Bill in the present Session of Parliament, intituled a Bill to extend the boundaries of the borough of Warrington, to provide for vesting the undertaking of the Warrington Water Works Company in the mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of Warrington, and to make better provision for the health, local government, and improvement of the borough, and for other purposes." Alderman Surrox seconded the motion. Councillor MONKS said that before a vote was taken, he should like to ask a question as to the opinion of the Town Clerk with regard to the passing of the Bill. Alderman CROSFIELD said that when a vote was taken of the ratepayers upon this question, there was a majority in favourof the purchase of the Water Works. He was away from home at the time, but he understood that there was a majority in favour. That being the case, he supposed the responsibility was taken out of the hands of the Council. He wished to say for himself that he declined to take any responsibility in the matter, because he could not approve of the purchase. If the ratepayers were satisfied to give a hundred thousand pounds more than a thing was worth, it was their look out. He thought it Was a very serious thing to do, and a very risky thing to do. They might waken up some morning, and find that the water had bolted. He only rose to express his own opinion that be thought it was a dangerous and foolish bargain. The TOWN CLERK said that the success of the bill in a great measure depended upon the report of the Local Government Board. He anticipated that they would have some objections to the boundary, and it would be necessary to reconsider that subject if the report was strongly against the extension proposed. He thought that the best plan would be to pass the resolution that night, on the understanding that the Bill should be fur- ther considered. Alderman HARRISON said that Alderman Crosfield's objection seemed to be as to the amount of purchase money. He thought he did not object to the purchase, assuming that it could be made at a reasonable price. He was sorry to find that Alderman Crosfield seemed to be rather inclined to be a croaker. He seemed to think that the water might sometime disappear, and it was possible that it might. But was there any probability that anything of the kind ssould happen? He did not think there was. There was no probability of the water going in some other direction. Every possible precau- tion would be taken with a view to having a proper examination, and being assured that the water would not adopt the eccentric course Mr. Crosfield had pointed out.

Councillor MONKS sail that he did net take the samt view as an objector that Alderman Crosfield did. The view he held was that they had not made their bargain, that they had not had their preliminary examination, and that they were not in a position to say whether the bargain was likely to be mode or not. He supposed very much would depend upon the report of the experts they called in whether they thought it desirable to confirm the unofficial offer made by the Corporation. It seemed to him to be a very unbusinesslike proceeclng to commit themselves to a bill like that. He pointed out that there was nothing to prevent them, after they had made theie bargain and settled the terms from obtaining a provir sional'order to buy the Water Works, or, if they though- proper, from going in for a short Act of Parliament. That, he thought, was the proper course for them to take. He did not wish to press the Town Clerk in the matter, but he took his answer to be adverse to the chancesof the bill. Alderman CROSFIELD : He only spoke with regard to the extension. Councillor MONKS : I take his answer to the question I asked.

The TOWN CLARK : It is not anticipated that the Loca Government Board will have any objections except to that part of the bill relating to the extension: Councillor MONKS: CU they have the power? The Town alien Yes. Councillor MONKS said that when the bill first came before the Parliamentary Committe:t there was net one of them knew anything about it, and he thought it was an extraordinary thing that a bill like that should be conceived, ptinted and got in order without the sanction or the knowledge of the Parliamentary Committee. The drifting policy that. had been displayed in the matter was, to his mind, most unsatisfactory. He was not satis- fied that the extension of the borough would be the ad- vantage that many of them claimed for it. It had been incidentally mentioned to him by Alderman Harrison that b/ the extension of the borough boundary the revenue would be affected to the extent of £250, by the people outside the present boundary Alaiming to have their gas at the same rate as those within the borough. Nothing had bean said about the capital expenditure that they Would be called upon to make. He heard on all hands that buPding in the outskirts had stopped, because no one would spend money until the boundary ; was extended when they would call upon the Corporation Ito put down sewers, tio. He could not see where they were to get the rateable value from to compensate them for this expenditure. With reference to the voting of the racepayers that had not the slightest effect upon him. He did not believe it had been an honest vote— (" Yes,' and "Oh oh ") —and he was told on very good authority that there had been a system of canvassing and sending out papers--- Councillor GRERNALL : Who has been canvassing? Councillor MONKS: I don't know. The whole matter had been pushed along in a premature and unsatisfac- tory way, and he felt it to be his duty to give all the op- position he could to the passing of the bill. Councillor VOISRY said that the opposition to the bill was mainly with regard to the purchase of the Water- works, but when they considered all the precautions that were to be taken before the purchase was completed, he thought those objections fell to the ground. He also referred to the sanction the ratepayers had given the bill, the main clauses of which, he said, were good. Alderman HARRISON said they would stultify them- selves if the progress of that business was obstructed that night. Alder man Buttons took the strongest exception to the observation of Mr. Monks that the vote had not been an honest vete. Before the vote was stigmatised in the way it had been there should have been evidence forth. coming to sustain the allegation Mr. Monks had ven- tured 'to make, which was that the ratepayers who sent them there were not to be trusted in anything they were doing, that people had been going about canvassing and he knew not what, and that the vote when it came to be counted was no representation of the opinions of the borough. He took entire exception to that—(hear, hear)—and he thought Mr. Monks should show where his authority came from for making any such statement. Until he did that he should hold Mr. Monks responsible for the statement. Mr. Monks also said the Parliamen- tary Committee knew nothing about this bill— Councillor MONKS:! said I was told by a member of the Parliamentary Committee. Alderman Bromess said if that member was there that night he challenged him to make it appear that that was a correct representation. (Hear, hear.) Why, it was nearly twelve months since the General Purposes Com- mittee appointed a special committee far the purpose of

making inquiry and reporting on the boundaries question. The Committee went to work and reported to the General Purposes Committee, and it was not time for the Parlia- mentary Committee to act until that report had gone to the General Purposes Committee, and they had given instructions for the bill to be proceeded with. The Parliamentary Committee, which was only a sub-com- mittee of the General Purposes Committee, had mainly to do with the bill after it got into committee in London. He had seen more than one popular vote, but he had never seen a vote that appeared to him to require less canvas- sing for than that vote, and he was utterly ignorant of any canvassing. (A Member : There was no canvassing.) This he knew, that when the gas works were to be pur- chased—and Mr.'Monks was an active agent in the pur- chasing of the gas works—there was a good deal of can- vassing done, and even then to his mind the vote obtained was not half so solid a vote as the vote for the present bill. On the occasion of the gas works purchase the owner as well as the occupier was qualified to vote, but on this occasion nobody but the occupier had the chance of voting. If the owners had been qualified there would have been 5,000 more votes that could have been re- corded one way or the other. He thought that the majority of 800 was a very satisfactory approval of the work of the Corporation, and it was'a mandate to go on with the bill. (Hear, hear.) Councillor HurcnissoN said he should vote for the Bill, but he did not wish to be tied down either to the extension or waterworks schemes. The resolution proposed by the Mtvoa was then voted upon as follows— For—Aldermen Sutton, Burgess, Harrison, Wright,and Chandley ; Councillors Greenall. Blackhurst, Taylor. Pierpoint, Tinsley, Fleming, Heaton, Shaw Green, Hutchinson, Garner, Muir, Flood, Voisey, Ashton, Marsh, Jenkins, Hepherd, H. Fairelough, and J. Fair- clough-25. Against—Alderman 'Crosfield and Councillor Monks

The Mason declared the resolution carried, as it had I been approved by an absolute majority of the Council. He should, he added, be glad if every member of the Council would join in carrying that Bill forward. (Hear, hear.) He should like the help of Alderman Crosfield. (Hear, hear.) Councillor VOISEY Said there were two ways of oppos- ing the Bill. One ISM in the way it had been opposed up to now, and the other was by sh swing a certain amount of apathy in passing it through the House of Commons. Every person charged with the work was now in duty bound to do his duty ,to the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) The meeting then ended.

div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON T. OUGHTRINGTON PAM—Played on the ground of the former, at Howley, on Saturday, before about 300 spectators. The visitors kicked off at four o'clock with the wind, and play began to rage in mid- field, but Onions getting possession, made a splendid run, and that player passing to Clayton, he sent in a light- ning shot and scored the first goal, and immediately after Onions scored a second with a beauty. The visi- tors then had a spell at pressing, Mather and Phillips be- , ing too good for them, but some rough play on the part of the visitors made the game unpleasant. About five minutes of half time Clayton getting possession scored a third goal, a fast low shot. The second half was not of much importance, the visitors rushing four through from scrimmages and free kicks in front of goal. The game ended—Park, 4; Warrington, 3. Warrington team :—Simkins, goal ; Phillips and Mather, backs; Watson, Phillips, and Cant, half backs ; Clayton, Chant- ler, Onions, Ellison, Warburton, forwards.

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.-RUGBT.

The local football season will be wound up to-day with two matches in which both the St. Helens leading organ- isations are concerned. Warrington will meet the St. Helens Club on the Wilderspool ground in a West Lan- cashire League match, and about the same time the St. Helens Recs. will be trying conclusions with the Runcorn team on the ground of the latter.

The meeting between Warrington and Aspull led to one of the toughest struggles of the season, and although the " wirepuller° " quickly opened the scoring roll, the " Aspullers " finished with two or three points to the good. The home team undoubtedly missed, in the for- ward department, the powerful aid of the brothers Turner, for it was in the scrimmages and on other occasions ' when strong forward play is needed that they were seen to least advantage. The home backs played well without exception, and the nassing at times was of the finest order. A fatal mistake was made in withdrawing Evans from full back to fill the place of Massey during his tem- porary disablement, for in that short interval Aspull got the lead which gave them the match.

Under the guise of Crompton's v. Smith's team, those old rivals Runcorn and Widnes met on the ground of the former on Saturday. Through various unpleasant inci- dents, which are better buried in oblivion, the teams have not had engagements with each other for several years, and the meeting on Saturday aroused deep inter- est, fully five thousand spectators being present. While Runcorn have had a phenomenally brilliant season, Widnes have a heavy balance of losses over victories, but during Easter they brightened up considerably knd won tour successive matches in as many days, and they were expected to make a tough fight on Saturday. For the first fifteen minutes Widnes had quite as much of the play as their opponents, and perhaps a little more, and Laws certainly should have scored, but missed a grand chance. Afterwards the combination and superior tac- tics of the home team told the inevitable tale, and Run- corn kept up an almost continual bombardment of the Widnes goal line, and it was surprising that the score was not much heavier than 1 goal (dropped by Davies) 1 try (Crompton) and two minors to two minors. The game was contested throughout in the most friendly spirit, and was full of interesting inciaents from a spec- tator's point of view.

div.head: MAD DOCTOR COMMITS MURDER.
div.p: A MAD DOCTOR COMMITS MURDER.

An inquest was held, on Monday, at tho Swan Hotel, Blackwater, near Farnborough, on the body of William Rouse, gamekeeper, who was fatally shot on Friday night by Dr. Samuel George Milner, of Upper Norwood. A witness named Knight, a friend of the deceased, stated that Milner passed him on the road twice on the evening in question, and on both occasions asked him the way to Reading. He also on the first occasion asked for relief, and as they suspected him they followed him along the road. Milner began to run. They ran after him, Rouse being in front. Milner fell, and Rouse fell on him. Two shots were heard, and Rouse got up and exclaimed, "I'm a dead man." He was removed to the Swan Hotel, where be subsequently expired. Thomas Lovegrove, laztdlord of the Swan, stated that he was aroused after closing time by Milner, who asked to be let in, saying he had been attacked by two men. He had shot one, and he believed he was dead. Witness let him in, and a few minutes afterwards Constable Reynolds came and arrested him. Milner was bleeding and dirty, and looked as if he had been struggling. Constable Rey- nolds stated that when he arrested him Milner struggled violently and attempted to draw a revolver from his pocket. He took him into the room were Rouse was lying, and Rouse immediately identified him as the man who had shot him. Milner became so violent that he had to handcuff him and strap his legs together. Witness had since ascertained that Milner was a lunatic, and had escaped from his keeper. When charged at Aldershot he gave his correct name and address. The jury, after a brief consultation, returned a verdict of manslaughter.

div.head: AN UNKNOWN MAN FOUND DROWNED.
div.p: AN UNKNOWN MAN FOUND DROWNED.

An inquest was held by Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, at the Ship Inn, Newton Common, on Tues- day afternoon, touching the death of a man whose body had not been identified and who was found in the Sankey Canal about 390 yards from the Newton Common locks, on Monday morning. It appeared that about half-past five on the morning named Owen Evans, a collier at Collins Green Collieries, was returning to his home in Graf ton-st., Earlestown, along the capal bank. At the spot indicated he saw a body floating in the water and he immediately gave inforniation to the Police. Constables Bowes and Cameron proceeded to the spot and-dragged the body out of the water,and removed it to the Ship Inn. Evidence to this effect was given by the man Evans, after which P.C. Howes sta,ed that the body had not been identified and they had no clue as to who the deceased was. The body was very much decom- posed and had apparently been in the water for two or three weeks. There were no marks upon it. It was that of a man about 26 years of age, 5 feet al inches in height,of medium build, with sandy hair and a small sandy moustache. He was dressed in a brown cloth overcoat, single breasted, with brown hone buttons. It had three pockets on the outside, a ticket. pocket, and one pock°, inside. The pockets were lined with black sateen, and the sleeves lined with striped sateen. He had also on a grey red tweed jacket with black composition buttons, two pockets and a ticket pocket on the outside and one inside pocket. There was a• waistcoat to match. The trousers were of blue check tweed cloth, lined with white calico ; brown merino jersey, blue and white striped cotton shirt, flesh coloured stockings, and laced boots. In the pockets were found a wooden pipe, an old knife with one blade, a., old German silver double-cased Geneva watch, attached to a silver guard of a curb pattern. The watch bore the name " Fielding " and was numbered 100,022.—the jury returned a verdict of " Found drowned." Up to Wednesday afternoon the body had not been identified. The police authorities have had photographs taken of the body for identification—if possible after the remains have been interred.

div.head: PRIMROSE DAY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: PRIMROSE DAY AT WARRINGTON.
TORY MEETING AT LATCHFORD.
The be ti Conservatives celebrated Primrose Day on Saturday in the Usual manner, primroses being . .
lentiful. At the Conservative Club a wreath was

displayed over the entrance to the hall,and the gate leading to Mrs, Reynolds' residence, at Latchford, was similarly- decked. In the evening the member for the Knutsford Division, the Hon. A. de Tatton Egerton, addressed the members of the Grappenhall Habitation (1573) of the Primrose League at an entertainment held in Christ Church Parish Boom Latchford. He said Lord Beaconsfield was a man who was far-seeing in all his work. He began life as a Liberal, he ended it as a Con- servative, but not as a Conservative of the old Tory type. He recognised that the time had come when Con- servatism should no longer run in a narrow groove, but should progress with the times in which it found itself. He laid the foundation of what was now the Unionist party, which-was a union of Conservatives and of those Liberals who think more of their country than of their party. They were working one and all to main- tain the emPirein its integrity, and to support the cause of law and order in this country. Lord Salisbury was following in the "footsteps of Lord Beaconsfield in carrying out a great foreign policy, to maintain our empire as the leading empire of the world. We had Ireland at the present time becoming quieter, and the reason was that we possessed a firm and substantial Government, a government which did not vacillate, and which had carried out what it considered to be the best for the country, Lord Beaconsfield, during one of the Administrations, had charge of the finances of the country, and no one would have been more gratifiecF:than himself to have

listened the other nightio the Budget as propounded by that great financier, Mr. Goschen. The Budget that had been proposed by Mr. Goschen was one which appealed to the country at large.; Mr. Goschen had benefited by careful management in times past, he had benefited by three years' work which he had expended upon the finances of the country, and now Om, had a budget in which there was the respectable surplus of £3,500,000, which had been devoted by him to reduce certain taxa- tion in the country. He considered that Mr. Goschen had made the fairest distribution of the profits he had at his command that any Minister had ever made in times past or could make in the future. He had given a little to everybody where the shoe pinched, and not only had he had a surplus, but he had by his great financial pro- jects been able to reduce the National Debt by no less a sum than £23,000,000 dining the past three or four years.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL PARISH CHURCH.
SALE OF WORK.

On Wednesday.and Thursday a Sale of Work in aid of a fund for the restoration of the church bells was held in the Large-room at Grappenhall, and proved a great success. The room had been taste- fully decorated for the occasion by Mr. Southern, of Manchester, and had a very attract i e look. Amon& those present at the opening ceremony on Wednes- day were the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton, M.P. Mr: and Mrs. J. C. Parr, the Rev. Canon Greenall, the Rev. Hayden Coope, Mr. and Mix. W. Lang, Mrs. Broadbent, Mrs. W. Stubs, Mr. and Mrs. Lister Kaye, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Carleton, and Miss Kidd. Canon Greenall, at, the commencement of the proceeoings, said that as Rector of the parish it fell to his lot to say a few words. They were inclebted to the kindness of the ladies for that Sale of Work, as it originated , with them. They had. collected together the beautiful articles that were seen before them, and which were not only artistic, but useful. They thanked the ladies for the trouble they , had taken in the matter. He regretted that Mrs. Eger- ton, who had promised to be present to open the sale, was absent owing to sickness. They were, however, glad to have present Mr. Egerton, who had consented to take her place. They would all feel regret in not having present a lady who was the moving spirit in getting up that sale. He alluded to Mrs. Greenall, who was also absent because of illness. They would be glad now to know that she was approaching her usual health Pnd strength. The object of the sale was to raise funds to pay for the restorgtion of the church bells, which sadly needed repair, and which had been used since 1790. To meet the expenditure that had been incurred they now wanted a sum of £163 7s. 9d. If they added to this a- further £4O for expenses connected with the sale, they required a total of £2OO. H 6 hoped they would at least secure so much, and, might he add, as inuch more as possible. Mr. Egerton, in a few appropriate words, then declared the bazaar open. The stall-holders were as follows : (1) Mrs. Edward Greenall, Mrs. Henry Greenall, Mrs. • Appleton, and Miss Eddowes. (2) Mrs. Parr, Mrs. Reynolds, Mrs. Wynne Jones. Mrs. Halton, Miss Reynolds, and Miss Wade. (3) Mr;. Thomas Greenall, Mrs. Few, and Mrs. W. Stubs. (4) Mrs. Atkin, and the' Misses ; Atkin. Refreshment Stall: Miss Chandley, Mrs. Woods, and Mrs. Lomas. Flower Stall: Mrs. and Miss Long, Miss Milner, Miss E. Harvey, Mrs. Greg, the Misses Boardman, and Miss Pearson. A band from Manchester, under the conductorship of Mr. J. C. Dewhurst, was engaged, and discoursed selections of music each day. Entertainments of various kinds were given at intervals, and were much appreciated. The sale of work realised over £257.

THE EAItLESTOWN CLUB AND THE LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. A meeting of the Lancashire League was held at Bolton on Thursday week representatives from eleven clubs being present. Higher Walton and Heywood Central were granted permission to play their League match on May 3rd. The conduct of the Earlestown club, who have systematically defied the League and refuse to complete their remaining League matches within the time laid down, was under consideration, and it was unanimously resolved to expel them from the League. After considerable discus- sion it was also decided that their record be expunged from the books of the League. The removal of Earles- town will make several changes in the relative positions at present occupied by the clubs en the League record. ,THE EARLESTOWN CLUB'S DEFENCE. The following letter has been sent us :—Sir, I have noticed in several papers a paragraph stating that the Earlostown F.C. had been expelled from the Lancashire League, for refusing to keep it engagements. Now I think the supporters of this club are entitled to an ex• planation, and with your permission I will take up a little of your valuable space, in trying to place the facts of the case before them. I may state in commencing that the Earlestown players are all employed in various works in the neighbourhood, within a radius of a mile from their field, and that no player has received a penny out of the club fund during the present season except for lost time. The Lancashire League is composed of one representative from each of the clubs affiliated, out of which a Management Committee of five members has been appointed. This Committee on the 15th January, sent out a circular to all the clubs connected with the League, to the effect that no League fixture would be allowed to be altered after the 24th February. 1890. It also sent out a circular en the 6th March, calling atten- tion to rule 9 (which states that no one but a referee appointed by the League would be allowed to officiate in 'League fixtures), and adding that that rule would be rigidly enforced. Now then, what dots; this League Committee do? The Heywood Club had for referee in their match with Earlestown at Hey wood one of their own committeemen, not on the League list. The Ch., irman of the Earlestown Club who was with the team on this occasion handed in a written pro- test against the referee before the match commenced. Heywood won but the protest was laid before the League Committee and the result was that the committee "knocked a bole" through their own rule and awarded the match to Heywood. The Bury Club were due to Hay their League fixture at Earlestown, on Saturday, 29th March. Bury without consulting Earleston applied to the League Committee a fortnight previously to post- wine its match with Earlestown. as they had a cup tie on the same day. This application was granted and the Earlestown Committee werenot informed of the decision until three days before the match should have been played, thereby throwing the Earlestown Club without a ,match and occasioning a loss of from £8 to £lO. On the 15th inst., the Bury Club wrote to Earlestown for a date on which to fulfil this engagement and stated that on no account would Saturday or Monday be accepted, in addition to which they also excluded two Mondays. Toe Bury Club, at the same time, were well aware that the Earlestown Club could not play on any day except Saturday as no less than seven of the players wets and are employed at one works, and to leave their employ. ment in circler to play football generally means dismissal. In addition to this, the "gate" on any day except Saturday would not meet the cost of posters alone, net to mention other expenses and loss of wages. The League Committee, however, cancelled a Saturday's match in order to meet the wishes of the Bury Club, and we think they ought in justice and in all fairness to have compelled a Saturday's match in return, even though it had been arranged for a Saturday in May. It is stated that the League have already granted permission to one club to play a League fixture in May, and we cannot understand why this has not been granted in the case of Earlestown. I will now give you another instance of how the League Committee has managed its business. The Hyde v. Earlestown match ended in a win for Earlestown by two goals to one. The Hyde Club lodged a protest against alleged rough play and against a supposed unfair referee. The referee on that occasion was Mr. Edwards, of Liverpool. who is generally considered one of the fairest and most efficient referees in Lancashire The pretest was considered at a League Committee meeting, and (although the Earlestown F.C. secretary opposed the hearing of the protest on the ground that the referee was not present at the meeting) this wonderfully clever committee, without calling upon the Earlestown club or the referee for any statement as to what actually did take place, decided that the match must be re-played. The Earlestown club has only failed to meet one League engagement during the season and that was with Blackburn Park Road, when a portion of the players missed the early train by which they had to travel, and the remainder got out at the first station. This theeFommittee of the Earlestown club could not possibly prevent at the moment, and they have since expressed their willingness to pay the penalty and play the match at the convenience of the Blackburn club. One other engagement and the only one to which any further reference can possibly be made against Earlestown was one with Heywood Central. The Earlestown players journeyed to Heywood to fulfil the fixture, but found it was impossible to play owing to the dense fog. Cerres- pondence tool! place with the view of playing this match, but had not been concluded when the League came to their strange decision. The Earlestown Committee have, during the present season, erected substantial dressing rooms on the ground at a cost of nearly £5O, and this with other special expenses for fencing, &c., has kept the clubs very low—so low, in fact, that on several occa- sions during the season the club has been considerably in debt and travelling expenses have had to be paid out of pocket. The childish petulance of the League Com- mittee displayed in their decision to expel the Earles- town club because we wished to play the deferred matches in May, will, of course, be a serious loss to the club as matches with Bury, Oswaldtwistle Rovers and Hyde which had been arranged to be played at Earles- town are thereby cancelled The Earlestown Commit- tee are endeavouring to arrange other good matches to the end of May, and if they receive the support of- the public, which they have tried to merit, the Treasurer may yet close his books at the end of the season with a balance on the right side. To conclude I would respectfully invite the Committee of the League—to use a term in one of the athletic papers—to "sit down and have a good think" about the discourtesy with which they have treated the Earles- town club. The Committee of that club have done all itt their povvor to fulfil their engagements and consider that their just claims liaTle been ignored by the League Com- mittee who have dealt with them in anything but a fair and proper manner. Apologising for taking up so much space, on behalf of the Committee, I am, yours kc., J. TAYLOR, (chairman), Earlestown, April 23rd, 1890.

A good healthy body is almost sure to be found a 590- ciated with a good conscience. A close student of human nature is rarely willing to place large matters of trust in thehands oranother until he has seen the one whom he is to trust. He looks for the fresh health and vigour, the honest frank counten i - ance and manly form, and, n fact. all that is attractive in men. He doubts the dyspeptic with sallow skin, drawn-out features, the evident weak and irritable nature. He feels as Shakespeare makes Jaius Cow' say :

- "Let me have nvn about me that are fat— Sleek-headed men, and such as sleep o' nights. You Cassius hath a lean and hungry look ; He thinks too much. Such men are dangerous.' He does not doubt the honesty of the poor unfortunate. but he fears disease of the body will affect the, mind,.. bring misfortune upon the individual, and loss to him-

OCIA• It may be, injustice to the weak, but if the man has not the mental strength, or if he is wrapped up in 11'15 misery, he cannot take in the situation of the world, does , not see (hat ideas are broadening, and that isms and teachings are advancing. How can an employer hope for success from such a man? The dyspeptic look, the wax-like complexion, and sallow features show disease. The far-seeing man notes all these signs, and knows that 'c the great light of man, the brain is effected, or will be, at no distant date. He discards the poor victim of disease who goes wearily out into the world. Discouraged at last he takes to his sick bed. Hu seeks medical aid. Lacking the broad ideas of the successful man of the world, he tries the same medical treatment that he has tried many times before. The same bigoted counsel is sought, the same drugs are administered by the same old family friend that treated him months and years before,and his parents before him, and in such a way he drags out his miserable , unsuccessful existence. Is he to blame? Why not? When he sees daily' and hears from every side, proclamations of a remedy known as Warner's "SAFE " Cure, to be had of all chemists, which is becoming more popular daily, hourly, while he is becoming weaker. Mr. William Shepherd, 164, Downham Road, 'sling' ton, London N., suffered for upwards of twenty veil from indigestion in its worst forms, having pet:iodic-1i spells of vertigo, fainting, and chills. During this time , he expended hundreds of pounds in dcctors and med_i- cines, but without any permanent benefit. He wrets-. over his own signature: " After trying Warner's 'S" Cure,' Cure,' I found it produced a most marvellous effect, an" • I am now in a perfect state of health." Such a man as we have described, nine times out o ten, unconsciously to himself or to his physician, has" kidney disorder, which is fast wastin his body and life. f ' He sees the merits of Warner's" SAFE Cure at evel turn, and hears it proclaimed from the house tops, an • yet he does not use it, because it is said by his illibete r physician that it is not professional, and not admitted by the code. Meanwhile the man of the world Press°. forward, cares not a fig for this or that school; his e r_lra , in life is success, and he looks hopefully forward to world beyond, believing and trusting in man in gil• world, and to his faith for the world beyond.

div.head: SINGING IN PUBLIC HOUSES.
div.p: SINGING IN PUBLIC HOUSES.

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, Mr. Harry Dale, late of the Mill Stone Inn, Sankey-St., applied for a transfer to him of the licence of the Hop Pole Inn, Horsemarket-st. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that he did not know of any particular ob- jection to the transfer. He would, however, like to Point out that in time gone by women of questionable Character had frequented the house, and since the pre- sent applicant had been at the Hop Pole complaints had been made by neighbours of the music and singing„ which Went on from an early hour in the morning till late at night. He had not received any complaint from the Police or any person which would justify him in bringing a charge against the applicant, but he would like M. Dale to take notice of what he said, so as to avoid anything of the sort happening in the future. The sing- ing and music which went on there was something new to Warrington and something which the town seemed hardly prepared for. The applicant was a man of good character, and nothing was known against him. No Complaints were made whilst he was landlord ef the Millstone.—Alderman Harrison : Have you heard any- thing beyond the fact that music is played there ?—No, sir.--Alderman Harrison : Because, per se, there is abso- lutely no harm in that.—The applicant said that the music going on in the daytime was simply his family Practising in their own private apartments.—The Chief Constable said the police had to be very much on the alert in such matters, because there were others, beside themselves, taking notes. His desire was to prevent any complaints at the Licensing Sessions, in August.—The Mayor observed that the Chief Constable was evidently actuated by a friendly spirit towards the applicant and the trade, and he hoped his kindness would be appre- ciated. The transfer would he granted.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

--- The annual meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. There were present the Revs. G. F. Roberts, and H. C. E. Carleton; Messrs. Kilshall, Swinton, Blackburst, T. Jones, Beaton, D. Jones, Davies, R. Owen, Harrison, Long, Aukland, Dobson, Jolley, Gill, Hibbert, Smith, Ratcliffe, Clarke, ' Balharry, Humphreys, W. Houghton, J. Houghton ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant ' 'llO, C. H. Ward (workhouse master). and H. MI slines (supiriutendent of Padgate Schools). ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN AND VICR-CHAIRMAN. This being the annual meeting the CLERK took the Chair pro. tem. and said the first business of the meeting would be the election of a chairman for the coming year --Mr. BALHARRY moved that the Rev. G. F. Roberts be re-elected, and this proposal was seconded by Mr. W. Notionrox.—Mr. HEATON moved that Alderman Harri- son be elected chairman.—Mr. T. JONES seconded this Proposal.—The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS expressed a desire to withdraw in favour, of Mr. Harrisoii' and the latter gentleman intimated that he should like to give way in favour of Mr. Roberts. The Matter, however, came to a vote when twelve members held up their hands in favour of Mr. Harrison, and eight for Mr. Roberts the former being therefore declared elected.—Mr. flarrison, in acknowledging his ,election, said he had been a member of the Board about 25 years. , After hp had been 18 years on the Board he was appointed Chairman a position which he occupied for 12 months, Vd before he retired it wO an understood thing betwixt imself and some members of the Board that, if it were their pleasure, he should again alio* himself to be nomi- nated. DIVULGING COMMITTEE SECRETS. Mr. W. HOUGHTON said at after a recent meet- "g of Padgate Schools Committee information was carried from the Committee room and imparted to People in the town, and of course very much agnified. This resulted in a very disagreeable '..;.l.oomstance occurring at the meeting after, and no. doubt had resulted further in feeling being raised against members of the Committee individually. Lie thought some strictures from the Chairman of the oard would have a very good effect. (Hear, hear.)— Ihe CHAIRMAN said he sympathised most completely With what Mr. Houghton had said He himself had been the victim o( the same sort of thing in con- nection with his position as a member of the Town Ceun- eb- He considered everything that was said in Com- !nittee was sacred within the four walls. Information nact been carried out and garbled in such a way as to Z,ower to a deliberate misrepresentation, and he did not 'link there was anything more entitled to their strong condemnation than for any gentleman to act in that WaY• (Hear. hear.) He hoped and trusted that, if any gentleman had hitherto done so, perhaps through illadvertence, he would be more careful in the future. (Rear, hear.)—Mr. W. HOUGHTON: It is the most dis- ereditab'e thing I have known for the last seven years. (Rear, hear.)

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

SHIP CANAL MISSION, STOCKTON HEATH. An entertainment in connection with the Band of Hope was held in the mission room, Stockton Heath, the other evening. The chair was taken by Mr. Henshaw,who gave a suitable and earnest, address. A very enjoyable pro- gramme was then given of songs, recitations, and dia- logues, in which the following took part part :—M. Travis, C. Mathias, L. Heesom, M. J. Beswick, A. Hallows, N. Dodds, J. Hobin, A. Gregory, Miss Risley, Miss Reid, Mr. Spencer. At the close a humorous sketch was given, entitled" The landlord in a fix," whicfi was well rendered by the following :—Mr. C. Perren, Mr. W. Perren, Mr. J. Dixon, Mr. P. Whitley, Mr. A. Rooks, Miss Perren, Miss Hobin ; W. Beswick, S. Briggs. - -

THE SHIP CANAL CRICKET AND QUOIT CLUBS. Mr. W. Browning, as secretary of the No. 6 (The!wall) district of the Ship Canal Cricket Club, has arranged a capital list of fixtures for the coming season, which opens on the first Saturday in May. Last year's fixtures are, for the most part, repeated, and consist largely of ' home and home matches with the other sections of the canal. Dr. Byrne will again captain the team, Mr. F. Smith filling the capacity of vice-captain. The other officers are—President, 3in John Price; vice-president, Mr. J. A. Ewart : treasurer, Mr. W. Kenway ; Commit- tee, Messrs. R. Bushell, H. A. Dix, J. H. Price, F. John- son, J. Lewis, R. Gifford, and W. Robinson. On May 3rd, the trial match will take place, when teams will be chosen by the captain and his deputy. Mr. E. Hayden has been elected captain of the Quoit Club (of which Mr. Price is president for the ensuing year), and there is every iea.son to believe that, under his guidance, the club will be more prosperous than was the case last year.

FATALITY AT ELLESMERE PORT. Mr. Tibbits, deputy coroner of West Cheshire, held an inquest last night week, at the Grosvenor Inn, Elles- mere Port, on the body of Joseph Forster, aged ten years, a waggon greaser, employed by the Ship Canal Company. George Smith,a foreman on the Ice-section of the canal, said he engaged deceased a week ago to grease the wheels of waggons. Deceased told witness he was 15 years old. On Wednesday witness told deceased to . fat some , waggons. In fatting the waggons the lad was obliged either to go under the waggons or to put his hand between the wheels, Witness had just left deceased under the wagon when he heard a scream, and turned round and saw him lying in the four-foot.—William Jeffery, horse driver, stated that on Wednesday he was in charge of a horse drawing waggons. He heard some one call out, " Unfasten the horse." He did so and when he turned round saw that deceased had been run over.—The verdict of the jury was that "deceased died from fracture of the skull, caused by a waggon passing over his head, and that the foreman, George Smith, was culpably negligent in employing a boy of the age of deceased to perform such dangerous work." PETITIONS AGAINST BILLS. Eight petitions have been lodged in the Private Bill office of the House of Lords, praying to be heard by counsel in opposition to the Manchester Ship Canal (Tidal Openings, ke.,) Bill when it comes for consideration before Lord Camperdown's Select Committee. .The peti- tions of Corporation of Liverpool and the Mersey Decks and Harbour Board are identically word for word the same so far as the allegations are concerned. After setting forth at length the protection given to them by Parliament under the Canal Act of 1885, they state that by the present Bill it is proposed in effect to fill up the tidal openings shown on the sections for the Act of 1885, and to construct in lieu thereof three new tidal openings which will practically diminish the width of the author- ized tidal openings by no less than 2.700 feet. In their petition the Local Board, traders and manufacturers of Widnes state that they are advised that the effect of the works proposed to be authorized will very seriously interfere with the river Mersey, and obstruct the entrance to the Widnes Docks and Sankey Canal. The other peti- tioners are the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany, Dean and Chapter of Chester, the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Company, and the Liverpool Maga- zines and the British and Irish Gunpowder Manufactur- ing Companies, Limited. THE NEW BILL IN COMMITTEE.

The Manchester Ship Canal (Tidal Openings) Bill was on Thursday before a Committee of the House of Lords, Lord Camperslown presiding. Mr. Pember, Q.C., Mr. Balfour Browne, Q.C., and Mr. Cripps. Q.C.' were coun- sel for the promoters. and Mr. Pope, Q.C., Mr. Bidder, Q.C., and Mr. Squarey were for the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board ; Mr. Pope, Q.C., was also for the Cor- poration of Liverpool, and Mr. Moon appeared for Use Shropshire Canal Company. The London and North- Western and other railway companies had peti ioned against the bill, but counsel on their behalf did not appear. Mr. Pember said the objects of the bill were somewhat manifold, and as there was not tune at his disposal bercire the hour for adjournment, he would only refer to the part dealing with tidal openings. The bill sought powers to MI up a number of tidal open- ings along the embankment of the canal and to con- struct a number of sluices in their , place. The canal was embanked at all points en the foreshore in order to preserve the necessary water level during low water, and these embankments caused what was called a loss to a certain extent in the tidal capacity of the estuary of the Mersey. The canal was excavated to a depth of 26ft.' and this depth was the ruling depth for the whole thirty-five miles. It still remained necessary to provide for the admission and TPrlli4aiOn of tidal water in the canal, and therefore the tidal openings which had been in the original scheme were left. These tidal openings did not appear on the deposited plans, Mr. Leader Williams treating them as merely subsidiary works to be altered according to his pleasure as he carried out the scheme, but unfortunately they were *hown in Mr. Leader William's sections. Hellee these tears. A part of Mr. Leader Williams's ultimate method was the construction of several very large sluices, two of which were at Randall's Creek, near Runcorn. They were about thirty feet wide. Ten were A the mouth of the Weaver. and were of the same width. It was obvious that they no longer depended upon the whole of these 45 tidal openings, and that they were no longer necessary. This bill, therefore, sought to make , certain alterations with regard to them. At this point the Committee adjourned until next day at II o'clock. It was stated that only four scientific witnesses would be called on each side.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

ACCIGENT AT THE TANNING COMPANY'S WORKS. On Tuesday morning an accident occurred at the Penketb Tanning Company's works to a young man named Ernest Godwin, of Warrington. It seems that he was working at the rolling machine when he accidentally got his right hand under the roller. severely crushiniz his fingers, so much that he had at once to he taken to the Warrington Infirmary, where it was found necessary to amputate the little finger. WEST.PYAN MUTUAL IMPROITEMBNT SOCIETY. At a general business meeting in connection with the above society, it was resolved to start a field club for the purpose of monthly natural history rambles during the summer session. All members are cordially invited to join in these expeditions, which may also be participated in by non-members and friends on the payment of the usual subscrip- tion the society. The first ramble will take place shortly.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR H. COSSHAM,
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR H. COSSHAM,
M.P.

Mr. Handel Cossham, member of Parliament or East Bristol, died at the National Liberal Club, London, on Wednesday. after having been seized with a fainting fit in the library of the louse of Commons. Mr. Cossham lived at the club during the Session. Dr. Bond. who accompanied him to the club after the seizure, assisted him to rearh the lift, by which he ascended to the first bedron v floor, where his room was situated. *Dr. Bond's assistant was present when the patient expired. Th e cause of death wae heart disease,, and consequently no inquest wilt. he necessary. The body has been removed to Bath. AP soon as death occurred, telegrams were sent to his wife, to the president of the Liberal Association of his di vi,iion at Bristol. and to the manaoer of the dN., '1,,r1',1 collieries. Mr. Cossham died within two hour f his first seizure. The event caused much excitmen ,t the House, and was almok the sole topic P of eon vers.?' ,n in the lobby. Mesthur Examiner,—A rekon vole be thinkin am lost, but aw ammut, ave only bin on'th shelf a bit. ACV don't rekon mi'sel a mashor, but aw mak no akount a bein beind in'th fashon, so wen aw seed ;Wry body guin in for th' fluenza aw thout i'me not guin be dun, al ave smak. An aw went in fur th fluenza, and by jove Mesthur, if yo kno anybody as is out o work just ax urn get th fluenza ; an tha'e only want a bit a rag in the'r poket, an thal sune ave a regler job. Wel. Mesthur, wen th poor folk begun a takin th fluenza in Warraton,th big uns went in fur th' watter on th' brane, so aw ses to misel I'm not guin to be dun, al av a smak to. So aw went in fur th' watter on th' brane; aw seed a bill on th' wall as sed that Mesthur Diggle., an th' Mayor an um wor guin talk bout th' latest fashion— watter on th' brane—in th' Co-Op's all, one Friday fleet. Aw ses al ave twopenoth,an aw went,but th' Mayor wernt the'er an Om ad to tak th' next mon, Mesthur Smith, th' belmon, an he wor a reel good un, a gradely " sub" fur th Mayor. If yode a seed im Mesthur Examiner percht in one korner that cheer' al th' rest a'th cheer wor fild , we konsequenee, yode a lafft ; th Mayor cud'dent a dun better. He tried to keep order, an th Mayor cud'dent a dun mour, cud he? .

11 We!, stir- Mesthur Diggle wor the'er an that wor 'enuf fur me, an he ad sum watter in botles on'th table. He sed he'd gotten sum fro Winik, sum fm Apperton, sum fro a brook at Sanky ; an one o'th a udince sed as that brook wor alose dry; and sum he getten fro sky. An I then he went on telin us about th watter, an tried to freeten us out o hying th' Watter Works, by shoin us a piece o a pipe as he sed wor chokt up we summot in th watter. Aw thowt to misel Mesthur Diggle that'al not do —it is'nt good enuf ; I've bin drinkin watter lurwer thun that ear pipe, and it asent chokt ml pipe up yet. 'An then aw thowt to misel, sum on us wanted wafter surnweer el's beside down th' pipes. If he's bin in th Publick All, when its bin pakt wi Torys or Radakles he's smelt sum'ot aside o.'d.'Col!one. Did you na're think, Mesthur Examiner, that if th J.P's. ad change th'r tune fur a bit an say " Five scrubs down an a shower," a'stead o "Five shilling an kosts," it ad do sum on urn mour good. If i'de mi way i'de ave akt o parliament, an kompel evry body to ave a scrub down an a shower evry wik, an ad ave a scrubin down Board, an mak Mesthur Diggle th' cheermon an then he'd he in is glory. After all, Mesthur Examiner, aw think the'ers summat in them ould sains. An one ses, " Kienliness is next to godliness," and how con us as is allus workin' in th' facktorys in the dust an' sweat, keep oursels cleon an' sweet about plenty o watter, an' sumwe'er to use it? Wot con lodgers do in little houses, beside washin the'r and's an' face ?

An' then the'ers sewers wantsa gond washin', an' many a thing. I say to mi mates, th' Korporation shud 'aye th' watter in the'er own 'ands, an' if tha'l tak as mich care in twin' th' Watter Works as tha dun in byin' the'r own beef, I say, mates, let us go in fur it. It at then be our own, an we shal not be so feard a usein' a drop.— Gradley yours, _
WORKIN' MON.
