div.head: WIN WICK AND ITS CHURCH.
div.p: WIN WICK AND ITS CHURCH.

This week we give a view of the ancient and interesting Church of Winwick. "Win wick," wrote Mr. Alfred Rimmer in the "Manchester Guardian" some months ago, "is one of the most delightful spots in this part of England. The road from War- rington is very pleasant, and it increases in interest as we pass by the grounds and shrubberies attached to Winwick Hall. These are celebrated for their rhododendrons, which are hardly surpassed anys where for splendour. They are of very old growth. It is said they most closely resemble those growing by the Black Sea whence they originally came. The living of Winwick, it is scarcely necessary to say, is one of the most valuable in England; Halsall in Lancashire and Doddington, in Cambridgeshire, being bracketed in the same priveleged category. According to the lastretunis,the living of Halsall, in Lancashire, ill put down at .£3,500 a year, Winwick at £3,200, and Doddington (which has a population of 1,358, Dissenters included), at the more modest sum of .£1,700. But the charm of Winwick lies in its picturesque situation, almost uninvaded by modern improvements. Round the church are some very noble yews. The spire is visible from more than one railway, and its solid tower shows it to be of ancient date. • The side windows of the church are uniform, and belong to the later Tudor period, when so many of the ecclesiastical buildings which now stand were erected. The patronage of Win- wick Church has been vested in the Stanley family since the days of Henry VI. Often in Lancashire there are little circumstances that bring some Bites of Shakespeare to memory. Sir John Stanley was the first of the patrons of Winwick, and at the same' time he was lord of the Isle of Man, which was granted to the family in 1405. In Act 2 of " Henry V 1.," second part, the Duchess of Gloucester is com- mitted to his charge. She i 4 habited in a white sheet and has a taper burning in her hand for penance : Duchess: Stanley, I prithee go, and take me hence, I care not whither, for I beg no favour, Only convey me where thou art commanded. Stank/4 Why Madam, that is to the Isl,e of Man, Thereto be used according to your state— Like to a Duchess and Duke Humphrey's lady. Many and learned have been the debates as to whether Oswald fell at Winwick, or Oswestry, or in Northumberland. Oswald was the champion of Christianity, and he was opposed by Fends, whose life was one long battle against the Cross. He was the enlightened King of Northumbria. On one occasion, when sitting down to a feast, he heard that at his gate there Were a number of poor who wanted sustenance, and he ordered the silver dishes to be taken untested and divided amongst Clem: "May this hand never grow old," said Bishop Aldan, when he 'Seized the King's hand and blessed it: and, according to the legends of the time, when Oswald was deteatedi and slain by Penda and the savage conqueror mutilated him, the "white hand" which Aidan had blessed remained without blemish. But much more recent events make Winwick interest- ing. During the Civil War the Duke of Hamilton entered England with 17,000 men, and Sir Marina- duke Langdale marched south from Northumber- land with a large force. Cromwell met them, and, falling on Sir Marmaduke's division, he quite routed it. and cut off all communication with the Scots. But the Duke's army was still intact, and they re- treated to Winwick, where a sanguinary battle was fought, the site of which is still pointed out. Crom- well, as usual, was victorious. At Winwick there is a free grammar school, founded by Gaulter a Legh in 1600,and here Richard Mather was a scholar. He went afterwards to Liverpool to take charge ef a public school, and subsequently took his degree at Brasenose College, and entered the Church. But the worldliness he saw in the ambitions and preferments of ecclesias- tics induced him to resign his living, and he was one of the early settlers in Massachusetts. His young- est son was Increase Mather, and his grandson was the celebrated Cotton Slather, whose descendants are amongst the foremost people in the New World. While in Liverpool, it is said, the great and self- taught astronomer Jeremiah Horrocks was his pupil. In Winwick Church is a monument to Mrs. Legh, of Lyme, who died soon after ,her marriage, and whose history is romance itself. She was the heiress of Shrigley Hall and the large estates that belonged to it. At the age of fifteen she was at a boarding school in Liverpool, and, of course, was looked upon as a prize. There was a Miss Frances Wake- field, who was the daughter of Dr. Davis, the head master of Macclesfield Grammar School, who had two nephews, Edward Gibbon Wakefield, and William Wakefield, and she hit upon a plan to abduct the heiress for her nephew Edward Gibbon. They went in a carriage to the school in Liverpool where Miss Turner was, and by false Pretences they induced her to go to Gretna Green, where the his- toric blacksmith married the young people, for, 18 he said, "two guinea's and champagne." They escaped with their prize to France, but the lady was rescued by her uncle in Calais. The Wake- fields were afterwards tried at Lancaster, and sen- tenced to three years' imprisonment. Mr. Legh, of Lyme, was the magistrate before whom they were first brought, and he afterwards married the young lady. She died at the age of nineteen, and a sculptured monument is erected to her in Winwick Church. There are many other monuments of in- terest in the church, which is in a district of ex- ceptional beauty ; and whether we approach it from Newton or Earlestown, or Warrington, the walk is • a delightful one." In the "Manchester Weekly Times" of last ; Saturday, there are views of Winwick Church, and , likenesses of the new Rector (the Rev. Canon Pen- • rhyn), and the curate (the Rev. J. Carson). In the text accompanying these illustrations we are told that there is a curious and interesting legend con- nected with the founding of Winwick Church. Ac- cording to this tradition, the selection of tile site ' was the'result of the strange interference of a pig. It is said that when the building of the church was contemplated, it was decided that the edifice should be erected at the bottom of the hill upon which the Present structure stands, and the work of building was begun. In the night, however, the stones were mysteriously removed, and morning after morning ' the workmen found their work undone and the ' materials carried away to the present site. The builders at length gave up contending against so , marked an interposition, and the church was erected where it now stands, and the miraculous pig was carved upon the west side of the spire to r commemorat. the wonderful event. This is the . legend, and it is not without some attraction. • Baines in his "History of Lancashire " supposes the effigy of the pig to be a rude attempt to represent the crest of the Gerard family, whose chapel is in the north aisle of the church, but Mr. J. E. Worsley, F.S.A., of Winwick, who has gone into the matter fully, and who doubtless knows more of his native village and its beautiful old I, church than any other living man, seems to think this idea very improbable. Winwick . is not the only church with its miraculous church- . buildingstory. Roby, in his" traditions of Lanca- shire," gives a wild legend (" The Demon Builders")

connected with the building of the parish church of St. Chad, at Rochdale, which is said to have been removed by evil spirits. Beamont says that a tradi- tion like that related of Winwick, in which super- natural hands assisted, is told also of Christ Church in Hampshire. The legend has it that the foundation was laid on the heights of St. Catherine but night after night the work was thrown down and the stones carried to a neighbouring eminence. Unwilling to disobey this implied command the new site was adopted, when daily a mysterious stranger was observed to come and labour at the work. He received no wages, and was never seen to eat. If a beam were too short, he lengthened it by drawing it out, as if the material were elastic. In due time Ow church was consecrated, and the monks named it Christ Church, in honour of their supposed helper in the work.

The carving of the pig is to the right of a niche near the west entrance. The fact of its being in such close proximity to the niche led Mr. Worsley to suppose that at one time the empty niche had been occupied by a figure of which the pig was in some way a part, and that this figure was that of St. Anthony, with whom the representation of a hog is invariably associated. He reasonably con- cludes that the Winwick pig was no other than the emblematic pig of St. Anthony and was placed near the niche containing an image of the saint, and fur- ther, as St. Anthony, was the patron of bells and bell towers, on account of the power he was sup- posed to DOBBBBB in common with consecrated bells of exorcising evil spirits, would in those days be thought appropriately placed upon a bell tower. In support of this theory, he refers to the figure and pig on the Bodmin Seal, a panel discovered by him in Gloucester Cathedral, and to various other authorities. The tower and the body of the church were built in the 14th century. The Hauock Chantry Chapel, founded in 1330, differs materially from the rest of the church. At the base of some of the pillars of the north aisle there is a sculptured head of a bishop. The mitre is of a form used in the 12th century,and this makes it possible that these pillars were form- ally portions of a much older structure. The Legh Chapel (Legh of Lyme) is of interest, especially on account of the unique brasses contained in it. One of them, that of Sir Peter Legh, who took holy orders after being left a widower in 1491, represents the knight with his priestly garments over his armour. The chancel impaired by time and injured in the Great Rebellion, was restored to its original form in 1847 by the Rev. James J. Hornby, rector. It contains an obituary window, the gift of the late Earl of Derby, when Baron Stanley, and is in memory of James, seventh Earl of Derby, who suffered in Commonwealth times for his devotion to the Royalist cause. A beautiful fragment of an ancient cross was dug up in 1830, and is now to be seen at the east end of the church. This cross head is one of the largest and most interesting specimens of its kind in the country. It is about sft. long, and is only exceed- ed in size by the fragment in the crypt at Lasting- ham, which is two inches longer. Its unusual size !tnd wonderful ornamentations are in themselves sufficient to give the Winwick fragment a high place of interest among sculptured stones. The ends of the fragment have .on them curious carvings. One end shows a man held downwards being sawn asunder apparently by two demons. After the great battle of 645 between Penda, King of Mercia, and Oswald, King of Northumbria—fought near Win- wick, the body of the vanquished King Oswald was dismembered, and the head and one arm were set up at Oswestry, and to this the rude carvings are supposed to refer. On the spot where Oswald fell there is now a spring which has ever since borne his name. From the holiness of his character, the well was once in high repute as possessing peculiar healing virtues. Portions of the soil, it is affirmed, were even taken to be administered to the sick. It is now in existence, but very greatly dilapidated. Winwick is the birthplace of Sir Phipps Hornby, third son of the Rev. Geoffrey Hornby, a former rector. He entered the Royal Navy, and fought against the combined F encb and Italian fleets, off the island of Lissa. A French ship struck to the Pelage (Hornby's vessel), and her flag was secured by her captain. It now hangs in Winwick Church.

div.head: LATE MR. J. G. MOMINNIES.
div.p: THE LATE MR. J. G. MOMINNIES.
SALE DF HOUSEHOLD FURNITURE, &c.
Acting upon the instructions of the executor of the late Mr. J. G. McMinnies, a two days' sale was conducted on Thursday and yesterday by Mr. T. Sutton, auctioneer, at the late residence of the

deceased, Summer House, Warrington. The first day's sale comprised-the furniture and utensils, glass, china, cutlery, oil paintings, water colours, and engravings, of the dining room, drawing room-, entrance hall and library. There was an exceed- ingly large attendance at the sale on Thursday, so large indeed that the house was crowded through- out and a considerable number of people,were un- able to get into the large dining room, in which the sale for the most part was conducted. Under these circumstances it was deemed desirable to sell part of the furniture in the garden outside, but the rain coming on necessitated a return to the in- terior of the house. It was generally remarkeC that everything was found in admirable condition and good prices were on the whole realised, the competition in some cases being very keen. Yesterday there was again ' a large attendance of buyers, and good prices were realised for most of the lots. The sale comprised the books, proof engravings, linen, &c., dressing and bedroom furniture, and bath-room and garden utensils. Although there were numerous books offered, the whole of the deceased gentleman's library was not disposed of, as same of the best volumes had been retained by Mr. McMinnies' nephew to whom the bulk of the property was left. There was some spirited bidding for a large open bookcase in brown oak which was finally knocked down for £9. A second open bookcase was sold for £4, and a third for 355. Among the books original editions of Thackeray's " Pendennis " and "The Newcomes," of two volumes each, were put up together, and, after a brisk competition, they were sold for £5. Three signed proof engravin:zs of Gustave Dore's great pictures realised from £4 10s. to .£5 each. The subjects of these engravings were, " Christ's entrance into Jerusalem," "Dream of Pilate's Wife," and "Christ leaving the Prastori um." The will of Mr. McMinnies, which was proved two or three weeks ago, appoints his nephew, Mr. W. P. McMinnies, sole executors and leaves him " all his real and personal estate not disposed of by his will." To his housekeeper, Miss Ellen Jones, he bequeaths. free of legacy duty, the sum of £5OO, "if she should be in his service at the time of his death," and to her niece, Miss Frances Jones, the sum of £250, which is also free of legacy duty. The personal estate was sworn at gross £12,934 Ile. 10d., but this does not, of course, Include any real estate.

An elderly man, on Thursday evening, walked on to the Admiralty Pier at Dover, took out a razor, cut his throat and jumped into the sea. He was taken out dead. He had previously stated that he was a publican from Windsor.

div.head: tetttrs to tbe Obitor.
div.p: tetttrs to tbe Obitor.
WANTED, A BRANCH POST OFFICE.

Sir,—The people of Warrington are long-suffering in- dividuals. For months upon months those in the centre of the town have had to ramble nearly half a mile tor a penny stamp or a half-penny post-card, and they have done so without serious complaint. Perhaps they have been quietened with the prospect that was held out to them of a branch Post Office being opened somewhere about Market-gate, but if so, they have been grievously deluded. Week has followed week, and they have stlll to make the compulsory pilgrimage, as no sign of k branch being opened has yet appeared. Ido hope, if we are to have a new branch, some action will be taken— and that, speedily—to relieve those who like myself have become April 24th, 1890.
DISGUSTED.
WESLEYANISIN. AT RUNCORN.

your correspondent "A Wesleyan niember " is one of those who, he says, are "wholly in the dark re- specting the business of his church, financial or other- wise," then I beg to say it is his own fault. No society could give fuller details of how every fund is raised and dispensed than the Wesleyan Methodist. Every treasurer or steward is a layman, and, like most other officials, elected annually by laymen. Without referring to Connexional affairs, but keeping to local matters, permit me to say that the chief authority financial and otherwise "in the Runcorn Circuit is the Quarterly Meeting, at which the three ministers and about sixty laymen are entitled to sit and vote. Every Wesleyan member is there represented by his class leader, so there is no taxation without representation. Like representatives to the Imperial Parliament, those who should attend sometimes fail to put in an appear- ance, and therefore cannot personally give those they represent an account of the business done. If" Wesley- an Members" Leader is one of these, the remedy is in his own and fellow members' hands.—Yours respectfully, EDWARD TAYLOR. 69 Greenway-rd., Runcorn, 19th April, 1890.

div.head: • MORE FACTS.
div.p: • MORE FACTS.

Sir,—l have no need to seek the aid of either priest or layman for any information on religious topics. For- tunately I possess a good pair of eyes, and can see, read, and study for myself. It your readers would only take the advice of your correspondent, "Thomas Williamson," and read the Bible for themselves, instead of following the " traditions of men," and the instructions of men-made Prayer Books, they would see there is no mention of the feminine biod whom the Catholics worship. Not a word is said of any such personage as the Mother of God. There are slight references to the mother of Christ, but we are not told to do honour to her in any shape or form. Nor are we to do honour or obeisance to any saints, calvaries, or crucifixes, for the fabrication and worship of images is absolutely and positively for- bidden.

My companion was neither impressed with the cere- monial nor with the error of her ways, but she was impressed with the idolatry which she saw, and to such an extent as to strengthen and confirm her Protestant convictions.

As to the greatness of England under Catholicism, it was only when our kings threw off its intolerable yoke that our country began to rise from that slough into which all nations which embrace it seem destined to descend. History proves that while Catholic countries are stationary or receding in all matters that tend to national progress and elevation, Protestant countries advance by leaps and bounds. The last attempt made by the last Catholic king of England, the saintly but perfidious and lustful James 11, to force Romanism upon the English people ended very disastrously for him and for his cause ; and I, for one, believe that when the nation realises the insidious attempts that are again being made to enslave it a similar reward will attend the efforts of those who are now doing their best to propa- gate what has been described as a "gigantic supersti- tion."—Yourel &a. A DISSENTER.

div.head: " TWEEDLEDUM AND TWEEDLEDEE,"
div.p: " TWEEDLEDUM AND TWEEDLEDEE,"

Sir,—The above heading is suggested to me by the recent correspondence of Mr. Foulkes and others. With- out wishiag for one moment to impugn the sincerity of their motives, I desire to point out the vapidity aid consequent uselessness and absurdity of such immaterial controversy. Mr. Foulkes is an old offender in this re- spect. His wearisome effusions and everlasting twaddle about sacerdotalism,must have long ago given offence to a majority of your readers. Take for instance his last diatribe as a specimen, which he unblushingly thrusts under the eye of every reader, wherein his egotism is positive as well as slangy—" My cause is gonna truth, and I intend to peg at it." Who made him Sn arbiter of truth? There is a vast deal too much unsoundness in Mr. Foulkes for him to teach anything but bigotry, in- tolerance, and uncharitableness, none of which are the handmaids of truth, but nevertheless they are to be found rampant in almost every Church in the land. What Mr. Foulkes needs most in his search after truth, in regard to rel.gion, is a careful study of historical facts connected with the foundatio'n and progress of the various systems of religion throughout the world, and of the histories of the many sacred books from which they derive their inspiration, our own Bible included. He will then see how variegated are theforms of religion, how capable they are and always have been of progressive human deVelopment. He will also find out—perhaps for the first time in his life—how far even Foulkism is from the truth, for not until all these varied forms are welded into one perfect Universil, shall we arrive at sound Truth. The superfluity of his past cor- respondence will be apparent even to himself ; churches and parsons will cease to trouble him, and everything else which now vexes his soul will melt into thin air, under his new state of rationality ; consummation devoutly hoped for. In conclusion,l commend to'Mr. Foulkes a quotation out of his favourite book :—" There may be diversities of operations, but it is the same spirit which worketh all in all."—Apologising for my intrudence, I remain yours truly, W. KNOWLES. Latchford, April 23rd.

div.head: 'RACK RENTED TRADESMEN, HOUSEHOLDERS' , AND LODGERS.' •
div.p: 'RACK RENTED TRADESMEN, HOUSEHOLDERS' , AND LODGERS.' •

Sir,—Kindly permit me to remi rid your readers that within the past few months two important Unions have been founded, allied in their objects, almost equal in their national interest, and each• relying solely upon peaceful combination to attain their ends.

Modern ' Landlordism ' is sapping the vitality of Retail Trade and the mental and physical energy of our labouring classes. The "Tenant Tradesmen's National Union" urges fair rent and fixity of tenure for shop- keepers so long as agre?d covenants are duly performed, also the right of a tenant to the full value of the good- will and permanent improvements. The " Working- men's Home Union " strives for fair rents, thorough sanitation, and -reasonable comfort in the dwellings of the toiling mdsses. Both Unions aim at arousing and supporting the legitimate action of local authorities and securing due proportionate representation. in Municipal Councils and in Parliament. Let it once be fully recog- nised that rack renting and heavily taxing the retail shopkeepers ,rnean dearer food, dearer clothing and dearer furniture for the people as well as less purchasing power to the limited incomes and hardly earned wages —that heavy rents, for small houses anctlocigings Mean less money 'al spend with the shopkeeper, less food, less clothing and less of other necessaries of life—and that insanitary dwellings mean less physical power in the labouring cla4ses, less ability to give a fair day's work for a fair day's pay as well as feeble development in the children—and the most reluctant mind will accept my contention that these two Unions are urgently needed, should work in the closest harmony and receive wide- spread adherence- and support. Producers, retailers and consumers are alike interested in these matters Individual shopkeepers, householders or lodgers are equally powerless in this struggle with rapacious land- .lordism,but when once a complete combination is formed
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

During its brief existence of two years, the Run- corn Musical Society has achieved considerable dis- tinction amongst similar institutions, for the char- acter and quality of its concerts, and it has gained a firmer hold of the music-loving public than any previous choral society in the town. The perform- ance of the Messiah in December was admitted to .be the finest exposition of Handel's noble music ever heard in the town and neighbourhood. Much of this excellency is to be attributed to the conduc- tor, Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, whose enthusiasm, not less than his musical ability, has inspired the choristers to aim at the nearest possible approach to perfection. It is to be hoped that the society will continue its career next winter with redoubled vigour, and a determination to surpass in the future what has been achieved in the past.

, Primrose Day was well observed by the Tories of Runcorn and Widnes districts, and there were few who did not wear a yellow favour in his buttonhole, Many Liberals, apparently determined that their political opponents should not have a monopoly of "Nervy spring-time's harbinger," also sported a few pretty primroses in their coats. The members of Frodsham Primrose League had quite a happy time on Monday evening, when they lield their annual meeting. The treasurer announced a handsome balance in hand, and the wardens an increase of 52 in the membership, but unfortunately the lady hon. sec. had no report to make which was an unpardonable omission, as the ladies apparently have quite as much, if not more, to do with the working of the League than the gentlemen. Not being initiated in the mysteries of the order, one cannot understand why there should be 20 dames and only 19 knights, leaving one dame all forlorn. Is there not one of the 566 "associates" worthy of the honour of knighthood at the hands of the Ruling Councillor? .

Mr. Robert Foulkes is most unfortunate in his attempts to set the mundane matters of this sub- lunary sphere on a properUsis. He attended the Frodsham Primrose meeting with the intention to unburden his mind 'of some grievance, but his oratory was as little appreciated as at the vestry meeting, and the audience, despite the chairmanis promise that Mr. Foulkeasboubt be heard, expressed their wish that a conjarifig entertainment should be proceeded with in preference to listening to the remarks of the Anti-Ritualist. Alas! it is the lot of reformers to be misunderstood, and unappreciated, and Mr. Foulkes fares no better than the rest. For about the tenth occasion, Mr. F. H. Gossage has been elected chairman of-Widnes Local Board, and as the reigning descendent of the " father of Widnes," it is fitting that he should have that honour. His re-election on Tuesday last will give ' Universal satisfaction to the townspeople. Into several of the pastimes which are denomin- ated "'manly," the ladies have within recent years made an invasion, and there is now a fully trained and equipped Ladies Cricket Club in existence; but it would be strange indeed were they to now make another step forward and embark in the rough and tumble game of Rugby football. In Runcorn the ladies are constant and enthusiastic followers of the winter pastime, and when the local club is making use of their skill and high position in the football world, to further a philanthropic object, it is not to be wondered at that a lady is willing to enter the arena and essay a kick at the oval. On Wednesday evening next; J. Valentine, the noted Swinton three-quarter, brings a Lancashire tcam to Runcorn to risk a fall with the wearers of the green, and the proceeds, Which, if the weal her be propitious, may confidently be put at £5O, are to be handed over to the District Nurse. The object is very appropriate, for no one should know better than the battered footballer the value of good nurs- ing, and it is quite as appropriate, if much more ncvel, that a lady should set the ball in motion in behalf of so Samaritan-like an object. Miss Bertha Speakman, daughter of Mr. Speakman, C.C., will, it is stated, perform this important duty.
RUNCORN MUSK:AL SOCIETY.

The third concert of the iteasori in connection with this society was given on the fifteenth inst., to a large and fashionable audience,- and proved to be one of the most enjoyable entertainments of the winter. The principals were—Miss Conway. Miss Emilie Lloyd, Mr. James Sauvage(late of Carl Rosa Opera Company), and Master Tons° LlwyfoSauvage, solo pianoforte. The first part of the programme consisted of sacred items from the compositions of Handel, Gounod, and lgendelssohn, and commenced with the chorus ." Sing unto God" (Judas Maccabseus). The choir, which consisted of 120 voices, also rendered " As the hart pants" and "Judge me, 0 God," and through- out showed that the pitch of efficiency previously attained had been maintained under the able and enthu- siastic conductorship of Mr. E. Wynne Humptireya. Miss Conway, who posse.ises a soprano voice of rare purity and flexibility, rendered " There is a green hill" With pathos and power, and she was recalled. A similar com- pliment Was also paid Mr. Sauyage for his interprstation. of" Glory to Thec," the powerful ton, a of his bass voice being heerd cousidnable advantag,e. Miss Lloyd is no stranger to Runc,orm and her re-appearanee was hailed with delight by the numerous audience, and 'ler charm- ing rendering of "The Valley'of Shadows" (Barri) well merited the enthusiastic encore with which she was re- warded. The grand scena from Mendelssohn's ••Elijah" was an enjoyable item. Miss Pierpoint (an angel) sang the • recitative in good style, and • Miss. Con- way (widow), and . Mr. Sauvage (Elijah) gave the duet in a manlier Via& called forth much applause. The second parf4. of the programme consisted of choruses and ballads, and opened with the

"Gipsy Chorus," from Balfe's " Bohemian Girl," which was given by the choir with precision and verve, and was loudly applauded. The bright, tuneful glee "The Bells of St. Michael's Tower," highly delighted the audi- ence, and a repetition was demanded and responded to. Miss Lloyd made a deep impression by her vocalisation of the ever verdant song," She wore a wreath of roses," and in response to a vociferous encore she gave a spirited and dramatic rendering of" Punchinello but perhaps her greatest success was achieved in the beauti- ful song "The garden of sleep," which was given with exquisite expression; and she was recalled and gave "Meet me in the moonlight." Miss Conway contribu- ted Bishops' favourite song " Bid me discourse" and "On the banks of Allan Water," and she was equally happy in her interpretation of the different styles of music, and was loudly encored for both songs, and she replied by singing "Coming thro' the Rye ' ,ind " Come lamas and lads" two old ballads, which greatly pleased the audience. Mr. Sauvage sang the tarantula " Gia la luna," an Italian song in a manner that called forth an unanimous recall, and he then gave "The Friar of Orders Grey." Efe brought out the humour of the song in unique and characteristic style and was treated to an ovation in consequence. The qualities of his voice, and his skilful use of them were heard to great advantage in the song " Laughing" and the encore song "Sion, the Cellarer " both of which wrought up the audience to a high pitch of enthusiasm. In these songs Mr. Sauvage was accompanied by his sox, Master Tons° Sauvage, who also performed the pianoforte solo " Rondo Brilliante " with the skill of a veteran, and the delicate touch of a genius, and he was encored. The last item on the programme the part song "The Cambrian Plume" was rendered by the choir in capital style and the concert concluded.with the singing of the National Anthem. In addition to his duties as conductor, Mr. Humphreys accompanied the principals, and Mr. W. B. Kay, the accompanist to the Society, played the accompaniments of the choruses. Owing to a mis- carriage of the news parcel containing this account of this concert we were unable to insert in last Saturnay's edition of this journal, but in order that the success of the society may be recorded we gladly find space in the present issue.

div.head: FRODSB.AM.
div.p: FRODSB.AM.

PRODSRAM PRIMROSE Lsantrz.—The annual meeting was held in Frodsham Town Hall, on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. James Reynolds, LP, Rul- ing Councillor. The room was decorated with prim- roses, flags, and mottos. There was a capital attendance, which included many ladies. Mr. A. Thomas, the treasurer, submitted a financial statement which showed that there was a balance in hand of £2O 17s. The accounts were passed. Colonel Ashton, the warden, pre- sented the annual report, which stated that the number of members at the present time was 605—(applause)—of whom 19 were knights, 20 dames, and 566 associates. Of these there are 26 members in Alvanley, 41 in Helsby, and the remainder in Frodsham and Frod-ham Lordship; showing an increase during the year of 52. (Applause.) The Chairman proposed :—" That the members of the Frodsham District Habitation (No. 1662) of the Primrose League desire to express their unabated confidence in her Majesty's Government, and to recognise the firm, un- deviating, and judicious foreign policy of Lord Salisbury, which is So strongly calculated to uphold the interests of the country and preserve 'peace with honour.'" (Ap- plause.) 'the Chairman, after remarking that they were all happier and more comfortable in consequence of hav- ing the present "stable government" in office, dealt with the Irish question, contending that the Irish people were the most favoured people under the sun as far as agricultural matters were concerned, and yet they were always quarrelling with their bread and cheese. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Robert Rogers seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. G. W. B. Rodway and carried. A vote of thanks to the retiring officers having been accorded, the following officers were appointed for the ensuing year :—Ruling Councillor, Mr. James Reynolds, J.P ; treasurer, Mr. Alfred Thomas, J.P. ; hon. sec., Mrs. John Ashton; warden, Col. Ashton. The Chairman then called upon Mr. Foulkes to address the meeting in accordance with a promise made at an earlier stage of the proceedings. Mr. Foulkes commenced his oration, but the meeting declined to listen to his observations, and a conjuring entertainment was proceeded with.

div.head: MARKET.,
div.p: MARKET.,

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. There is not a great deal doing in this market, but everything is apparently firm, and those who lately have sold freely are wanting advances. The estimate of sales has been raised to 12,000 bales, and "spot in American and 13razilian qualities is raised 6d. There is little doing to-day either in twist or weft, and bundles move slowly at quotations. Cloth is rather slow, but some lines have been done in Eastern goods, though on the whole sellers' efforts are but poorly rewarded. LONDON PRODUCE, FRIDAY. Sugar quiet all round, fine yellow and mediums easier; dry goods unaltered ; foreign slow ; beef quiet ; April buyers 12s 2tri and dealers 124 3d. Coffee on the spot very steady ; Rio futures firmer—Septem- ber sold 76s 3d, December 745, May buyers 75s 6d and sellers 76. 34. Tea quiet. Rice steady. Jute quiet. Linseed oil 23s 301 to 23s 71d. Turpentine, 29s 9d to 30s. Petroleum unaltered. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY. The beef market is inactive, and prices show no change. Pork rules dull at unaltered values. Prices keep fairly steady for bleon, eon- sidering the reluctance dealers display to purchase beyond their immediate requirements Hams continue in strong .de- maw, at extreme prices, while shoulders sell freely at un- changed currencies. Cheese firm, with a moderate inquiry. Butter closes uli, though prices are nominally unaltered. Lard shows little change, but is, if anything, in buyers' favour.

MIL STANLEY AT BRUSSELS. Mr. Stanley arrived in Brussels on Saturday, and was received with enthusiasm by the people. King Leopold gave a banquet in his honour, and presented to him the Grand Cordon of the new Order, the Congo Star. HEALTH OF THE QUEEN. We understand that the rheumatic affection in the left knee from which the Queen suffered before she went abroad has been considerably relieved. Her Majesty had much benefited in health ty her sojourn at Aix-les-Bains, although the weather was not favourable. She will arrive, accompanied by the Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg, at Port Victoria on Wednesday next, and will come to Waterloo Station on her way to Windsor Castle. THE NATIONAL LEAGUE. Mr. J. J. Clancy, M.P. presided at the fortnightly meeting of the Na,ional League held in Dublin on Tues- day, and after paying e tribute to the worth of his late colleague, Mr. Matthew Harris, went on to dissect the recent speech of Mr. Balfour, several assertions in-which he flatly contradicted. It was announced that since the meeting a fortnight previously the receipts had amounted to £267, and that grants to £212 altogether had been made to evicted tenants. THREE CHILDREN SUFFOCATED. On Saturday night a fatal fire occurred at the house of Mr. Pagus, miller of Cowgate, Kirkintilloch, Dumbarton- shire. The house has three storeys, and the fire had thoroughly spread through the dwelling before it was ascertained that the three children of James Baxter, hair- dresser, were sleeping there. The smoke prevented entrance by the door' but by means of a ladder the children were brought out at one of the windows. They were removed to houses near, but they all died. MR. MORLEY AT ROCHDALE. Mr. John Morley, addressing a meetino. at Bochdale,on Wednesday night, commended the creeds of Mr. Cobden and Mr. Bright in regard to Free Trade as one of enlight- ened national interest, and a creed which depended upon the coincidence of national interest with the interest of civilised nations at large. He combated the arguments of Sir M. H. Beach and Mr. Chamberlain as to the policy now being pursued by the Government and the Liberal Unionists, and urged a number of objections to the Irish Land Bill.

THE SPEAKER'S CONDITION. The condition of the Speaker of the House of Commons had further improved on Friday morning, when Mr. Peel was able to move from the bedroom into his sitting- room. THE RAILWAY STRIKE. All traffic between Cork and Dublin on the Great- Southern and Western Railway has ceased. The direc- tors are determined not to yield to the men without a prolonged struggle. THE FASTING MAN.' Succi was in remarkably good condition when exam- ined by his medical man at noon yesterday, and there is now no reasonable doubt that he will accomplish his forty days' fast this (Saturday) afternoon. THE SCULLING CHAMPIONSHIP. The sculling match for the championship of the world and £2OO a side, which was rowed yesterday over the championship course on the Parramatta river, between Peter Keep and Neil Matterson, resulted iv a victory for the former. Both oompetitors are ,V.ve South %%lien men. • THE FRENCH IN DAHOMEY. Pants, FRIDAY.—A Cabinet Council will be held to- morrow to consider the state of affairs in Dahomey. It is believed the Ministers will decide to send an expedi- tion from France. YESTERDA.Y'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House inet at four o'clo,ik. CUSTODY OF CHILDREN.—EarI MEATH moved the second reading of the Bill regulating the custody of children. He denied that there was any intention to proselytise children. The Lord Chancellor objected to the prin- ciple of the Bill. Etrl KIHBERLEY pointed out that the law would require many alterations, if the adoption of children was legalised. After discussion, the Bill was withdrawn. The South Indian Railway Bill was read a second thee, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Clerk of the House having reported the continued indisposition of the Speaker, Mr.. Courtney took the chair at 2.15. PUBLICANS AND COMPENSATION.—The Chancellor of the Exchequer, in reply to Sir Wilfred Lawson said pos- sibly his bill would be ready next week or in three oj four days. POST OFFICE SERVANTS.—Mr. RAIIKES, replVing, to Mr. A. J. Williams, s,iid there was a precedent in the Post Office for the restrictions respecting the right of public meeting laid Clown in the recent circular issued to the Post Office civil servants. TEA AND CIIRRANTS.—Mr. Cx.aneinci replying to Mr. Goschen said he was afraid he could only repeat the answer he gave yesterday, and again point out that in his view co-operative societies would benefit rather than be prejudiced by the immediate application of the re- missions (hear, hear). POLICE VOTES, &C.—Sir Jo aar GORST moved the second reading of the electoral Disabilities (Naval Military and Police) Bill. The Government promised to extend the Bill to include voluntary as Well as involuntary absence in pursuit of occupation. After prolonged discussion the bill was read a second time, and the House considered the resolution of the committee respecting the provision of funds for the drainage of Suck river, Ireland. Mr. Storey and Mr. Waddy objected to British money being applied for these private purposes. The House accepted the resolution by 245 to 95. SUPPLY.—The House then went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service estimate the first vote relat- ing to the slave trade. Various reductions were moved, and discussed, and at a quarter to seven progress was reported. LLSFT SITTING.]
